## laptop-toplevel

**2026-10-08 · laptop-toplevel: wlr-foreign-toplevel-management is the window source without an adapter.** This closes the 2026-10-07 wave4-wm follow-up ("wlr-foreign-toplevel-management is a follow-up"). The `strand-toplevel` thread binds `zwlr_foreign_toplevel_manager_v1` (up to v3) and every `wl_seat` next to `ext-foreign-toplevel-list-v1` and `ext-workspace-v1`, and `wm::merge` picks the window source in this order: the IPC adapter; then, with no adapter (or one that failed to connect), the wlr protocol whenever it is bound; then `ext-foreign-toplevel-list-v1` read-only. Picking a whole source, not mixing the two protocols per window, keeps one id space per state (the `Reset` rule for a late adapter already covers a source change). design.md's "Compositor-agnostic first" names the protocols it uses and says the standard ones come first; the wlr protocol is a de facto standard on wlroots compositors, so adding it is in that spirit and removes the hello bar's one gap on labwc rather than adding a concept. design.md now says so in that bullet. The adapter keeps priority because only it relates windows to workspaces. With an adapter, nothing from the wlr protocol is used (its states would only duplicate what the adapter reports).

**2026-10-08 · laptop-toplevel: wlr window ids and the list join.** The wlr protocol gives a toplevel no identifier, so a window's id is `wlr-<key>`, where the key is this client's own counter per handle (stable while the handle lives, never reused in a connection). `Window::toplevel` (the `ext-foreign-toplevel-list-v1` identifier M4's thumbnails will capture by) is joined by app id and title: the n-th oldest wlr toplevel with a given app id and title pairs with the n-th oldest list toplevel with the same pair, and only when both protocols show the same number of them. Otherwise it is `None` until they agree, which avoids a wrong pairing while one protocol's `done` has not arrived. The id is not the joined identifier, since a late join would change a window's key and turn a title update into a remove and an insert.

**2026-10-08 · laptop-toplevel: focus, the keyboard's screen and actions.** `focused` is wlr `activated`; `minimized` and `fullscreen` map one to one, and `maximized` is read but has no schema field. When exactly one window is activated and it is on exactly one output, that output is the focused screen, and the one active workspace on it is `workspaces.focused`. This refines wave4-wm's "focus with the protocols alone", where several outputs meant no focused workspace. With no activated window, or one spanning outputs, the old rule stands. `win.focus()` is `activate` on the first seat still offered. Every seat is bound, so when that seat's global is removed (multi-seat, a seat hot-removed) `activate` names the next one rather than answering `Unsupported`; it answers `Unsupported` only when no seat is left (`tests/protocol.rs::win_focus_falls_back_to_another_seat_when_one_is_removed`). `win.close()` is `close`, and `win.minimize()` is `set_minimized`. `Ok` means the request was sent; the change arrives as state, and a compositor may ignore it (sway has no minimize). An id the protocol does not show is `UnknownWindow`, and with no wlr protocol the answer is still `Unsupported` (`NotConnected` while an adapter is expected).

**2026-10-08 · laptop-toplevel: no maximize or fullscreen actions in the language.** The task asked for the protocol's maximize and fullscreen toggles as well. The schema's `Window` declares `focus()`, `close()` and `minimize()`, and the builtin stubs and design.md declare the same. Adding `maximize()`/`fullscreen()` would add syntax that design.md does not name, which CLAUDE.md rules out without a design change. It would also need every adapter to implement or refuse them. So the protocol thread's `WindowOp` covers only the three schema actions. The protocol state carries `maximized` and `fullscreen`, so adding the actions later is a schema change (strand-services-schema, the compiler's builtin stubs, design.md) plus one `WindowOp` arm each. Left to the design owner.

**2026-10-08 · laptop-toplevel: labwc in the compositor matrix.** Arch packages labwc (0.20.2 at this writing), and the matrix's container is Arch, so labwc joins the pacman lists and runs headless (pixman, `WLR_HEADLESS_OUTPUTS=1`, two desktops named `1` and `2`). With no IPC there is no compositor CLI to use as truth. The two IPC-truth tests skip labwc, and `the_stores_follow_a_compositor_without_ipc` uses each test window's own `xdg_toplevel` configures (activated or not; `TestWindow::activated`) and close requests, plus the workspace state labwc sends. The design bar's pixel test does not run there, because its expected dots come from compositor truth that labwc cannot give. The forced fallback on real sway (`tests/sway.rs`, `tests/wm_services.rs`, adapter off) covers the same paths in the check job, since sway 1.9 offers the wlr protocol. Ubuntu 24.04's labwc was not tried: the check job's image does not need it.

## laptop-services

**2026-10-08 · laptop-services (audio): `DeviceRef::Id` carries `object.serial`; item writes carry the record they were made on.** The wave4-wm (audio) entry left a follow-up: a `DeviceRef::Id` from a stale item could reach the device that took its id, and refusing it needed the store's item to carry the serial too. The private PipeWire hands a freed id to the very next node (the test sees it on the first try), so the case is real. `DeviceRef::Id` is now `Id { id, serial: Option<u64> }` (`DeviceRef::id(id)` for "whatever holds the id", `DeviceRef::device(id, serial)`); the audio thread refuses a reference whose serial differs from the node's (`UnknownDevice`), and a node without a readable serial matches any, as `AudioState::serials` already compared them. The change stream gains `AudioChange::Serials` (the whole id → serial map, in the first batch and when it changes) so handle users build references with `Mirror::device_ref`. The schema record stays exactly the schema's (no serial field: that would add a concept the language does not need), so the store tells a stale item apart by what the logic thread already holds: `Write` gains `held`, the record the writer held for an item write (the client used to send only the list's current item under the key, which after a reuse is the new device). The store refuses a write or `make_default()` whose held record names another `node.name` than the device under its id now, answering the write with the device as it is; otherwise it sends the serial it shows. A device replugged under its freed id with the same node name is taken as the same device. Proof: `tests/audio.rs::a_reference_never_reaches_a_device_that_reused_its_id` (a real reuse on the private PipeWire, every action refused, the new device untouched), `tests/audio_service.rs::the_audio_store_follows_and_writes_pipewire` (a stale item's write and `make_default()` change nothing), `src/audio/model.rs::tests::a_reused_id_is_a_new_device`, `src/audio/thread.rs::tests::a_reference_with_a_serial_names_only_that_device`.

**2026-10-08 · laptop-services (audio): without an inotify instance the audio thread retries on its timer and makes the watch again.** The wave4-wm (audio) reconnection entry already let a thread without a socket watch retry every 10 s; the watch was made once, at start, so a thread that met the per-user inotify instance limit (128 by default, which parallel test runs and busy desktops reach) stayed on the 10 s timer for its whole life even after instances were freed. The watch is now made again each time the thread starts waiting for the socket (every failed attempt, every loss), its io source added to the loop then; the first failure is a warning saying the thread retries every 10 s, a later success an info line. The bounded 10 s timer stays the fallback rather than another signal: the only other kernel notice of a created name is fanotify, unprivileged only since Linux 5.13 and under a per-user limit of its own, and a stat poll would be the same timer. `audio::deny_inotify(remote, deny)` (doc-hidden) lets a test deny the instance to one thread by its socket, as `EMFILE`. Proof: `tests/audio.rs::without_inotify_it_reconnects_on_its_timer` (denied throughout: reached within 10 s of the daemon's return after the doubling) and `a_watch_that_inotify_refused_comes_back` (allowed again after 1 s: past the doubling the daemon is reached in under 6 s, which only the watch can do; with the watch made only at start it took 9.2 s and the test failed).

**2026-10-08 · laptop-services (core): held item writes, latest write wins per item.** The handoff's known limit ("a stale held write from one handler can land after a newer one from another handler in the same throttle window") reproduced three ways in `KeyedSignal::write_item_tagged`, the item-write path of every service list (`s.volume = v` for `s` in `audio.sinks`). A throttled handler's `HeldItems` had no rebase, so (1) another handler's write of the same item that went through without changing it (the value already there) did not touch the held write, which landed later and won; (2) any change of the list (another item's report, another item's write) dropped every held write of the handler, losing writes of items nobody else touched; (3) of two handlers holding writes of one item, the first to land dropped the other even when the other was made later. A field write already settles this as "latest value wins" (2026-10-05 rate guard), so items follow it per item rather than adding a rule: each item write gets a per-list order number when made; when one lands (through the gate or from a hold, changed or not) it drops other handlers' held writes of that item made before it; any other change of a held item (a list operation, an applied report) drops the held write of that item; held writes of other items are kept. The fix is in strand-core (`keyed/reactive.rs`, and `Runtime::edit_deferred` in `rate.rs`), outside this stream's crate, because the race is in the core's hold queue: strand-services only sees the writes once they are sent, each with a tag taken when it lands, so it cannot tell an older write from a newer one. No interface changed. Proof: `crates/strand-core/tests/feedback.rs::a_newer_item_write_supersedes_a_held_one_of_that_item`, `held_item_writes_survive_changes_to_other_items`, `of_two_held_item_writes_the_later_one_wins` (all three failed before the fix) and `a_change_of_a_held_item_supersedes_its_write`.

**2026-10-08 · laptop-services (introspect): one kept D-Bus connection per bus.** `strand_introspect::properties` built a tokio runtime and a zbus connection for every question, so each 10 s (`TTL`) refresh of a `from dbus` check was a `Hello` and a new unique name on the bus (the reloads gate allowed for that short-lived connection). It now keeps one connection per `Bus` for the process in a current-thread runtime held in a static: no thread of its own (it runs only inside a caller's `block_on`, callers taking turns), so the idle connection costs no wakeup and adds no thread to `strand run`. Connecting is single-flight under an async mutex, so callers asking at once share one. A call that fails other than with an answer (an I/O error: the bus restarted) drops the connection and asks once more on a new one; one that gets no answer within the 2 s bound drops it too, so a hung bus is never kept; an answer that is an error (no such name or object) keeps it. The one-connection-per-bus cost is held for the life of the process, as the services' own connections are. `crates/strand/tests/reloads.rs` still allows a connection that only introspects during the reloads; that allowance is now looser than needed, and tightening it is left to that file's owner. Proof: `crates/strand-introspect/tests/connection.rs::refreshes_reuse_one_connection_and_a_restarted_bus_gets_a_new_one` (a monitor of the private bus's `Hello` calls counts one connection for five questions, one for four callers at once, one after an error answer, and one new connection after the bus restarted; the old code made five for five).

**2026-10-08 · laptop-services (core): a kept held item write is re-based onto what kept it.** Review of the entry above found its third case only half fixed: when another handler's older write of an item landed, the newer held write of that item was kept but still carried the item as it was before that landing, so the next change of anything in the list (a report of another item) re-based the hold, saw the item differ from that stale value and dropped the newer write; the older write won. The same happened when the service answered the landed write with a corrected value (a clamped volume). Both now follow the rule the entry states, "latest write wins per item": when an item write lands, the later held writes of that item it keeps take the landed value as their base; and when `receive_items` applies a report whose verdict is `Settle` for an item (the service's answer to our last landed write of it, tagged, possibly a different value), the held writes of that item are re-based onto the answer instead of dropped, because every one of them was made after the write answered (older ones were dropped when it landed). A report that answers no write of ours (an untagged value no pending write sent, an unknown newer tag) is an outside change and still drops them, as a field's held write is dropped by any change. Proof: `crates/strand-core/tests/feedback.rs::a_later_held_item_write_survives_a_change_after_an_earlier_one_landed` and `a_service_correcting_an_earlier_write_keeps_the_later_held_one` (both failed before), with `an_outside_report_after_an_earlier_write_landed_drops_the_later_held_one` as the control.

**2026-10-08 · laptop-services (introspect): dropping a hung connection never waits for another caller.** The entry above made connecting single-flight by holding the async mutex over the connection map while connecting, so a caller whose question timed out and went to drop its connection waited for that mutex with no deadline; with another caller connecting to an unresponsive bus at that moment, `properties` took up to twice its 2 s bound. The map is now a plain `std::sync::Mutex` never held across an `await`, and a separate async mutex (waited for within the caller's deadline) only makes connecting single-flight; dropping a connection takes the map alone. Proof: `crates/strand-introspect/tests/connection.rs::a_question_that_times_out_does_not_wait_for_another_callers_connect` (a question to a peer that never answers, while another caller connects to a socket that never speaks: 3.0 s before, under 2.4 s after).

## laptop-trim

**2026-10-08 · laptop-trim: a surface's size goes to logic only when a binding reads it.** `tests/services.rs::the_real_services_sleep_when_nothing_changes` failed on the 16-CPU laptop (logic 9 to 11 wakes in 5 s of 1 s cpu samples, limit 7) and passed on 4-CPU machines. The suspect was the delayed allocator trim (`run.rs`, `Trimmer`), but logging each wake of the logic loop showed otherwise: no trim was armed during the samples. The extra wake came about 6 ms after a sample and carried one message, `ToLogic::Size` for the popup, whose width follows its text: `pct(cpu.usage)` going from `5%` to `13%` resizes it from 21 to 29 px, and the main thread sent every configured surface size to logic. The machine dependence lies in the value, not in the threads. `/proc/stat` covers every core, so the test's background load reads as about 5 to 15% on 16 cores, crossing the one-to-two-digit boundary on most samples, and as more than 10% on 4. Pinning the container to 4 CPUs with `taskset` failed the same way, since `/proc/stat` still shows 16 cores. The limit is right: design.md wants a shell to wake only when something it shows or reads changed, and the compiler already marks the nodes whose size logic reads (`Prop::Watch`, "nodes nobody measures carry nothing, so their size changes never wake logic"); the renderer's layout facts obey it, the surface configure path did not. `Forward::configured` (demo/host.rs) now sends `Size` only for a surface node carrying `Prop::Watch`. A surface watched later loses nothing, because the renderer reports a newly watched node's laid-out size at once (the root's rect is the surface's size). No interface changed. Proof: `demo::host::tests::an_unread_surface_size_does_not_wake_logic` (the widths of `5%` and `13%` configured on an unwatched popup send nothing; once watched, the size goes), independent of the machine, and the services test passing repeatedly in debug and release.

**2026-10-08 · laptop-open (winstate): `win.maximize()` and `win.fullscreen()` are window actions, and they toggle.** Owner decision: `Window` gains `action maximize()` and `action fullscreen()` next to `focus()`, `close()` and `minimize()`, and a `maximized: bool` field next to `minimized` and `fullscreen`. This supersedes laptop-toplevel's "no maximize or fullscreen actions in the language", which left the choice to the design owner. The schema text, the compiler's builtin stub, the `windows` store (`WindowAction::{Maximize, Fullscreen}`), `WmAction::{MaximizeWindow, FullscreenWindow}` and design.md's compositor bullet all declare them. grammar.md lists no methods, so it is unchanged. `minimize()` sets: sway's `move scratchpad` and wlr's `set_minimized` never restore, Hyprland and niri answer `Unsupported`, and the way back is `win.focus()`. Maximize and fullscreen have no such way back, so a set-only pair would also need `unmaximize()` and `unfullscreen()`: two more names to learn. A toggle needs none. One taskbar or title-bar button then both enters and leaves the state, and `win.maximized` / `win.fullscreen` say which way it will go. Every compositor's own command is already a toggle (Hyprland's `fullscreen`, niri's `FullscreenWindow` and `MaximizeWindowToEdges`, sway's `fullscreen toggle`). Only the wlr protocol has set and unset requests, so the protocol thread picks one from the state the compositor last sent, which is the state the services show. What the toggle gives up is idempotence: two calls restore the window. `minimize()` is unchanged. The field `fullscreen` and the action `fullscreen()` share a name. The checker already tells them apart by the call (`w.fullscreen` is the field, `w.fullscreen()` the method), so the schema parser now joins the docs of a field and a method that share a `DocKey::Member` (field first) instead of keeping only the first. Hover on either shows both. Any other repeated key still keeps its first doc (`crates/strand-compiler/src/schema/mod.rs::tests::a_field_and_an_action_of_one_name_share_their_docs`). Tests: `crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs::tests::window_state_actions_check_next_to_their_fields` (served and builtin schema) and `crates/strand/tests/wm_audio_shells.rs::window_buttons_maximize_and_fullscreen_on_sway` (clicks in `strand run`).

**2026-10-08 · laptop-open (winstate): how each compositor runs them.** Hyprland 0.56.2 (`src/config/lua/bindings/LuaBindingsDispatchers.cpp`, `src/config/legacy/DispatcherTranslator.cpp` at v0.56.2): in the Lua dialect, `hl.dsp.window.fullscreen({ mode = "maximized" | "fullscreen", window = "address:0x…" })`, whose default action is Hyprland's toggle. The classic `fullscreen 1|0` dispatcher acts only on the focused window, so the classic form is `[[BATCH]]dispatch focuswindow address:0x…;dispatch fullscreen N`. That focuses the window first, which a taskbar click would do anyway. A batch is answered with each command's reply joined by `"\n\n\n"` (`dispatchBatch`), and it counts as done only when every part is `ok`. On a Lua config the batch is refused command by command with the Lua parser's error, which switches the connection to Lua as before. `j/clients`' `fullscreen` is the internal mode: 0 none, 1 maximized, 2 fullscreen (3, both bits, from 0.42 to 0.5x). The adapter used to count any non-zero mode as fullscreen, so a maximized window read `fullscreen`. Now mode 1 is `maximized`, and `fullscreen` is bit 2. niri 26.04 (`niri-ipc/src/lib.rs` at v26.04): `MaximizeWindowToEdges { id }` and `FullscreenWindow { id }`, both toggles that take the window's id. `MaximizeColumn` acts on the focused column and takes no id, so it is not a window's maximize and is not used. Maximize-to-edges is the one that sets the window's xdg `maximized` state. sway: `[con_id=N] fullscreen toggle`; sway has no maximize, so `win.maximize()` answers `Unsupported` ("sway has no maximize …"). Through the wlr fallback sway ignores `set_maximized` and the reply is `Ok`, because the wlr protocol cannot tell. wlr fallback: `set_maximized`/`unset_maximized`, and `set_fullscreen(None)`/`unset_fullscreen`. The fullscreen requests need handle version 2, and an older one answers `Unsupported`. `ext-foreign-toplevel-list-v1` alone is read-only, so both answer `Unsupported` there, like the other window actions. Tests: the adapters' unit tests (`src/wm/{hyprland,niri,sway,mod}.rs`); the fakes (`tests/hyprland.rs`, including `::a_refused_batch_switches_to_lua_too`, `tests/niri.rs`, `tests/protocol.rs`); real headless sway (`tests/sway.rs`: fullscreen on and off in sway's tree and the window's configure, maximize `Unsupported`; the forced wlr fallback toggles fullscreen too).

**2026-10-08 · laptop-open (winstate): niri's window state comes from the wlr protocol.** niri 26.04's IPC `Window` has no fullscreen or maximized field, so `windows.all[i].fullscreen` was always false on niri, a gap that predates this task. niri offers `zwlr_foreign_toplevel_management_v1` to unsandboxed clients, and its states are the window's xdg states. So an adapter that reports no window state (`IpcSnapshot::window_states`, false only for niri) takes `maximized` and `fullscreen` from the wlr toplevels (`wm::merge_with`). Neither side knows the other's ids. A window pairs with the wlr toplevel of the same app id when each side shows exactly one with that app id. Twins pair by app id and title in order: niri's windows by id, which is the order they opened, and the wlr toplevels in the order they were announced. Twins whose counts disagree get neither state, rather than a guess. The app id alone covers the common case, so a title change that reaches one protocol before the other does not make a lone window's state flicker. Hyprland and sway report both states over IPC and keep their own. Test: `src/wm/mod.rs::tests::an_adapter_without_window_states_takes_them_from_wlr`.

## laptop-resilience

**2026-10-09 · laptop-resilience: the compositor matrix runs nightly too.** The `compositors` job ran on push and `workflow_dispatch` only, so a new Hyprland, niri, sway or labwc release in archlinux:latest that breaks an adapter stayed hidden until the next push. It now runs on the nightly schedule as well (its `if` is gone; the `nightly` job is unchanged and still runs only the fuzzers and the latency run). On push nothing changes: the same steps, and the same job name `compositors`. On the schedule the job is named `compositors (nightly: archlinux:latest Hyprland, niri, sway, labwc)`, and `scripts/compositor-matrix-ci.sh` now names each failure with the compositor and its package version (`::error title=compositors: hyprland 0.57.0-1::…`) and writes `target/matrix/summary.md` (compositor, package version, result), which a new `if: always()` step appends to the job summary, so a nightly failure says which compositor and which release broke. Splitting the job into one job per compositor would have named the failing compositor in the job list too, but it would build the test four times (or add an artifact hand-off) and change the push behaviour the owner asked to keep, so the version goes into the annotation and the summary instead.

**2026-10-09 · laptop-resilience: Hyprland dispatches go out in Lua first.** From 0.56 a Lua config is Hyprland's only kind, so the classic form the adapter sent first (wave4-exit-ci) cost every connection on a current Hyprland one refused request before its first action ran. The adapter now sends the Lua dispatcher object first and the classic form only when Hyprland refuses the Lua one as a classic Hyprland does. That refusal comes from `dispatchRequest` in `src/debug/HyprCtl.cpp`: without a Lua config (0.54.3; 0.55.4 and 0.56.2 with a hyprlang config, the same code after the Lua branch) the first word of the request is the dispatcher name, `hl.dsp.focus({` is none, and the reply is exactly `Invalid dispatcher`. The fallback is symmetric: a reply that refuses the dialect sent (`Invalid dispatcher`, or Lua's own error for the chunk `return hl.dispatch(…)`, as before), in any command of a batch, sends the action once in the other dialect, and the dialect that was understood is kept for the rest of the connection; a reconnect starts in Lua again (Hyprland may have restarted with another config). An action's own failure (`No such window found`, a dispatcher's message) is not a dialect refusal and is not sent again. This covers `ws.focus()`, `win.focus()`, `win.close()` and the toggles `win.maximize()`/`win.fullscreen()`, whose classic form stays the focus-then-`fullscreen` batch. The initial dialect is not chosen from `j/version`: the adapter does not otherwise read it on connect, a version cannot tell a 0.55 Hyprland's config type, and the one refused round trip falls only on hyprlang configs, which 0.56 no longer has. The fake answers a Lua form `Invalid dispatcher` in its classic mode now, as Hyprland does, and the tests check both orders (`a_lua_config_hyprland_gets_lua_dispatches`: no classic attempt; `a_classic_hyprland_gets_the_batch_after_refusing_lua` and the replayed-traffic test: one refused Lua form, then classic for the connection, Lua again after a reconnect).

**2026-10-09 · laptop-resilience: an adapter that cannot understand its compositor degrades to the standard protocols.** Before, a reply the adapter could not parse ended the session like a lost socket: the last state stayed on the bar (frozen) while the adapter reconnected forever, and niri's lenient parsing read a reply or event of another shape as empty lists (a bar without windows) with no word anywhere. Now a session ends either with an I/O error (a lost socket: reconnect, keep the last state, as before) or "not understood" (`wm::understood::SessionEnd`), and the second sends `AdapterMsg::Degraded(text)`: the run drops the adapter's state and serves windows and workspaces from wlr-foreign-toplevel-management, ext-foreign-toplevel-list and ext-workspace-v1 exactly as when the adapter fails to connect (the same `merge`, a `Reset` of the ids, actions routed to the protocols), `Sources::degraded` holds the text, and the adapter retries on its existing backoff (100 ms doubling to 10 s), so a fixed or upgraded compositor recovers without a restart and nothing else wakes meanwhile; its next state clears it with another `Reset`. The thresholds, chosen to fit how each adapter already works: a reply to a state request that is not the JSON the adapter reads, or lacks a field it needs, degrades at once, since the state cannot be known without it; the fields that matter are now required in the serde types (Hyprland: a monitor's name, `focused` and `activeWorkspace`, a workspace's id and name, a client's `address`, `mapped` and `workspace`; niri: workspace `id` and `idx`, window `id`; sway's types were strict already), the rest keep their defaults and unknown fields stay ignored. An empty Hyprland reply (the socket closed without an answer, as when Hyprland exits) stays an I/O error. Events: every adapter already re-read the state after an event it could not apply (Hyprland's known events with odd data, sway's undecodable events); niri now does too instead of ignoring them, and the re-read's replies decide. So one odd event, and an event name the adapter does not know (ignored as before; never re-read), stay harmless; only `MAX_STRIKES` = 8 consecutive stream messages that are no event at all (a niri line or sway payload that is not JSON, a Hyprland line without `>>`), with no event between, degrade: eight is far beyond a stray line and still a fraction of one burst, and each of them already cost a re-read. Bytes that are no i3-ipc frame degrade sway at once (the framing is lost). Actions: a syntax the compositor refuses in every dialect it has (Hyprland's Lua and classic, both refused as dialects; niri's `error parsing request`; sway's `parse_error`, narrowed below to its unknown-command reply), for an action every supported version has (see "one unsupported action is only rejected" below), answers the action `Rejected` and degrades, because every action would fail on IPC ids while the protocols could run them. Such a refusal cannot be re-checked without running an action, so it holds while the compositor reports the same version (`wm::understood::Refused`): retries read the version and stay degraded instead of flipping the bar between the two id spaces; another version, or none reported, is tried again.

**2026-10-09 · laptop-resilience: the degraded adapter is a `ServiceDiagnostic`, not an overlay notice.** The text names the compositor, its version (Hyprland's `j/version` `version` or `tag`, niri's `"Version"`, sway's `get_version` `human_readable`, read when the adapter degrades; "version unknown" otherwise) and what was not understood, for example `the Hyprland IPC adapter does not understand Hyprland 0.57.0: the reply to j/clients (missing field `address` …); windows and workspaces come from the standard Wayland protocols until it does (retrying)`. The existing rules put on the overlay only what the user must act on, and make a failure the service retries a log line and a `strand watch` notice; this one is retried by the adapter itself and the bar keeps working on the protocols, so it is `notice: false`. A running body had no way to raise a non-notice diagnostic (only a failed run did), so `Cx::warn(message)` adds one (`Envelope::Warning`, through the same `diagnose` as a failed run, with its dedup). The three stores share one service, so only one raises it: the oldest live subscription of the hub (`WmSubscription::reports()`), which needs no knowledge of which stores a shell reads; each store tracks the last `degraded` text and the reporter warns when it changes to a new one. The return to normal is logged at info by the service; non-notice diagnostics have no "resolved" form, and adding one was not needed for a log and `strand watch` line.

**2026-10-09 · laptop-resilience: one unsupported action is only rejected; the syntax is judged by the actions every version has.** niri answers every request it cannot deserialize `error parsing request` with nothing more (`src/ipc/server.rs`), so that answer cannot tell "this niri reads another syntax" from "this niri has no such action". niri 25.08 has no `MaximizeWindowToEdges` (its `niri-ipc/src/lib.rs` has only `MaximizeColumn`), and the adapter supports niris that old, so treating that answer as a refused syntax made one `win.maximize()` click move a healthy 25.08 to the protocols until niri was upgraded. sway's `parse_error` and Hyprland's dialect refusals share the risk: a command or dispatcher added in a later release is refused by an older one in the same words as a syntax it no longer reads. The adapter now counts a refusal in every dialect as the syntax's only for an action every supported version of each compositor has, `ws.focus()`, `win.focus()` and `win.close()` (`wm::understood::tells_syntax`: niri `FocusWorkspace`, `FocusWindow`, `CloseWindow`; sway `workspace`, `focus`, `kill`; Hyprland `workspace`, `focuswindow`, `closewindow` and their `hl.dsp` forms). The same refusal of a later action (maximize, fullscreen, minimize) answers that action `Rejected` (niri's text adds `this niri does not know `Action MaximizeWindowToEdges``; Hyprland returns the reply in the connection's dialect and keeps that dialect), and the adapter stays up. A compositor whose syntax really changed is still caught by the next focus or close, which a bar sends far more often than the toggles. Probing with a harmless action after each refusal was the alternative: niri has one (`FocusWindow` of an id no window has does nothing), but sway's and Hyprland's answers to a probe that matches nothing were not seen live, and the rule by action needs no extra request and no guess. Tested by `tests/niri.rs::a_niri_without_a_later_action_rejects_only_that_action`, `tests/hyprland.rs::a_hyprland_refusing_a_later_action_in_both_dialects_rejects_only_it`, `tests/sway.rs::a_sway_refusing_a_later_command_rejects_only_it`, and `wm::understood::tests::only_actions_every_version_has_tell_the_syntax`.

**2026-10-09 · laptop-resilience: a retry after an event stream that was not understood waits for an event, and a degradation is reported once.** Only the refused-actions case was pinned by version; after eight messages that are no event, every retry connected, read the state (whose replies were fine), sent `Connected(true)` and its `State` before reading any event, and so cleared the degradation with a `Reset` of the ids, until the next eight lines degraded it again with another `Reset`. A compositor whose event format changed thus swapped the bar's window and workspace ids on every backoff cycle, and raised the diagnostic again each time (the store's `last` went to `None` on recovery, and `diagnose` drops its dedup for a run older than `RETRY_MAX`): a warning and a `strand watch` line about every 10 s, and a 100 ms backoff again whenever the garbage came slower than `STABLE`. The previous paragraph's "retries stay degraded instead of flipping the bar" held only for refused actions. Now each adapter keeps a `wm::understood::Degradation` across sessions. After a stream that was not understood, the next session is on probation: it subscribes and reads the state, but sends `Connected(true)` and its state (and starts the backoff's stable clock) only once its stream has carried an event, any event the adapter knows or not, which is the same test `Strikes` already applies; until then it answers actions `NotConnected` (the coordinator routes them to the protocols while degraded anyway) and drops reloads. niri restates its state as events at the start of every stream, so a niri that is understood again comes up at once; Hyprland and sway come up on their next event, which any focus or title change sends. And a session that ends not understood without having come up sends no second `Degraded`: the service already has a reason, so the diagnostic is raised once per degradation, and only a session that came up and then failed reports again. The first reason is the one shown until then, even if a later retry fails another way; the log has the rest at debug. Tested by the three `an_unknown_*_event_is_harmless_but_a_stream_of_no_events_is_not` tests, which now go on through about 1.5 s of retries against a stream that stays garbage (each retry reads the stream; no `Sources` with `connected`, no other change, the reason unchanged) and then recover on an event (each fails with the guard removed), and by `wm::understood::tests::a_degradation_is_reported_once_and_a_stream_one_waits_for_an_event`.

**2026-10-09 · laptop-resilience: only sway's unknown-command reply refuses its syntax.** The sway adapter read any `parse_error` reply to focus, kill or workspace as "this sway no longer reads the command syntax" and degraded, pinned to sway's version. But sway sets `parse_error` for every `CMD_INVALID` result (sway 1.10 `sway/commands.c` `cmd_results_to_json`: `parse_error` is `status == CMD_INVALID`), and `cmd_focus`, `cmd_kill` and `cmd_workspace` return `CMD_INVALID` for states: `Can't run this command while there's no outputs connected.` (a laptop with its lid closed and its external monitor just unplugged, or a click queued while the last output went away), and, for `workspace`, `Expected workspace number` and `There is no previous workspace` (a workspace literally named `number` or `back_and_forth`). One such click moved a healthy sway to the protocols, and `Refused` kept it there after the outputs came back and across sway restarts of the same version, until sway was upgraded or strand restarted. Now only `execute_command`'s own refusal, `Unknown/invalid command '…'` (the handler table has no such command), counts as the syntax's (`wm::sway::refuses_syntax`, still only for the actions every sway has, `understood::tells_syntax`); every other `parse_error` answers the action `Rejected` with sway's message and the adapter stays, so the same action runs once the state allows it. A changed argument syntax of `focus`, `kill` or `workspace` (a `checkarg` `Invalid … command` reply, or a criteria token sway no longer knows) is therefore not caught as a refused syntax; those replies are `CMD_INVALID` too and their wording is not a stable marker, whereas removing or renaming one of those commands, the change that would make every action fail, still is. Not pinning a sway refusal by version at all was the alternative the finding offered; it would have stopped the "no way back" but still flipped a healthy sway to the protocols and back on every such click, which the design's "without flipping back before it understands it" rules out. Tested by `tests/sway.rs::a_sway_refusing_an_action_for_its_state_rejects_only_it` (focus, close and workspace answered the no-outputs reply, and workspace answered `Expected workspace number`: each `Rejected` with sway's text, no `Sources` change, not degraded; then focus and workspace run), `wm::sway::tests::only_an_unknown_command_refuses_the_syntax`, and the unchanged `a_sway_refusing_the_command_syntax_degrades` (`Unknown/invalid command 'focus'`).

## laptop-media

**2026-10-09 · laptop-media: a new track starts its time at 0 in the same update as its title.** On a `PropertiesChanged` carrying `Metadata`, `media` carried the old track's position forward to now and asked for `Position` in a task; until that answer came, a shell showed the new title with the old track's time (`media_follows_the_active_player_without_polling` failed about 1 in 5 runs on "the new track starts at 0"). The service now remembers the track each player's `Metadata` last named and, when a `Metadata` names another track, sets the carried position to 0 at once; the `Position` answer still corrects it, and an answer to an older question is still dropped. Tracks are told apart by `mpris:trackid` (an object path, or a string from players that send one), else `xesam:url`, else `xesam:title` with `xesam:artist`, comparing the first key both `Metadata` name, so a player that adds a trackid to a track it first named by title alone has not changed track; when they share no key, only two that name nothing are the same. A `Metadata` change for the same track (new art, a length) keeps the carried position. A track change signalled as an invalidated `Metadata` is judged when the whole re-read lands, after the changes signalled since are applied over it, so a stale read naming the old track does not reset the new one; if that read's own position answer is current, it stands. Resetting on every `Metadata` change would have been simpler, but players send `Metadata` for art and length updates mid-track, and that would have jumped the time to 0 until the answer.

**2026-10-09 · laptop-media: a whole re-read naming another track resets the time only while no newer position fix can stand.** The first version reset the time to 0 whenever an invalidated `Metadata`'s whole re-read landed naming another track. When a `Seeked`, or the answer to a later `Position` question, had already landed since that read was asked, the reset overwrote that newer fix; the read's own position answer was stale and dropped, so nothing corrected the time until the next state, track or rate change. Every read now carries the player's latest question number from when it was asked (`Ask::asked`, `Read::asked`), and the re-read resets only while that is still the latest (no position question or seek since). When a newer question is still in flight, the read leaves the carried time alone and that question's answer says where. When the read's own question is the latest, its answer overrides the reset anyway, so in practice the reset matters for a read that asked no position (only some other property was invalidated). The track the read names is noted either way, so later comparisons use it. Keeping a separate "last fix applied" counter would also reset while a newer question is still in flight, but it adds a second counter for a round trip of old time. The `Seeked` handling moved into `Players::seeked` so the case is unit-tested (`a_position_fix_newer_than_the_whole_read_survives_it`).

## laptop-labwc

**2026-10-09 · laptop-labwc: a stopping protocol thread waits for the compositor to take the requests it sent.** `compositor_matrix.rs::window_state_actions_follow_the_compositor` failed once on labwc 0.20.2 in GitHub run 37913227852 ("win.fullscreen() by request" never showed, all three views unchanged, labwc.log empty). With the matrix made loopable (`MATRIX_FILTER`, `MATRIX_LOOP` and `MATRIX_WAYLAND_DEBUG` through scripts/container/matrix.sh, scripts/compositor-matrix-ci.sh and scripts/compositor-matrix.sh) it failed 4 of 200 idle runs, 3 of 200 with WAYLAND_DEBUG and 15 of 200 under full CPU load, on either `reply_to` request. WAYLAND_DEBUG on both sides showed the fresh `wm::run`'s `set_fullscreen` (or `unset_fullscreen`) leave the client and never reach labwc. `reply_to` ends its run as soon as the `Ok` arrives, which stops the wlr thread, and the thread closed its connection at once: when the stop came in the same command batch as the request, before the request was even written (wayland-client does not flush on drop), and, once writing came first, before labwc had read it, because libwayland-server (1.26.0, `wl_client_connection_data`) destroys a client on `WL_EVENT_HANGUP` before reading what is still in its socket. Writing before the reply alone still failed 2 of 200 and 1 of 300 (the second shape, seen in the logs). So the thread now writes a batch's requests before it answers them (an `Ok` means written; a write that fails answers `NotConnected`) and, on a stop after any request was sent, sends a `wl_display.sync` and waits for its `done` (500 ms at most, `SETTLE_WAIT`; a hung compositor still cannot hold the thread longer) before it closes the connection: requests are dispatched in order, so the `done` means every request before it was read. The bug was in production code, not the test: any short-lived run that acts and stops (a script's one-shot action) could lose its action the same way. After the fix: 0 of 300 idle and 0 of 200 loaded runs. `wm::protocol::tests::a_request_followed_at_once_by_a_stop_still_reaches_the_compositor` pins it deterministically: the request and the stop in one batch while the fake compositor reads nothing, the thread must keep the connection until it does (it fails on the old code and on writing alone). The fake compositor moved from tests/protocol.rs to tests/common/fake_wlr.rs for it, and gained `paused`. labwc.log was empty because labwc logs only errors without `-d`; the matrix starts it with `-d` (and `WAYLAND_DEBUG=server` with `MATRIX_WAYLAND_DEBUG=1`).

**2026-10-09 · laptop-labwc: every end of the protocol thread after a request settles, and an `Ok` means on the connection, not written.** Review of the stop fix above found two gaps. First, the thread had a second way out: a state send that fails because the run's receiver is gone returned at once, without `settle`. Aborting `wm::run` drops the receiver and then the `ProtocolClient` (whose drop sends the stop); a compositor event in between marks the state dirty, the send fails, and the thread closed the connection before the stop's settle could run, so a request just written could be lost to libwayland-server's hangup handling the same way. That return now settles too when a request was sent (`wm::protocol::tests::a_request_outlives_a_dropped_state_receiver` fails without it: the fake compositor, paused, still sends a new toplevel after the receiver is dropped, and the thread must keep the connection until the fake reads the request; the fake's `paused` now still flushes its own events for this). Second, the paragraph above says "an `Ok` means written", but the batch writes with no wait (`send_queued(.., Duration::ZERO)`), so behind a full socket the requests are still queued in wayland-client when the `Ok` goes out; the poll loop writes them, or `settle` on the way out, so nothing is lost. We kept the zero wait (a reply should not block on a slow compositor) and corrected the stated guarantee instead: an `Ok` means the request is on the connection, written or queued, and every end after a request writes the queue and waits (500 ms at most) for the compositor to read it.

GPU crates still stay cold (no device, their code untouched) until something needs them, so the PSS budget is unchanged. ## m4-infra

**2026-10-09 · m4-infra: lavapipe is selected by `VK_DRIVER_FILES`, with a fixed llvmpipe vector width.** Ubuntu's `mesa-vulkan-drivers` installs every Mesa ICD (Intel, Radeon, nouveau, virtio and others), so the check image and CI set `VK_DRIVER_FILES` (and the deprecated `VK_ICD_FILENAMES`) to `/usr/share/vulkan/icd.d/lvp_icd.json`; the plan's `lvp_icd.x86_64.json` is the Arch name and does not exist on Ubuntu. `LP_NATIVE_VECTOR_WIDTH=256` keeps llvmpipe's code path the same on AVX2 and AVX-512 machines so GPU-tier pixels do not depend on the CPU; `LP_NUM_THREADS` stays unset (rasterisation results do not depend on the thread count, and one thread would slow every GPU test). `STRAND_REQUIRE_GPU=1` is set in CI's env, `ci.sh` and `run.sh`'s defaults, like the other `STRAND_REQUIRE_*`. The Mesa version comes from Ubuntu's updates pocket (25.2.8 today), as sway and the fonts do; the `GPU tier device` step prints it to trace a pixel change.

**2026-10-09 · m4-infra: the hardware GPU leg runs in the check image, not the Arch image.** The plan expected Ubuntu 24.04's ANV not to drive the laptop's Panther Lake GPU (8086:b080 on `xe`) and put `gpu.sh` in the Arch matrix image. The updates pocket's Mesa 25.2.8 drives it: `vulkaninfo` lists "Intel(R) Graphics (PTL)" and `vkcube-wayland` presents to a headless sway rendering with GLES2 on the render node, all in the check image. So `gpu.sh` uses `run.sh`'s image and build tree (the test binaries it runs are the ones `run.sh` builds), passes only `/dev/dri/renderD128` (run.sh refuses any `card*`, the in-container script checks none is present), swaps the ICD by the render node's PCI vendor, and starts its own sway in a private runtime dir. Failures warn unless `STRAND_STRICT_GPU=1`, as the m4-owner decision asks.

**2026-10-09 · m4-infra: the lock VM is a baked Ubuntu disk image booted with a direct kernel, not virtme-ng on the container's rootfs.** The critique listed what breaks with virtme-ng over a shared rootfs (a 0600 kernel, virtiofsd's sandbox in an unprivileged container, a read-only uid-mapped root, setuid `unix_chkpwd` through 9p). `Dockerfile.lockvm` builds the guest as a Docker stage (Ubuntu 24.04, its kernel, sway, grim, the binary's runtime libraries, pamtester, user `tester` with password `strand-test`, `/etc/pam.d/strand` including common-auth and common-account), turns it into an ext4 image with `mke2fs -d` in a second stage (no loop device, no root on the host; ownership and the setgid `unix_chkpwd` survive), and the final image holds only QEMU, that image and the kernel (chmod 0644). The guest boots it with `snapshot=on`, so every run starts clean and scenarios may rewrite `/etc/pam.d`; a tiny PID 1 (`lockvm/init`) mounts two 9p shares (the checkout at its own path, and a control dir with the command and its exit status) and powers off with sysrq. No virtiofsd and no network. Boot to command takes about 0.5 s under KVM and 6 s under TCG; the smoke's whole run is about 3 s of guest time. The TCG override is `LOCKVM_TCG=1` (the task's name; the plan's `STRAND_LOCK_VM_TCG` is not used, since `STRAND_*` variables are forwarded into `run.sh`'s containers).

**2026-10-09 · m4-infra: CI gets a `lock-vm` job.** GitHub's standard Linux runners expose `/dev/kvm` (GitHub changelog 2024-04-02, hardware-accelerated Android virtualization on 2-vCPU runners) once a udev rule makes it 0666; the job applies that rule with `sudo` on the runner (never in the container scripts) and fails, without emulating, if the runner has no `/dev/kvm`. It runs nightly, on `workflow_dispatch`, on tag pushes, and on branch pushes and pull requests whose changes touch the lock paths (dorny/paths-filter: strand-auth, the session-lock and lock-fallback modules, the lock tests, `scripts/lockvm/**` and the harness); otherwise it skips its steps and passes. Confirmed in run 37955474449 (2026-10-09): the runner's `/dev/kvm` was `crw-rw---- root kvm`, 0666 after the rule, and the smoke passed under KVM (guest up in 0.89 s, 4 s in all). Today it runs the harness's smoke; S-lock replaces the command with its scenarios, and the integrator owns ci.yml after wave 0.

**2026-10-09 · m4-infra: the lock-vm paths filter follows the critique's S-lock ownership, widened by globs.** None of the lock files exist yet, so the filter names them as the critique's stream table assigns them to S-lock (which wins over the plan), adds the ones it had missed (`services/auth*`, `auth.schema`, `check/lock.rs`, the plan's `strand/src/lock.rs`), and matches `*session_lock*` and `*lock_fallback*` anywhere under `crates/` so a test or module placed elsewhere still triggers the tier. S-lock keeps the list in step with its real file names; nightly and tag runs cover any miss. The m4-owner paragraph above said CLAUDE.md names `/dev/kvm`; it does not yet, so that sentence now says the decision is the authority until the owner edits CLAUDE.md.

## m4-render-split

**2026-10-09 · m4-render-split: strand-render's monoliths split by concern, with no feed.rs or backend.rs yet.** F0 split `renderer.rs`, `flatten.rs`, `raster.rs`, `anim.rs` and `layout.rs` into directories (the map is in architecture.md, "`strand-render` module map") as pure moves: no logic, signature or name changed, private items that moved became `pub(super)` (or kept `pub(crate)`), and each `mod.rs` re-exports what the rest of the crate used, so no caller changed. The critique named `renderer/{frame,wake,feed,backend,lists,pose}.rs`. `frame.rs`, `wake.rs`, `lists.rs` and `pose.rs` hold the code that exists for those concerns today. `feed.rs` (effects' `feed`/`feed_frame`) and `backend.rs` (GPU promotion) would have been empty, because neither concern has code yet, so their owning streams create them; the place promotion will hook into is `Renderer::paint_frame` in `frame.rs`, where the display list goes to `Raster`. Code the critique did not name went to modules of its own (`text.rs`, `layout_pass.rs`, `apply.rs`, `specs.rs`, `surfaces.rs`, `tooltip.rs`), so that no stream's file is a catch-all. `layout_pass.rs` is not called `layout.rs`, so that it is not confused with `crate::layout`. In `pose.rs`, "pose" means exit poses and closing surfaces, the pose code the renderer has today. In `anim/`, the existing concerns went to `motion.rs`, `pose.rs` and `sizes.rs`. The critique's `anim/{keyframes,morph,stagger,pages}.rs` are new features, so their streams add them. In `layout/`, list virtualisation went to `list.rs` (lists), a node's taffy style and fillet-relevant shadow overhang to `style.rs`, and text measuring to `text.rs` (letters). The renderer's unit tests moved to `renderer/tests.rs`, so features.md and one test comment now point there. Two doc lines that sat above `glide_moved` went back to `diff_records`, which they describe. Verified with the unchanged tests: `cargo test -p strand-render` (the same 227 passing, 1 ignored, as before the split), `-p strand-compiler` and `-p strand --test demo`.

**2026-10-09 · m4-docs: `DropPayload` in strand-scene, `NodeEvent::Drop` in strand-render.** `NodeEvent` lives in `strand_render::input`, so the M4 variant goes there. Its payload is produced by `strand-surface` for external drops (`InputEvent::DragDrop`), which cannot depend on render, so `DropPayload` sits in `strand-scene` next to `InputEvent`. An in-Strand drag sends only the source node; logic maps it back to its `drag:` value, so no logic value crosses into render. `Prop::Drag` and `Prop::Accepts` carry type names, which is all render needs to pick a target.

**2026-10-09 · m4-docs: the unlock gate is a type.** design.md asks for a small, separately reviewable PAM helper and a lock that fails closed. `strand_auth::UnlockToken` is minted only by `strand_auth::Client` from a success reply and is neither `Clone` nor constructible elsewhere; `strand-surface`'s `State::unlock` takes it, so no other path can unlock. That adds an edge from `strand-surface` to `strand-auth`'s lib, which depends only on libc and zeroize; the binary alone links libpam.

**2026-10-09 · m4-docs: keyframes travel inline.** `Prop::Play` carries the compiled `keyframes` block (`PropValue::Keyframes`) instead of `[name, seq]`, so render keeps no table of keyframes that a reload would have to update; the settings are the ones `check::keyframe_settings` already allows (`duration`, `delay`, `repeat`, `alternate`, `easing`).

**2026-10-09 · m4-docs: an SVG part names its layer with `Prop::Name`.** The 2026-10-05 render decision makes `#id { … }` blocks child nodes; the new kind `SvgPart` carries the id as `Prop::Name`, the prop that already holds a declared name, rather than a new prop.

**2026-10-09 · m4-docs: the lock fallback bypasses the Router.** While render's built-in fallback lock is shown, keys on lock surfaces go from the binary straight to `lock_fallback`, so the code that must work when everything else has failed does not depend on the Router, the logic thread or the text worker. The Router stays S-lists' alone; parallax, tilt and jelly read it (`pointer`, `drag`) and never edit it.

**2026-10-09 · m4-docs: tray click coordinates are left to S-surface.** The plan gave the tray actions optional `x`/`y`. A user-facing argument would be new syntax with no way for a config to know the anchor's output position, so architecture.md only fixes the outcome (real coordinates instead of 0, 0) and leaves the route (an argument, or the host filling them in from the calling node) to S-surface's decision.

**2026-10-09 · m4-docs: clipboard is not M4.** decisions.md (wave3-pixels p3) left Ctrl+C/V "for M4 with drag and drop", but design.md never mentions a clipboard and no M4 box asks for it. It stays out; drag and drop's `wl_data_device` makes it cheap to add later.

**2026-10-09 · m4-docs: `strand_auth::Client` takes its `pre_exec` from its owner.** Every spawn must run `strand_services::child::restore_in_child` (architecture.md, "strand-services"), but `strand-services` depends on `strand-auth`, whose lib depends on no Strand crate, so the `Client` cannot call it. `Client::new(helper, pre_exec: fn())` takes the hook, and its two owners (the `auth` store and the main thread's fallback client) pass `child::restore_in_child`. That keeps the helper's spawn and respawn inside the reviewable crate without a dependency cycle; moving `child` into `strand-auth` would make the auth crate own a process-wide THP policy that is not its concern.

As earlier services did when they stopped being provisional, S-lock moves it to `strand-services-schema/src/auth.schema` (with an `AUTH` constant and a `schemas()` entry) and deletes the provisional block from builtin.schema in wave 1, the one builtin.schema edit S-lock owns after 0b. After 0b, a bundled-effect stream edits only its own effect's declaration there.

This removes a case rather than adding one.

Logic resolves the id through the `apps` service when it builds the `Drop` value, null when no installed app has it.

## m4-gpu-spike

**2026-10-09 · m4-gpu-spike: wgpu 30 presents to a layer surface on lavapipe; the readback path is the universal fallback.** The scratch crate `spikes/gpu-present` (its own `[workspace]`, not a member; `run-spike.sh` starts a private headless sway inside `run.sh`'s container and never touches the host session) opens wgpu 30.0.1 (Vulkan only) with vello_gpu 0.3.0 (`default-features = false, features = ["wgpu", "std"]`) and draws to a 256x128 wlr-layer-shell surface, using raw Wayland handles from wayland-backend 0.3.17's `client_system`. On lavapipe (Mesa 25.2.8, LLVM 20.1.2) and sway 1.9 with `WLR_RENDERER=pixman`, the WSI path works through Mesa's wl_shm software WSI. Surface formats are Bgra8UnormSrgb, Rgba8UnormSrgb, Bgra8Unorm, Rgba8Unorm and Rgb10a2Unorm; present modes are Mailbox and Fifo; alpha modes are Opaque and PreMultiplied. Setup (instance, surface, adapter, device and renderer) takes 76 ms, and 60 Fifo frames take 19.2 ms each (paced by the compositor). The grim shot matches the scene. Offscreen rendering, then `copy_texture_to_buffer`, a map and a swizzle into a `wl_shm` ARGB8888 buffer also works: setup takes 176 ms, and a frame takes 3.6 ms including the Wayland roundtrip. On the laptop's Intel PTL GPU (`gpu.sh`, renderD128 only), presenting **fails** against a pixman sway: `request_adapter` with `compatible_surface` returns `NotFound`, with `incompatible_surface_backends: VULKAN`. ANV's WSI needs linux-dmabuf, and a pixman compositor offers none. Against `gpu-session.sh`'s GLES2 sway, presenting works at 15.7 ms a frame (Fifo, 60 Hz) and readback takes 0.76 ms a frame. So promotion must test surface compatibility (an adapter request with `compatible_surface`, or non-empty `get_capabilities`) and use offscreen rendering plus shm readback when the WSI can't present. Readback works on every compositor and device we tried. It is also the natural path for a shader on a surface that has not been promoted (critique B.6).

**2026-10-09 · m4-gpu-spike: dropping the device frees memory on hardware but not on lavapipe.** The measurements are PSS from `/proc/self/smaps_rollup`, taken after `malloc_trim` (the spike uses glibc malloc, while strand uses mimalloc). They cover three create, 60-frame and drop cycles with 256x128 offscreen frames.
- **Lavapipe:** 2.4 MiB before the GPU starts, 108–112 MiB with the device up, and 83–85 MiB after everything is dropped. Threads return from 35 to 1, and `libvulkan.so.1` is unmapped, but `libvulkan_lvp.so`, `libLLVM.so.20.1`, `libdrm` and `libedit` stay mapped, and Pss_Anon stays about 13 MiB above where it started. The leftover is the same after every cycle, so it is a one-time cost, not a leak.
- **Intel ANV:** 2.4 MiB before, about 17 MiB with the device up (21–26 MiB when presenting), and 7.6–8.7 MiB after the drop. Every Vulkan library is unmapped and anon is about 1.3 MiB above where it started. This is also the same every cycle.
- **Device-up time:** 78–104 ms on lavapipe, and 45–51 ms on Intel once its shader cache is warm (274 ms cold).

As the critique predicted (D.4), "mappings gone" and "PSS back to baseline" don't hold on lavapipe. The CI idle test should assert three things: the GPU thread is gone, nothing wakes up, and PSS after a second promote and drop is within tolerance of PSS after the first (no growth). The advisory hardware leg can also assert PSS within about 6 MiB of the pre-GPU baseline, which ANV meets. If the owner needs memory back on lavapipe too, the only route is a GPU helper process, which this spike did not build.

**2026-10-09 · m4-gpu-spike: linking the GPU backend adds 3.0 MiB of `.text` and about 1.3 MB of cold PSS; proposed gate 18.5 MiB.** `spikes/text-measure/apply.sh` adds wgpu (vulkan, wgsl, std), naga (wgsl-in), vello_gpu, vello_common, raw-window-handle, pollster and wayland-backend `client_system` to `crates/strand`. It also adds `gpu_spike::run`, which `main` reaches when `STRAND_GPU_SPIKE` is set. That function validates a WGSL module with naga, creates a WSI surface from raw handles, creates the device and a shader module, and renders a vello_gpu scene that uses fill, stroke, a blurred rounded rect, a clip and blend layer, and a blur filter layer, then reads it back. vello_gpu's `text` feature is off, because strand draws glyphs as its own paths. The release profile is unchanged, so the GPU crates build at opt-level 3. The edits were reverted after measuring, and none is committed in `crates/`.

| Build | `.text` | `.data.rel.ro` | Bar PSS (`budgets.rs` design bar) |
|---|---|---|---|
| laptop/integration-m4 today (c349d04) | 14,532,055 B (13.86 MiB) | 466,976 B | 32,380 / 32,470 / 32,214 / 32,556 kB, mean 32,405 |
| `client_system` only | 14,588,887 B (+56.8 kB) | 466,592 B | 32,575 kB (one run, within noise) |
| `client_system` + GPU code | 17,683,543 B (16.86 MiB, +3.0 MiB) | 596,384 B | 34,003 / 33,905 / 33,568 / 33,416 kB, mean 33,723 |

The two builds were measured alternately with the same test binary. The GPU build adds `libwayland-client.so.0` to `ldd` (through `client_system`), but no `libvulkan`, which wgpu dlopens, and no Vulkan library is mapped in the bar. The "cold" claim therefore holds for devices and drivers but not for PSS: the bar grows by about 1.3 MB (+4%). Of that, the `strand` file mapping accounts for about 0.6–0.85 MB: relocated `.data.rel.ro` (+129 kB, dirty) and `.got` (+7 kB), plus code pages where LTO mixes hot and cold functions. Another 0.3–0.5 MB is mimalloc anon, which is within the run-to-run spread. The bar stays under the 34 MB target (mean 33.7 MB) and the 38 MB ceiling, but with about 0.3 MB to spare under the target. The stream that lands the backend should measure this again and, if it needs room, try section ordering or `opt-level = "s"` for wgpu-core and naga. The `.text` gate for the default (GPU) build should be **18.5 MiB (19,398,656 B)**, the measured 17,683,543 B plus 9.7%, with the number recorded here when S-gpu lands it. A CPU-only build keeps the 15 MiB gate, and today has 1.14 MiB of headroom under it. Enabling `client_system` switches the wayland backend for every crate in the build. It costs 57 kB of `.text` and a dynamic dependency on libwayland-client, which every Wayland desktop has.

## m4-scene

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: naga is checked in the compiler, behind a `shaders` feature, and the CPU-only build links none of it.** The plan puts `check::shaders` (naga parse, validate, `u_*` reflection) in `strand-compiler`, and the owner put the GPU in every build, so naga is in the shipped binary through wgpu anyway; a direct dependency of the compiler on the same naga version adds no code there, and `strand-dev`'s LSP needs it to check shaders without linking wgpu. Putting reflection in `strand-gpu` instead would make the compiler and the LSP depend on the GPU crate. The check sits behind a compiler feature `shaders`, which `strand`'s default `gpu` turns on, because the spike's CPU build had only 1.14 MiB of room under the 15 MiB gate and was measured without naga: the CPU-only build is the CPU core, with the interim `uniform_ty` limit and a shader that draws nothing, as with no device. A second naga version in `Cargo.lock` is a merge blocker, since it would link naga twice.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: render lowers its display lists into `strand-gpu`'s frame type; the GPU crate depends only on `strand-scene`.** Render calls the GPU backend, so `strand-gpu` cannot depend on render's display-list types. Moving those types into `strand-scene` would make the shared vocabulary carry render's internals. Instead `strand-gpu` defines `Frame` (kurbo paths, peniko paints, layers, texture ids, shader passes; vello_common types render already has through vello_cpu), render fills it in `renderer/backend.rs`, and the GPU thread builds the vello_gpu scene, so vello_gpu's CPU-side encoding stays off the main thread. `strand-surface` hands out `raw-window-handle` handles and never depends on `strand-gpu`; the binary joins the three.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: a software Vulkan adapter counts as no device, unless `STRAND_GPU_SOFTWARE=1`.** design.md promotes to the GPU to take heavy animation off the CPU. On lavapipe the "GPU" is the CPU, and the spike measured about 80 MiB that stays mapped after the device drops, against a 30 MB bar. A user whose only Vulkan driver is lavapipe is better served by the CPU fallback. The lavapipe test tier is to set the variable beside `STRAND_REQUIRE_GPU=1` (pending; see "the software-adapter variable is pending" below), which keeps its meaning for the harness (fail instead of skip) and does not change the binary's behaviour.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: a shader on a CPU surface is drawn offscreen and read back; a surface the WSI cannot present to promotes in readback mode.** The plan left this choice to 0c. Waiting for the surface to promote would leave a small aurora behind a bar's clock undrawn, since it never damages 0.2 Mpx, and design.md says the GPU handles shaders whatever their size. The spike showed readback works on every compositor and device tried, which presenting does not (ANV with a pixman compositor). So there are three backends (`Cpu`, `GpuPresent`, `GpuReadback`). A pass or a readback frame is a frame hold, like text: the frame waits up to 8 ms (`GPU_WAIT`) and then draws the previous result. While the device starts, and when there is none, the CPU fallback draws, so no first frame waits for the GPU.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: a surface presented by the GPU has one committer, the GPU thread.** Two threads committing one `wl_surface` could tear double-buffered state, and a pose spread over alpha modifier, viewport and margins could land half-applied. While presented, the manager sends configure acks and sets regions and margins as pending state that the next present applies, and render paints poses into the frames, which are full-damage frames anyway. A surface the manager must destroy stays alive until the GPU thread has released its swapchain (`gpu_release`, then `take_back`), so WSI never presents to a destroyed surface. In readback mode the main thread commits and poses are delegated as usual.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: demotion mirrors promotion, the drop is timed by render, and a failure is retried once per 30 s.** design.md fixes the promotion rule (large areas for more than 500 ms, switch when settled) but not the way back. Using the same rule reversed (500 ms of frames under 0.2 Mpx, then a settled frame) keeps a surface from flapping. The 30 s drop deadline is in `Renderer::next_wake` (the plan's `promote.rs::drops_after_30s_with_one_wake`), so the GPU thread never wakes on a timer. A lost device demotes at once with a full repaint, since it cannot wait for a settled frame. After a failed start or a loss, render asks again at most once per 30 s while demand lasts, so a broken driver costs one attempt per idle window rather than one per frame.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: the shader ABI is a prelude Strand prepends, with Strand's bindings in group 0 and the file's `u_*` in group 1.** The plan's reading named the built-ins (`time`, `size`, `scale`, `pointer`) but not how a file reaches them. A prelude, shared as `strand_scene::shader::PRELUDE` by the checker and the GPU thread, declares them with the vertex output and an input texture (a filter's subtree, a glass backdrop, or 1×1 transparent), so a file is just its uniforms and one `@fragment` function. Diagnostics subtract the prelude's lines. The checked text travels in the scene (`Prop::Shader`, `ShaderCode`), so render runs exactly what was checked and never re-reads a file that may have changed since; a save that fails the check keeps the last good build, as a module save does. `pointer` reads -1 outside the box, so a shader can tell "away" from the corner.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: idle-test tolerances.** The lavapipe test asserts no growth (PSS after the second promote-and-drop cycle within 3 MiB of after the first; the spike's after-drop PSS spread 2 MiB across three cycles), not a return to baseline, which lavapipe cannot meet. The hardware leg's "within about 6 MiB of the pre-GPU baseline" is the spike's ANV result (5.2–6.3 MiB under glibc malloc; strand uses mimalloc), so S-gpu sets the exact bound from its first `gpu.sh` run; that leg is advisory. design.md's +20–40 MB while promoted is checked only on hardware: lavapipe's device alone is about 106 MiB.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: m4-plan.md brought in line with 0c and with wave 0 as landed.** The `.text` gate is now the number (18.5 MiB), the GPU exit tests assert what lavapipe can meet, the S-gpu bullets point to architecture.md's "`strand-gpu`", the pose-commit question is marked settled, and the S-infra section starts with the four places where the landed infra differs from its list (m4-infra), rather than rewriting that list.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: time leaves reach a scope through `with_time`, and read 0 without it.** architecture.md said `TokenScope::resolve` takes a per-node time context. Changing `resolve`, `eval` and `lookup` would touch every caller in render and the compiler for a value most of them never read, so the context rides in the scope instead: `TokenScope::with_time(Option<TimeContext>)`, with `TimeContext { t, index, count }`, carried into an override's parent scope so `set { $spin: t * 20deg }` still sees the node's clock. With no context every leaf is evaluated at `t = 0` with `index` and `count` 0, so a frozen time signal is its value at `t = 0`; `reduced_motion` keeps a letter's `index` and `count` (see "`reduced_motion` stops the clock and keeps the letters" below, which replaced passing `None`). `wave(period, phase)` is `0.5 − 0.5·cos(2π(t/period + phase))`: it swings 0 to 1, which keeps `glow: 10 * wave(2s), …` a non-negative radius, starts at 0 like the frozen value, and takes `phase` in periods as design.md's `phase: index * 0.1` reads. `noise(x)` is 1-D gradient noise in −1..1 that is 0 at whole `x`. A zero or negative period does not resolve (the prop is unset) rather than dividing by zero.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: a template's numeric slots follow `PropValue::numbers_mut`.** `TokenExpr::Template` gained `numbers: Vec<Option<TokenExpr>>`, filled after the colours, in one depth-first field order: `Number`, `Angle`, a non-`Auto` `Length`, `Insets` top-right-bottom-left, `Corners` clockwise from top-left, a border's width before its paint, a gradient's angle (`linear`) or `from` (`conic`) before its stops' offsets, a shadow's `x`, `y`, `blur`, `spread`, then `List`/`Call` items. So `glow: 10 * wave(2s), $accent.alpha(0.4)` fills slot 0 and `border: 1.5, conic(from: t * 40deg, …)` fills slot 1. Producing such templates is F1's compiler work; 0b lands the slot and its evaluation, and every existing producer sends an empty list.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: canvas ops are the `Canvas` record's methods, and the enum stays open.** architecture.md left `DrawOp`'s variants to the canvas work, but an empty enum gives the VM nothing to record into and S-gpu would need a scene PR before starting. builtin.schema's `Canvas` record already fixes the calls (`line`, `rect`, `circle`, `fill`, `stroke`, `text`), so each became a variant, with fills and strokes ending the current path as in canvas 2D. `DrawOp` is `#[non_exhaustive]` so transforms and clips can be added without breaking other crates' matches, and `DrawOp::METHODS` is checked against the record by `scene_catalogue.rs`, so a method added to the schema without an op fails there.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: `svg_part` is the one scene kind with no schema element, and compiler-set props are kept out of the schema.** `NodeKind::SvgPart` comes from `#id { … }` selector blocks, not an element, so the catalogue test's "every kind is an element" check lists it as scene-only. The props the compiler sets and source never writes (`name`, `watch`, `two_way`, and M4's `uniforms`, `shader`, `accepts`, `row_count`, `row_first`) are listed in the test, which fails if the schema ever declares one, since a config could then write it. `uniforms` is class `Effects` so a `~` on the group defaults to `$motion.effects`; the other four snap.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: the backend and GPU status types live in strand-scene.** architecture.md names `strand_scene::Backend` but not where `GpuStatus`, its `AdapterInfo` or `BackendChange` live. Render reports all three, logic receives `GpuStatus` (`ToLogic::GpuStatus`) and a CPU-only build has no `strand-gpu`, so they sit beside `Backend` in `strand_scene::backend`, and `strand-gpu` will report its adapter as the scene's `AdapterInfo { name, driver, software }` rather than a type of its own. `GpuStatus::NOT_BUILT` is the reason string the plan names for a build without the backend.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: bundled passes read their reach from uniform slot 0, and a blur reaches three standard deviations.** `ShaderPass` keeps the fields architecture.md fixes (`code`, `uniforms`, `input`), so the reach of `bloom`, `chromatic` and `wobble` (their radius, offset and amplitude) comes from `uniforms[0]`, which each effect's builder fills first (in buffer units, divided back by the scale: see "pass uniforms are buffer values" below); the other bundled passes and every file pass reach nothing. `Bundled` has nine variants for design.md's eight effects, because `crt()` and `chromatic(px)` are separate spellings of one. `Effect::Blur { radius }` takes the radius as a standard deviation, as CSS's `filter: blur()` does (unlike a shadow's blur, which is twice it), and reaches `ceil(3·radius)`, where a Gaussian has fallen to about 1/255.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: the bundled effects' signatures.** builtin.schema now declares `bloom(radius: length)`, `crt()`, `chromatic(offset: length)`, `wobble(amplitude: length)` and `glass()`, each returning `Filter` like `blur` and the colour filters, so `filter:` and `backdrop:` accept them with no new type. The positional each takes is the one design.md's spelling shows (`bloom(r)`, `chromatic(px)`, `wobble(amp)`); further knobs are named parameters with defaults, which the schema language allows, so the stream that builds an effect adds them to its own declaration without breaking a config. Because `backdrop:` and `filter:` share `Filter`, `filter: glass()` type-checks; rejecting a misplaced one is `check/effects.rs`'s job (S-effects).

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: behaviour later streams own is an explicit, tested no-op.** The Router ignores `InputEvent::Drag*` (`input.rs::drag_events_are_not_routed_yet`) until S-lists routes drags; the demo host does not forward a `NodeEvent::Drop` to logic, whose own `NodeEvent` has no drop yet (`to_logic` returns `None`, `drops_are_not_forwarded_until_logic_takes_them`); render mounts `window: true` rows like any other, naming the field in its matches (`tree.rs::window_rows_mount_and_unmount_like_any_node`); the new `SurfaceHost` hooks (`compositor_caps`, `gpu_release`, `lock_changed`) are no-op defaults the manager does not call yet (`hook_tests::the_m4_hooks_default_to_nothing`), with `LockState` beside `SurfaceHost` in strand-surface since only the manager and the binary use it. The compiler still sends `play` as `[name, seq]` and `u_*` props one by one; `PropValue::Keyframes` and `Prop::Uniforms` wait for their lowering streams. `Keyframes::repeat` is `Option<u32>`, `None` repeating forever.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene: a spec's scrim is read only on popups and panels.** `SurfaceSpec::resolve` fills `scrim` from a `Color` or a solid `Paint` on a `popup` or `panel` and leaves it `None` on other kinds and for a gradient, so a value the checker should have rejected (S-surface's `check/surfaces.rs`) never reaches the surface manager as a scrim it cannot draw.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene (review): keyframe stops resolve like a pose.** `PropValue::Keyframes` holds props per stop, so `keyframes pulse { 50% { bg: $accent } }` carries a token and `50% { x: t * 2 }` a time leaf. `has_tokens`, `reads_time` and `TokenScope::resolve` now recurse into the stops as they do into `Pose` and `Uniforms`: a stop's token resolves (and follows a theme swap), a stop reading `t` makes the node frame-driven, and a stop that fails to resolve fails the whole value, as a pose entry does (`tokens.rs::keyframe_stops_resolve_and_read_time`). The block's other fields travel unchanged.

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene (review): one `var<uniform>` per `u_*`, packed densely in binding order.** The ABI let each `u_*` sit at its own binding in `@group(1)`, while `UniformSlot.offset` claimed a WGSL uniform layout as if they were one struct; separate bindings have no shared layout. Of the two consistent readings, one binding per uniform keeps design.md's spelling (`shader "aurora.wgsl" { u_speed: 0.4; u_tint: $accent }`) mapping one prop to one declaration and lets the checker match `var<uniform>` names directly, where a single struct would add a type the file must declare by a fixed name. So `UniformSlot` gained `binding`, and `offset` is now only the slot's first `f32` in `ShaderPass::uniforms`, dense in binding order (`ShaderCode::packed`, which the checker uses); the GPU thread copies each slot to its own binding range at the device's offset alignment (`shader.rs::checked_code_travels_shared`).

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene (review): pass uniforms are buffer values, and reach divides by the scale.** The ABI delivers lengths in px × scale, and the GPU thread uploads `ShaderPass::uniforms` as they are, so render packs them in buffer units; otherwise the GPU thread would need to know which of a file's floats are lengths. Damage is logical, so `Bundled::reach(uniforms, scale)`, `ShaderPass::reach(scale)`, `Effect::reach(scale)` and `Effect::reach_of(effects, scale)` take the surface's scale and divide a bundled pass's slot 0 by it (a blur's radius is logical and is not divided). A scale that is not positive counts as 1 (`effect.rs::reach_grows_damage_by_each_effect`).

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene (review): `reduced_motion` stops the clock and keeps the letters.** Passing no time context under `reduced_motion` also zeroed `index` and `count`, which are fixed per letter, not time: `letters { x: index * 8 }` collapsed every letter to 0 and `index / count` became 0/0, leaving the prop unresolved. Render now passes `TimeContext::frozen(index, count)` (`t = 0`). To keep one rule rather than two kinds of frozen, every leaf is simply evaluated at the context's `t`, and no context is `TimeContext::default()`: `t`, `wave(…)` with phase 0 and `noise(t * k)` read 0 as before, while a staggered `wave(1s, phase: index * 0.1)` holds its still value at `t = 0` and `noise` of a constant is that noise. Nothing moves, which is what design.md's "turns off … time signals" asks (`tokens.rs::reduced_motion_stops_the_clock_and_keeps_letters`, `::without_a_time_context_time_leaves_read_t_zero`).

**2026-10-09 · m4-scene (review): the software-adapter variable is pending.** architecture.md stated that CI's env and `run.sh` set `STRAND_GPU_SOFTWARE=1` beside `STRAND_REQUIRE_GPU=1`; neither does, nor does `ci.sh`. m4-scene owns neither file, so the text now says the integrator adds it with S-gpu's first test that needs it (the lavapipe idle test), as m4-plan.md already asks. Until then a lavapipe-only run treats the adapter as no device.

## m4-runtime-w1

**2026-10-09 · m4-runtime-w1 (F1): a time-bound value is its own `Value` variant, and logic errors where it needs a value now.** `Value::Time(Rc<TokenExpr>)` sits beside `Value::Token`; `Value::symbolic` picks one by `TokenExpr::reads_time`, so `$accent.alpha(wave(2s))` is a time value and `$space * 2` stays a token.
