**2026-10-10 · m4-gpu-effects (review): the hardware leg in release.** The leg reported above was a debug build, under which `gpu_idle` skips its 6 MiB baseline check, so m4-plan's advisory check had not run for this branch. Rerun after the review fixes as `STRAND_STRICT_GPU=1 scripts/container/gpu.sh cargo test --release -p strand --test gpu_idle` on the laptop's Intel GPU (ANV, `Readback` mode as before), with the panel's new `filter: bloom(8)` box: it passed. PSS 24,560 kB before the GPU and 29,196 kB after the first drop, 4,636 kB over the baseline, inside the leg's 6,144 kB (m4-gpu-w2 measured 4,455 kB); of that, 1,864 kB is strand's own code paged in, 822 kB libstdc++, 1,284 kB anonymous and mimalloc memory. The second cycle ended at 31,068 kB, 1,872 kB over the first, inside the 3 MiB no-growth bound. Strips matched the CPU's in both cycles (0 pixels past 6, worst channel difference 3). The promoted cost against design.md's +20–40 MB is still not measured, because ANV cannot present on the leg's pixman sway, so nothing is presented there.

**2026-10-10 · m4-gpu-effects (review 2): a failed pass is keyed without its time.** A failed bundled pass was "not asked again until its inputs change", but a clocked pass (wobble, aurora, particles) has `strand.time` in its want's key, and particles' uniforms carry their positions, so it was asked again every frame, each failure logging a warning and aurora keeping its refresh clock over a still CPU frame. A want now carries a `base` as well as its key: the key without the time and the pointer, and for a clocked bundled pass without its uniforms. A failed pass is asked again only when its `base` changes (its code, size, scale or input; for an unclocked one also its uniforms). For a clocked pass that means a changed colour or rate does not retry it either, until its size or input changes or the node goes; that is preferred over retrying a failing driver at refresh rate. While its pass's last answer is a failure, a node takes its CPU form whole: wobble has no clock, aurora no refresh clock, and the still-aurora and capped-particle notices are said (`Flattener::gpu_draws`).

**2026-10-10 · m4-gpu-effects (review 2): a tilt warms up again after the device goes.** `ShaderResults::answered`, which turns a tilt in 3-D, outlived the device, so a tilt hovered after the 30 s idle drop drew its card flat until a new device answered (hundreds of ms on lavapipe). When the device goes (dropped on idle, lost, unavailable), a node keeps `answered` only if it still holds its 3-D pixels (a tilt shown at rest, which keeps drawing them); any other warms up in 2-D again, as on its first hover. Clearing it while the device stays up was rejected: the frame then holds for the up device's answer, which takes one round trip, so the first hover's 2-D warm-up is not needed there.

No syntax was added. (Superseded 2026-10-10: decisions.md m4-owner-docs, "the owner accepts noise fields as `.wgsl` shaders".)

**2026-10-10 · m4-gpu-effects (review 2): the idle test proves its bloom.** `gpu_idle`'s `filter: bloom(8)` box was not checked, so the test would pass if its pass never ran or fell back. Its box is now #f5c2e7 beside a plain box of the same colour, and each cycle waits for the bloomed box to be brighter inside than the plain one by at least 24 (summed channels): the GPU's bloom screens the glow over the box (+78 measured on lavapipe), while the CPU's fallback glow is drawn under it and leaves the inside as plain.
## m4-interaction-finish

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: a layer surface's origin is arranged past our own exclusive zones, in global layout coordinates.** The wave-2 origin placed every layer surface over its whole output, so a tray panel anchored under a 36 px bar reported y = 0 and the app's menu opened over the bar; and origins were output-local, so a press on a second output sent a point on the first. `placement::arranged_area` now follows wlroots' `arrange_layers` (the order sway, labwc and river share; niri and Hyprland reserve the same way for the anchors a shell uses): exclusive surfaces first, layer by layer from `overlay` down, each reserving its zone plus its margin on its edge, a zone of -1 taking the whole output. Only our own surfaces are known; another program's bar is not (the protocol never says where a surface ended up), which the module doc records. Origins add the output's logical position, the space `SNI Activate(x, y)` and xdg positioners outside a popup use. Proved by `sway.rs::layer_surfaces_are_placed_past_our_zones_in_layout_coordinates` (grim reads the panel where its origin says, on two outputs, and back at y = 0 when the bar goes).

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: a tray action called by no input sends (0, 0).** The click point was a process-wide "last press" that every `tray.activate` read, so a timer or an `strand ipc` write activating an item sent the point of whatever was pressed minutes before. The point is now read when the action is built (`TrayCall`, the service's action type) and only when the calling thread runs a handler of an input event: the VM counts the handlers of `click`, `secondary`, `middle`, `scroll`, `activate`, `key`, `dismiss` and `drop` it runs (`vm::in_input_handler`), and the binary hands that probe to the tray at startup, so strand-services keeps no dependency on the compiler. (0, 0) is what the SNI spec's hosts send when they have no point; KDE's and waybar's items treat it as "place it yourself". A handler that awaits keeps its flag only for the synchronous part it runs before its first await, which is where a click's action is called. Proved by `tray.rs::the_tray_is_the_watcher_when_there_is_none` (an action outside an input scope sends `Activate at 0,0`) and `instantiate.rs::actions_know_whether_input_called_them`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: Hyprland is known by its globals, not by `HYPRLAND_INSTANCE_SIGNATURE`.** Two behaviours hang on Hyprland: it draws a layer surface stretched to its arranged box whatever its viewport (so a root's `scale` pose is painted there, decisions.md m4-surface-w2) and it blurs layer surfaces by its own rules (so the blur fallback's reason names `strand compositor-rules`). Neither is a protocol capability a client can query: no global says "honours `wp_viewport` on layer surfaces", and testing it would mean reading the screen back through screencopy at startup, a round trip and a permission for one bit. What can be fixed is where the answer comes from: the environment variable is inherited by anything started from a Hyprland session, so a nested sway or a `strand run` against another compositor's socket was treated as Hyprland and painted its scale. The registry is the connection's own: `caps::Offered::from_registry` marks `CompositorCaps::hyprland` when any `hyprland_*` global (Hyprland's own protocols, which every release since 0.3x offers: `hyprland_focus_grab_manager_v1`, `hyprland_surface_manager_v1`, ...) is listed. The matrix asserts it is set on Hyprland only (`surfaces_meet_the_live_compositor`), and the pose branches there read it. niri's lack of the alpha modifier is proven by `compositor_matrix.rs::a_posed_panel_looks_the_same_on_every_compositor`: `strand run` with a half-opacity, half-scale panel blends the desktop halfway to white in the half-size box and leaves the rest of the box alone on sway and labwc (delegated), niri (painted; the test fails if niri starts offering the modifier, so it keeps proving the repaint path) and Hyprland (opacity delegated, scale painted; CI).

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: password redaction remembers replaced values and redacts on fragments.** `Secrets` redacted only the inputs' current values once no password input was mounted, and forgot a value the moment its field emptied or its input went away, so a state that copied the password (`last = secret` before `secret = ""`) faulting after the unlock printed it, and a slice of it (`secret.slice(2, 6)`) or an upper-cased copy printed whenever no input was mounted. Now a value replaced by one it does not start is remembered (typing on adds nothing; a value inside a kept one is not kept twice), the newest four of them, as zeroized `Password`s; and a message still holding any 4-byte run of a known value, ASCII case ignored (a shorter password: the whole of it), is redacted whole. Four bytes is the trade: shorter runs would redact ordinary messages for any common pair of letters, longer would let a four-letter slice through; a false positive costs one log line's text, never behaviour. Keeping old values in memory outlives the lock (see the review paragraph below for the residual risk this records). Proved by `run/lock.rs::tests::a_password_fragment_is_never_logged` and the updated `password_values_are_redacted`, `a_fault_that_can_carry_values_is_redacted_whole_while_a_password_is_mounted`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: the supervisor requirement is documented with a unit and proven in the lock VM.** A process death while locked (main-thread panic, abort, SIGKILL) cannot be survived from inside the process, so architecture.md's residual risk stands: strand needs a supervisor. What was missing was proof that a supervisor is enough. `tests/lock.rs::a_supervised_strand_dying_while_locked_keeps_the_session_locked` runs strand under a restart loop that behaves as systemd's `Restart=on-failure` (restart on a non-zero exit or a signal, stop on a clean exit), kills it with SIGKILL while locked and with SIGABRT once it is back, and asserts from grim that the desktop never shows between each kill and the restarted strand's password field, that the test itself never starts strand, and that the right password unlocks and removes the marker. architecture.md now carries the user unit to use (`Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=0`). strand still ships no supervisor of its own: a second process watching the first adds a concept and a failure mode the session manager already covers.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: the blur ladder's inspector half is a `strand watch` notice per `blur` box.** The inspector proper (pick, identity, provenance) is M5's; what the blur ladder owes it is "the inspector says why" a `blur` fell back. The surface that exists today for per-node answers is `strand watch`, where runtime faults already carry `file:line:col`. So when the compositor is known not to blur, the host walks a surface's tree (nested popups left to their own surfaces) the first time its frame has blur regions, and again whenever their count changes, and sends logic each `blur` node with its kind and whether it draws the tint (`ToLogic::BlurFallback`); logic resolves each node through `Instance::origin` and makes one notice per box: `<file>:<line>:<col>: `box` in strand-Top asks for blur and draws its tint fallback (alpha + 0.15; `blur_fallback: none` turns it off): <why>` (or "draws no blur and no tint (`blur_fallback: none`)"), deduplicated and kept for watchers that subscribe later like every main-thread notice. `why` is `caps::blur_missing`, the reason without what the box draws, so a `blur_fallback: none` box is not told it draws a tint. The once-per-run warning stays as it was. The walk costs one tree pass per surface per change of its region count, only while the compositor does not blur; the region count itself is read each frame only then. M5's inspector reads the same notices.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: how Hyprland's blur mixes with Strand's.** CI's Hyprland 0.56.2 offers `ext-background-effect-v1` with blur (the matrix reports `background_effect: true` and 21 blur rectangles), so on current Hyprland the ladder's first rung applies: Strand sends each `blur` box's rounded region and draws no tint, exactly as on niri. The layer rules `strand compositor-rules` prints (`blur`, `blur_popups`, `ignore_alpha 0.5` per namespace) are a second, independent mechanism: Hyprland blurs behind every pixel of the matched surface whose alpha is above 0.5, whatever the region says. With both in place the blur is no longer limited to the `blur` boxes: an opaque-enough box without `blur` on the same surface gets blurred too, and the rounded shape no longer bounds it. Without the protocol (older Hyprland) the rules are the only blur, and Strand cannot tell whether they were pasted, so it keeps its tint (alpha + 0.15) on top: a box whose background is under 0.5 alpha can cross the rule's threshold only because of the tint, and a box above it ends 0.15 more opaque than on a protocol compositor (`blur_fallback: none` restores parity for such boxes). Decided: nothing is detected or switched automatically (no protocol says a layer rule applies); the printed rules now open with a comment saying they are only for a Hyprland without `ext-background-effect-v1` and what they do besides where it is offered, and the fallback reason names the rules only when the protocol is missing (it already did). Hyprland is known by its `hyprland_*` globals (see above), never by the environment.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: a carried drag shows the source as its icon, which supersedes m4-lists-w2's "no icon".** m4-lists-w2 left the icon out as a second render target for a cosmetic gain. It costs less than that: `Renderer::drag_image` flattens only the dragged node as a root with its lift and glide held and no animation stepped, rasterises its box into a CPU buffer of the box's size, once per drag, so there is no second live target and nothing redraws while the pointer moves (the compositor moves the icon). The icon is committed after `start_drag` on the icon surface with the grab point as its offset, because sway places an icon committed before the drag at the pointer with no offset. A fractional scale is drawn through the viewporter like other surfaces. Headless sway 1.9 leaves the last icon frame on screen after a drop until the pointer moves; the tests move it before checking the icon is gone instead of making up a commit for the compositor.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: what a drag gives other programs travels in `Prop::Drag`.** The surface manager needs the source's data when another program asks, and the value lives on the logic thread. Rather than a new cross-thread request, the compiler puts the exportable form beside the type name (`List [type, kind, text…]`) for the three things design.md says cross program boundaries (text, files, apps: a `text` value, a `Drop` record and an `App`); every other value keeps the bare `Keyword` and exports nothing. Readers go through `strand_scene::drag_type`/`drag_export`, so the encoding stays in one place. Files go out as `text/uri-list` (percent-encoded `file://` URIs) and also as their paths as text; an app as its `.desktop` file's URI when one is found under `XDG_DATA_HOME`/`XDG_DATA_DIRS`, and its id as text.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: another Strand process's drag arrives as a `Drop`.** A node id means nothing in another process, and design.md types drops from other programs as `Drop`. So a drag whose private type starts with `application/x-strand-node;` but names another process is read through what it exports, like any program's drag, and logged at debug as another Strand; with nothing exportable (a `Pin`) it carries nothing readable and is refused like any such offer. Sending typed Strand values across processes would add a serialisation format design.md does not have.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: `Prop::DropRows` replaces "make it a `list`".** m4-lists-w2 placed a plain container of non-draggable `for` items in its parent, because render could not tell `for` children from content. The compiler can: it sets `Prop::DropRows` on an `on drop` target with a direct `for` child, and render counts drops among a target's children when it is a `list`, holds `drag:` children, or has `DropRows`. This removes the need to tell users to wrap such a target in a `list`; a per-item target with its own content still has no `DropRows` and is placed among its parent's rows.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: review of the redaction: a floor, escapes and a recorded core-dump risk.** Three findings held. (1) Values under four bytes were remembered and matched whole, so one letter typed and cleared ("a", then "") blanked every later fault message holding an "a". Now a value under `FRAGMENT` (4) bytes is neither remembered nor matched: below four bytes a match cannot tell a password from ordinary text, and while its input is mounted a password of any length is still covered by the blanket rule (every value-carrying error replaced whole). (2) The fragment match was on raw bytes with ASCII case folding, so a password with a quote or backslash every three bytes, or a non-ASCII one upper-cased, printed through Debug or JSON escaping. The message is now compared in two forms, lower-cased with Unicode `to_lowercase`, as written and with `\\ \" \' \n \r \t \0 \u{..} \uXXXX` undone; letters whose upper case is longer (`ß`/`SS`) still escape it, which architecture.md's wording now allows. (3) The paragraph above said keeping old values widened nothing; after a submit the field is empty, so the remembered values are the one sure copy of up to four recent passwords for the rest of the process. Dropping them when the last password input unmounts would undo the change: while an input is mounted every value-carrying error is redacted whole anyway, so remembered values only ever act after the unmount. Decided: keep them, and record the residual risk in architecture.md ("The lock"): a core dump after an unlock can hold them; a session that cares sets `LimitCORE=0` on the unit. Making strand non-dumpable while it holds them (as `strand-auth` is) was rejected: it also takes away `/proc/<pid>` and ptrace from the user for the whole session, and the cores it prevents are the ones that diagnose the crash. Proved by `run/lock.rs::tests::a_password_fragment_is_never_logged` (a typo cleared redacts nothing; escaped, JSON-escaped and non-ASCII upper-cased copies are redacted).

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: review of the input flag, blur notices and the drag icon.** (1) The input-handler flag was entered again on every resume of a handler's coroutine, so `on click { await sleep(10s); tray.activate(item) }` read whatever point was current ten seconds later; the flag is now entered for the first stretch only, as the tray paragraph above already said (`instantiate.rs::actions_know_whether_input_called_them` clicks a handler that calls after an `await` and finds that call outside the input). (2) Blur notices were logged before their dedupe, once per box on every report, and a scrolling windowed `list` of `blur` items changes the region count and so reports often; and they were never retired. They now live apart from the other main-thread notices: logic keeps the last report per surface, logs and sends only notices not said before, and after a committed reload says them again from the kept reports for the nodes still mounted, at their new places, dropping a removed or moved box's old line (`run/tests.rs::each_blur_box_says_where_it_is_and_why_it_fell_back` reloads a moved and a removed box). The host still walks the surface's tree when the count changes: the walk is one pass over one surface, the same order of work as the flatten that just ran, and only while the compositor does not blur; tracking which boxes changed would need the walk anyway. A soft reload that swaps a `blur` box for a new node at an unchanged count is told at the next change of the count (a hard reload recreates the surfaces, which reports afresh). (3) The drag icon was rasterised into a surface-sized buffer (about 33 MB for a 4K panel) and cropped; `Raster::paint_window` now paints straight into a buffer of the box's size, rasterising each pixel by the same fixed-grid cell as a full paint (offscreen groups still drawn over the whole surface), so the icon stays bit-identical to the frame (`tests/drag.rs::the_drag_icon_is_the_source_drawn_alone_at_rest` compares it with the crop of the full frame, at an offset off the cell grid, and with its PNG).

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: the documented unit lifts systemd's start limit and backs off instead; the test's supervisor is that unit.** Review found that the unit architecture.md recommended (`Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=0`) kept systemd's default start limit, 5 starts in 10 s. A strand that died again soon after each restart while locked would get the unit marked failed after a few milliseconds, leaving the compositor's abandoned lock with no password field: the state the supervisor exists to end. The test's restart loop restarted forever, so it never showed this. The unit now sets `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` in `[Unit]`, and the brake moves to the restart delay: `RestartSec=100ms` growing over `RestartSteps=5` to `RestartMaxDelaySec=2s` (systemd 254; older systemd ignores those two keys and waits 100 ms each time). A strand that cannot start then costs one start every 2 s, not a busy loop, and the field is back at most 2 s after any death plus strand's start. The earlier reason for `RestartSec=0`, that 100 ms only delays the field, holds; but with no start limit a zero delay would spin forever. The test's supervisor is no longer a hand-written loop. `tests/lock.rs` reads the ini block from architecture.md itself (`Supervisor::documented`) and runs a shell loop with systemd's semantics: restart on failure, delays as `RestartSteps` interpolates them, and systemd's default start limit for what the unit leaves out. `the_supervisor_gives_up_as_systemd_does_unless_the_unit_lifts_the_limit` shows the loop giving up after five quick deaths under a unit with no limit, and checks that the documented unit has none. The lock-VM test now adds a crash loop of six deaths after its two rounds, each death as soon as the new strand runs. With `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` removed from the doc, that test fails with "start limit hit (5 starts in 10000 ms)" (run once by hand); with it, the session stays locked and the field returns.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: only press-caused handlers take the tray's click point.** Review said `key`, `activate` and `dismiss` handlers took the last mouse press's point. For `key` and `activate` that was already false: the host sets the point to (0, 0) on every key press (m4-surface-w2, `demo/host.rs::a_press_sets_the_tray_click_point`), so Return on a row or a key handler sends (0, 0), and a clicked row's `activate` should send the click's point, which it does. The real stale cases were the events no press of ours precedes: `dismiss` (a click away the compositor saw elsewhere, or focus loss), `scroll` (a wheel sets no point) and `drop` (the press started the drag on another node, or in another program). `vm::INPUT_EVENTS` is now `click`, `secondary`, `middle`, `activate` and `key`, so a tray action from the other three sends (0, 0). `instantiate.rs::only_press_caused_handlers_run_as_input` drives each event's handler.

**2026-10-10 · m4-interaction-finish: an exclusive zone that goes to none or moves places the others where it was.** `place_layer` placed the other surfaces on the output again only while the surface's zone was positive, and only on its current output. A live bar whose zone dropped to none (`height: 0`), or a surface that moved to another output, left the panels it had pushed down at origins that still took the old zone out. Their tray click points were then off by the bar's height. Each surface now remembers the monitor its zone was last counted on (`Surface::zone_on`). Placing it places the others on both the old and the new monitor when they differ, and a removal uses it too. A spec change places the configured surface at once instead of waiting for a configure. On sway the others got a configure anyway (sway configures every layer surface when it arranges), so the proof is on the fake, which configures a surface only when its own request changes, as a compositor may. The fake gained an opt-in `zxdg_output_manager_v1` (`SurfaceGlobals::xdg_output`) for the logical sizes the placing needs. `fake.rs::a_zone_that_drops_to_none_places_the_others_again` fails without the change. `sway.rs::layer_surfaces_are_placed_past_our_zones_in_layout_coordinates` gained the same steps on sway.

## m4-integration-w3

**2026-10-10 · m4-integration-w3: merge order and the offscreen pass that both effects branches rewrote.** The wave-3 integration merged laptop/m4-effects-finish first, then laptop/m4-gpu-effects, then laptop/m4-interaction-finish, as m4-gpu-effects asked (it edits S-effects' and S-runtime's files, recorded under its own section). A merge with `--no-ff` instead of a rebase keeps every stream's commits as they were reviewed. Both effects branches rewrote `Offscreen::prepare`'s group loop. effects-finish replaced the two passes (groups, then backdrops) with one pass ordered by where each group ends, so a backdrop inside an offscreen ancestor shows what is behind it. gpu-effects added a GPU group's read-back pixels and skipped GPU backdrops in the second pass. The merge keeps effects-finish's single ordered pass and puts gpu-effects' check at its top: a layer with `gpu` pixels takes them and is not drawn by the CPU, whether it is a filter group or a backdrop. Its pixels are then in `current` for the groups still open around it, as a CPU backdrop's are. `render_group` keeps gpu-effects' split (`rasterise` plus the filters, with the `bundled` flag) and applies effects-finish's `pixelate` mosaic before the CPU filters in both cases, so a GPU pass's input is mosaicked like the CPU blur and colour filters that already run before the bundled passes. `Layer::cell_local` needs both `mosaic` and `gpu` to be empty. The other conflicts were both sides added side by side (Layer fields, module lists, `Animator::jelly` next to `hold_still`/`release`, the host's per-surface maps, the features.md boxes, the decisions.md sections).

## m4-audit

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: the lock exit is ticked on a lock VM run of the integration tree, with the helper killed and deleted for real.** The exit stayed unticked with no reason after the merges, and its newest VM evidence (23 tests) predated the supervisor tests. m4-plan's tier C asks for "the helper OOM-killed or deleted"; `auth_crash` is an `abort()` inside the helper, which the client sees exactly as it sees a SIGKILL (end of file on the socket), so it stands in for the OOM kill as far as the client can tell, but two tests now do it for real: `pam_helper_killed_mid_check_shows_the_fallback` SIGKILLs the helper from outside once it has read the right password and hung (the new strand fault `auth_hold` keeps the default 30 s timeout under `auth_hang`, so the kill, not the timeout, ends the check; the test asserts the log says "the PAM helper stopped"), and `pam_helper_deleted_and_killed_keeps_the_session_locked_until_it_is_back` moves the helper binary away (renamed beside itself and put back by a guard, since the build directory is the host's) and kills the running one (from a copy of `strand` and its helper in the test's own directory, `Vm::installed`: CI's checkout belongs to the runner's user, so the guest's test user cannot rename anything in cargo's directory, which failed the first CI run of the test). The second found a real gap: the fallback's `strand-lock-auth` thread looked for the helper once, at its first check, so a helper deleted at that moment (a package upgrade mid-session) left the fallback unable to check any password for the rest of the lock session. It now looks again at each check until one is found; while none exists every password is refused (the session stays locked, which is the fail-closed reading). `scripts/lockvm/scenarios/all.sh` passed on 2026-10-10 at 70af44f: session_lock 7, strand_lock 27 of 27, faillock and pam.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: "no grim pixel shows the desktop" now means every pixel.** `Shot::desktop()` sampled one pixel of the test desktop's bar. The locked assertions (`until_locked`, `Vm::lock`, the no-locker and supervisor checks) now scan the whole shot for the bar's colour (`Shot::desktop_anywhere`, tolerance 3), so a lock covering part of an output fails. `Shot::desktop()` stays for "the desktop is back", where one pixel is enough.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: a GPU submission that never ends loses the device; a hung presented surface and a GPU stall while locked stay open for the owner.** naga bounds neither loops nor run time, and lavapipe has no driver reset, so a validated shader with an endless loop blocked the GPU thread forever in a readback's `poll(wait_indefinitely)`. Readbacks (passes and readback frames) now wait at most `HUNG_AFTER` (10 s, far past any real frame or pass, even lavapipe's on a loaded machine; a false alarm costs a CPU fallback): the pass answers `Failed` with its key (so render records it as failed and does not ask for it again), then `Lost` ("stopped answering") and `Exited`, and the thread leaks the device, renderer and swapchains rather than dropping them (a drop waits for the queue). `strand-gpu/tests/hang.rs` proves it on lavapipe. Not done, and recorded for the owner because each needs a design call: (1) a promoted `GpuPresent` surface does not read back, so a frame that hangs there is not caught by this deadline (the WSI's own acquire timeout is the only bound), and nothing exempts a lock's surfaces from promotion; (2) the lock's fault list (`run/lock.rs`, `reason()`) does not count a GPU stall as a fault, so a fullscreen clocked shader in a `lock` that hangs after its first frame on a promoted surface can freeze the lock's content without showing the fallback. The options are to never promote lock surfaces (their passes would read back, which this deadline covers) or to watch for a `Presented` that never comes while locked; either changes design.md's promotion rule or the lock's fault list.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: the GPU thread's caches are bounded.** `pass_reads` gained an entry per pass key (which includes the node's generation) and `Passes::pipelines` one per shader text, and neither was ever evicted while the device lived; a shown shader keeps the device alive, so remounted shader nodes and every hot-reload save grew them for the session. Both are now a small least-recently-used map (`strand-gpu/src/lru.rs`): 64 pipelines, far more than one screen draws, and 16 readback buffers keyed by size instead of pass key, since a pass's read finishes before the next pass is drawn and passes of one size can share a buffer. No interface change: render does not have to tell the thread which passes are gone.

Asserting `stalls == 0` on the real binary would make a functional assertion of how fast a debug logic thread answers on a shared runner, which CLAUDE.md forbids; the bench (`list_scroll_bench.rs`, a logic answering 50 ms late, `stalls == 0`) stays the assertion, and features.md's exit text now says which check covers what. The e2e test's bursts were flaky for another reason (run 38028157777: 3,800 of 96,976 pixels late): `still()` now also waits for the burst's own frame (`top` five rows on) and for nothing left on render's workers (the damage line's new `pending=` field, `Renderer::work_pending`: text layouts or image decodes in flight), before its quiet window.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: a lock with no way out is a check error.** A `lock` that draws, keeps its logic alive and never faults never shows the built-in field, so `lock { text clock.now }`, or a lock whose field submits through a handler that never calls `auth`, locked the session with only a TTY for a way out (and the restart marker locked again on the next start). design.md's "fails closed" promises a way out whenever something goes wrong; a config with no path to `auth.submit` is wrong before it runs, so the check refuses it: `check::lock_no_auth` is an error when nothing in the lock calls `auth.submit`, searched through its handlers and timers (every `if`/`match`/`for` branch, so a field revealed on a key press counts) and the components it shows. A `fn` cannot call an action (`check::impure`), so fns are not searched; a call outside the lock (a bar's handler) does not count, since only the lock has the keyboard while locked. It is judged only on a program with no other error, so a misspelt `auth.sumbit` gives its own error, not two. A runtime rule ("no password `input` mounted, show the fallback") was rejected: a lock that shows a clock and reveals its field on a key press is the common shape and would show the fallback over itself. The check does not prove the call is reached at run time (a handler on an element never shown, a branch never taken); it removes the config that has no call at all, which is the one design.md's wording cannot excuse. Tests: `checker.rs::a_lock_needs_a_reachable_auth_submit`, `negative/lock_no_auth.strand`; the unit tests' locks gained an `on key` submit.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: the run ends the GPU thread before the surface manager drops.** `run` declared the `GpuHost` before the `SurfaceManager`, so the manager (the display and every `wl_surface`) dropped first, and only then did the dropped `Gpu` send `Shutdown` to a detached thread that went on presenting and then dropped its swapchains on freed libwayland objects: the `RawHandles` safety contract ("the manager keeps the `wl_surface` and the connection alive until the GPU thread has answered `Release`") broke on every exit with a promoted surface. The exit path now calls `GpuHost::shutdown(GPU_SHUTDOWN)` first, which sends `Shutdown` to the running thread and any still ending and joins them, polling every 5 ms for at most 3 s. A thread that does not end in time (a hung driver: a readback gives up only after `HUNG_AFTER`, 10 s) keeps the connection: the manager is leaked with `mem::forget` rather than dropped under it, with a warning, since the process exits right after. Reordering the declarations alone was rejected: the dropped thread is detached, so it would still race the manager's drop. Test: `run/gpu.rs::host::tests::shutdown_joins_the_running_thread`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: an image worker that cannot start stops the shell, as the text worker does.** `Renderer::new` silently decoded inline when `ImageWorker::spawn` failed, so every decode and every `svg`/`lottie` file read ran on the render thread with jank as the only sign, against "file IO off the render thread" (m4-effects-finish). The shell and demo now build the renderer with `Renderer::try_new`, which returns the spawn error (reported like the text worker's `DemoError::Text`, as `DemoError::Io`); `Renderer::new` keeps inline decoding for tests and offline renders, where it is the intent. Refusing beats a warning: a thread that cannot be spawned means the process is out of threads or memory, and the shell starting half-working there hides it. Test: `renderer/tests.rs::an_image_worker_that_cannot_start_is_an_error_not_inline_decoding`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: the helper's test hooks are asked for by name; no plain test build has them.** m4-lock-w1 turned `faults` on in strand-auth's tests through a dev-dependency of the crate on itself. Cargo unifies that feature into the `strand-auth` binary it builds for the tests and copies the binary to `target/<profile>/strand-auth`, so `cargo test --release` (a packager's `check()` before `package()`) replaced the release helper with one honouring `STRAND_FAULT` and `STRAND_AUTH_PAM_CONFDIR`, the variable that swaps the PAM stack, at the path `cargo install` and the helper lookup use. `no_faults.rs` built into its own target dir and so never saw it. The self dev-dependency is gone; `tests/pam.rs` and `tests/no_faults.rs` have `required-features = ["faults"]` and run in their own CI step (`cargo test -p strand-auth --features faults`, in ci.yml's and ci.sh's test jobs), as strand's `[[test]] lock` already did. The new `tests/plain_build.rs` (built only without `faults`) checks that the helper a plain test build leaves behind holds none of the hooks' strings. `--all-features` still turns them on, by name, as any feature. A separate test-only helper binary was rejected: two helpers would let the tested one drift from the shipped one.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: the `strand` service is chosen only when libpam will read its file.** m4-lock-w1 chose `strand` whenever `/etc/pam.d/strand` or `/usr/lib/pam.d/strand` existed, on the premise that Linux-PAM reads the vendor directory. It does only when built with `--enable-vendordir` (openSUSE; not Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora or Arch). Elsewhere `pam_start("strand")` finds no file and uses `other`, usually `pam_deny`: every password comes back `PAM_AUTH_ERR`, a `Denied` verdict, so the right password is refused as wrong, no fallback shows (only `Failed` shows it) and no `login` warning is given — the lockout m4-owner chose `login` to avoid. The same held for an `/etc/pam.d/strand` the user cannot read (`exists()` true, libpam's open fails). Now the helper takes `strand` when `/etc/pam.d/strand` opens for reading, or when `/usr/lib/pam.d/strand` does and the system's own `login` service lives in `/usr/lib/pam.d` and not in `/etc/pam.d`: the fallback relies on `login` being found, so a `login` found only in the vendor directory proves this libpam reads it. Where `login` is in both or neither, the vendor file is not trusted and `login` is used, which authenticates either way (with the one-time warning). Asking libpam for its vendor directory has no API; reading the compiled path out of libpam's binary was rejected as more code in the security boundary for the same answer. Tests: `strand-auth/src/main.rs::tests` (`a_vendor_service_counts_only_where_libpam_reads_the_vendor_dir`, `an_unreadable_service_file_is_not_chosen`).

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: kept-cell values and notices go through the password redaction.** `Secrets` redacted runtime faults and write errors only. A cell kept over a changed default carries its value (`KeptCell.shown`, quoted text) into the `reload` and `notices` events' `kept_over_default`, its notice line (`<path>: kept "<value>" (default changed)`) into the log, the events and the overlay. A lock whose password state is not cleared on submit holds the accepted password after the unlock, and the deferred reload that lands then (or any later one changing that state's default) printed it. `Shell::apply` and `Shell::after_step` now pass every kept value and notice through `Secrets::redact` (`redact_kept`, `redact_lines`) before logging, streaming, queueing for later watchers or showing them, so they get the same current-and-remembered-value rule as fault messages. Not showing the values of cells bound to a password input at all was rejected: the binding is the compiler's knowledge, and a copy in another state would escape it, which value matching catches. **2026-10-10 · m4-audit: a shader's per-pixel private memory is capped at check time.** naga validates types and bindings but bounds memory only at its 1 GiB type limit, so `var<private> a: array<vec4<f32>, 50000000>;` passed the check and reached the GPU thread inside the strand process, where a driver that cannot give every invocation its copy (lavapipe's private arrays live on its threads' stacks) kills the process past any wgpu error scope; under a lock that leaves the session locked with no client. `check::shader` now sums the sizes (naga's `try_size`) of the private and workgroup globals and of every function's local variables, entry points included, and refuses more than `MAX_PIXEL_MEMORY` (16 KiB) per pixel. The sum over all functions over-counts what one call stack holds, which errs towards refusing; 16 KiB is about 1,000 `vec4`s, two orders of magnitude above the bundled effects (none declares an array) and well under what a driver thread's stack gives a SIMD batch. Override-sized arrays are sized by their default, as the pipeline will be. A shader that loops forever is the separate run-time limit (`HUNG_AFTER`). Test: `check/shaders.rs::tests::huge_private_and_local_arrays_are_refused`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit: correction — a lock's surfaces never reach the GPU thread, so a GPU stall cannot freeze a lock.** The entry above ("a GPU submission that never ends loses the device; …") said nothing exempts a lock's surfaces from promotion and offered "never promote lock surfaces" as an owner decision. The code already does the part that matters: `State::raw_handles` returns `None` for a `Role::Lock` surface and `State::hand_off` refuses one (strand-surface's `gpu_handoff.rs`, as architecture.md's "Surface hand-off" says: "none for a lock surface, which is never handed off"), so render's promotion of a lock surface reaches the GPU thread as an `Attach` without handles, which is readback mode. Its frames are bounded twice: render draws on the CPU whatever is still in flight past `GPU_WAIT` (8 ms), and a readback that never ends loses the device after `HUNG_AFTER` (10 s), after which the CPU draws everything. The lock's content, its password field included, keeps answering through a GPU stall; only a shader's pixels lag. So the lock's fault list needs no GPU-stall entry, and features.md's "lock fails closed under faults" holds without a carve-out. What stays open for the owner is the non-lock part of point (1): a hung frame on a presented surface that is not a lock is bounded only by the WSI's acquire timeout. Nothing tested the lock exemption, and the lock-vm job did not watch `gpu_handoff.rs`; `session_lock.rs::a_lock_surface_is_never_handed_to_the_gpu` (lock VM) now proves both refusals and that the manager keeps drawing the lock, and ci.yml's lock filter lists `gpu_handoff.rs`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 3): the `GPU_WAIT` bound behind the lock tick is tested.** features.md's lock exit said a lock's GPU work is "held at most `GPU_WAIT` per frame", but no test named `GPU_WAIT`: `gpu.rs` checked that a pass holds the frame, not for how long, nor that the frame paints when no reply ever comes. Two device-free tests in `strand-render/tests/gpu.rs` now deliver `Ready` by hand and never answer: a promoted readback surface (`a_readback_frame_the_gpu_never_answers_holds_at_most_gpu_wait`) and a `shader` pass on a CPU surface (`a_pass_the_gpu_never_answers_holds_at_most_gpu_wait`). Each asserts the hold ends no later than `GPU_WAIT` after the request (an instant taken after it, so no wall-clock margin is involved), that the frame is then wanted and painted by the CPU without the GPU's pixels, and that no later frame holds while the request stays unanswered. A uniform change alone wants no frame (nothing on screen changes until its pixels come), so the pass test changes the background in the same diff.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 3), deferred past M4: PAM messages during a check.** PAM's `TEXT_INFO` and `ERROR_MSG` reach the client only with the verdict, and the client gives the whole exchange 30 s. On a stack with `auth sufficient pam_fprintd.so` before `pam_unix` (pam_fprintd waits 30 s by default; some Arch and authselect fingerprint setups), the user never sees "Place your finger on the reader", the typed password never reaches `pam_unix`, the client times out and shows the fallback, whose own client meets the same wall. Fixing it needs a protocol message for interim text, the lock's field showing it, and a timeout that leaves room for interactive modules, which widens strand-auth's reviewed protocol and the lock's design (design.md names no such prompt) past M4's plan. Ubuntu's pam-auth-update sets `timeout=10` for pam_fprintd, so the password gets through there about 10 s late. Recorded in handoff.md's known limits; README's PAM section asks for a password-only stack until then.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 4): a spring that settles on a large frame does not promote.** m4-gpu-w2 assumed "the frame where its springs come to rest is small", but a node's damage is its whole old and new bounds whenever its signature changes at all (`flatten/hash.rs` hashes floats by their bits), and a spring's last step moves it by less than the settle tolerance: a slow spring opening a large panel for over 500 ms ended on a large frame with no spring in flight, which met "due, settled, large" and started the device as the animation ended (20–40 MB on hardware, lavapipe's libLLVM mapped for good: the cost RUN_GAP removed, by another path). `Promotion::frame` now remembers whether the last frame had springs in flight, and the frame on which they come to rest never promotes; the next large frame with none does (a shader clock running on). Demotion may still happen on that frame. Requiring one more large frame was preferred to treating any spring-tainted run as settled: an animation of springs and a clock together still promotes, one frame later. Test: `promote.rs::a_spring_that_settles_on_a_large_frame_is_not_promoted`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 4): a frame whose inline pass fails is answered once.** `draw_frame` answered `Failed { surface }` for a failing inline `Op::Pass` and then went on to present or read the frame back, so the frame also got `Presented` or `Pixels`: render demoted the surface for good (its `Failed` arm) with the GPU's pixels on screen, and the host's `Failed` arm cleared the frame in flight before its `Presented`. The frame now ends at the failed pass with the single `Failed` (its uploads and frees still submitted, so the image table stays true), and render draws it on the CPU, where the pass is then asked for on its own, fails with its key and is not asked again. Reporting the pass without a surface was rejected: an inline pass has no key for render to record it under. Test: `strand-gpu/tests/frames.rs::a_frame_whose_inline_pass_fails_is_answered_once`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 4): a hung frame records its inline passes as failed.** A promoted surface's frame that hangs (`HUNG_AFTER`) or panics is answered `Failed { surface, key: None }` (kind `Lost`): no pass key, so render's "not asked again while its base stays" never saw the `shader` that hung, and the demoted surface asked the next device (30 s later) for the same pass on its own, which hung and leaked a second device. Render now keeps each GPU surface's inline passes (id, key, base, from its last frame's wants) and, on such a `Failed`, records each as a failed pass result. All of the frame's passes are recorded, since the thread cannot tell which one hung; an innocent `shader` in the same frame draws nothing until its inputs change, the cheaper error than a second leaked device. A presented frame's hang is still owner item 2 (no deadline at all). Test: `strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::a_hung_frame_records_its_inline_passes_as_failed`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 4): `auth` verdicts outlive the store and carry their lock session.** Two gaps in the lock's auth path. (1) `auth.submit` from a lock that reads neither `auth.busy` nor `auth.failed` holds no reader, so the store stopped 5 s later (STOP_GRACE) and, mid-check, dropped its `check` task's result: a correct password's token and the client's 30 s timeout were both lost, the fallback never showed, and every retry did the same (the round-3 PAM deferral counts on "the client times out and shows the fallback"). The blocking task now hands its verdict to `UnlockSink`/`FailureSink` itself, so a stopped store still delivers; the store keeps only `busy`, `failed` and the warning. Holding a reader while a lock shows was the alternative; it would move lifecycle knowledge into the binary and still lose a check started before the lock was seen. (2) A check still in flight when a lock ended (the fallback's thread outlives `reset()`, and `auth`'s check outlives an unlock by the fallback) answered into the next lock: a stale token released it, a stale refusal re-enabled submitting during its own check. Each check now carries the lock session's generation (`LockScreen::session`, bumped by `reset()`): the fallback's checker is spawned with it, and `auth` reads it through the new `AuthConfig::session` (`SessionTag`) when a check begins and passes it to the sinks, whose signatures gain a `u64` (architecture.md, `auth`). Verdicts for an ended session are dropped. Tests: `strand-services/tests/auth.rs::auth_checks_through_the_helper_and_only_success_unlocks` (its stop-mid-check part), `strand/src/run/lock.rs::tests::a_verdict_from_an_ended_lock_is_dropped`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 4): shader files are read as a regular file of at most 1 MiB.** The loader (`reconcile/loader.rs`), the LSP and `strand check` read a `shader` path with an unbounded `read`: `shader "/dev/zero"` read until memory ran out and a FIFO blocked the compiler worker (ending hot reload), with the LSP rechecking at each keystroke. All three now go through `check::shaders::read_file` (a stat, then a bounded read), the rule `import()` files and the watcher already follow. 1 MiB is the import cap; a fragment shader is a few kilobytes. **2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 4): an SVG's `<image href>` reads no file.** Both SVG parse sites used `usvg::Options::default()`, whose string resolver reads any absolute path whole, unbounded and without a regular-file check, before looking at it (not behind the disabled `raster-images` feature; a `.svg` target is parsed again). A tray item's icon (any session-bus client), a notification's or a downloaded one could name `/dev/zero` and kill strand (on a lock, the restart marker brings it back), or a FIFO and block the image worker. Both now use `media::svg::options()`, whose string resolver returns nothing. Raster images inside an SVG are not drawn anyway, so only a nested SVG file is lost; a `data:` URL, bounded by the outer file, still resolves. **2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 4): Lottie files are bounded by their structure.** velato 0.12 draws a file as it stands (its own docs: "Repeater expansion is unbounded"; precomp reference cycles are not checked at import): a reference cycle (a precomp or matte that refers back to itself: a precomp instancing itself, a cycle of two, or a layer that is its own matte, `tp`) recursed until the stack overflowed, an abort no `catch_unwind` stops; precomps that fan out cost 2^N layers; a repeater of `1e18` copies cloned geometry until memory ran out. `lottie::load` now walks the model (memoised, checked for reference cycles) and refuses a file with a reference cycle, nesting past `MAX_NESTING` (32), or one frame's work past `MAX_WORK` (100,000 layer and shape instances, each precomp instance counted and each repeater multiplying what precedes it by its copies, an animated count at the most its keyframes and their easing hull reach). Refusing was preferred to clamping, which would draw something other than the file. Playback looping and time remapping are not reference cycles and are unaffected (owner, 2026-10-10: "reference cycle", not "loop"). Tests: `media/lottie.rs::tests::reference_cycles_are_refused`, `::looping_and_time_remapping_are_not_reference_cycles`, `::files_velato_cannot_draw_within_bounds_are_refused`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 4): `capped_clocks_paint_at_their_rate` maps wakes through the instant before each paint.** GitHub run 38057185680 failed it at 0569265 with "frame at 1.020833333s painted nothing". `host_loop` turns `next_wake()` back into presentation time with `due = last + (wake - at)`, and its first `at` was taken after `clocked()`'s T0 paint had returned, while the renderer reads its `now` at that paint's start: any delay between the two (a preemption on a loaded runner) made the first wake early by as much, and at 144 Hz over 4.2 ms painted refresh 3, between ticks. The first `at` is now the instant taken just before the T0 paint (`clocked_since`), like every later one, so the mapping no longer depends on scheduling; the capped case sleeps 6 ms after the T0 paint to prove it (the old mapping fails that way every time). No wall-clock bound is involved.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 5): a lock session begins when a lock is first asked for.** Round 4 tagged every `auth` verdict with the lock session its check began in, but the generation rose only when a lock ended (`LockScreen::reset`), so a check begun while no lock was active carried the next lock's tag. `auth.submit` outside a `lock` is legal (a popup's password prompt), so a correct password there, with PAM still answering (faildelay, faillock, up to the 30 s budget) when an idle or lid lock began, delivered a current token; `State::unlock` defers a token while the lock is pending and released the new lock as soon as the compositor said `locked`, with no password typed into it. `Guard::check` now also starts a new session (`LockScreen::begin`) when it first sees a lock asked for or held (`since` going from none to some), on the main-loop turn after the request and before the lock's surfaces can take input, so the lock's own checks carry the new tag. **2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 5): a drag export nobody reads is given up.** `send_request` registered a write source per `receive` of our drag's export, holding the pipe and a copy of the bytes, that ended only when every byte was written or a write failed. A receiver that asked and then held the pipe unread stopped it after one pipe buffer (about 64 KiB), and the source stayed for the life of the process, one more per repeated `receive`. Each write now has a time limit like the read side's: `DRAG_WRITE_TIMEOUT` (5 s) with no progress removes the source and closes the pipe; every write that makes progress moves the limit, so a slow reader that keeps reading is not cut off. Ending the drag (`end_ours`) does not remove pending writes: a receiver may call `finish` before it has read everything, and the limit already bounds what an ended drag can hold. Test: `strand-surface/tests/dnd.rs::an_unread_drag_export_is_given_up` (a 1 MiB export held unread: the receiver gets what fit, then the end of file; before the fix the write was never given up).

So a validated shader with an endless loop was asked of a new device, leaking one more, each time a bound uniform changed, the node resized, or its popup reopened (a new node) after the 30 s retry, without limit. Render now keeps, for the life of the process, the shader files (`ShaderResults::lost`, by content: path, text and uniform layout) whose pass, or whose promoted surface's frame, was answered `Failed` with kind `Lost` (a hang past `HUNG_AFTER` or a panic); flatten stops wanting their passes, so they are neither read back nor drawn inline, and the node draws nothing, with one warning naming the file. A reload that changes the text is new code and is tried again. A frame hang marks every user shader drawn inline in it, since any may be the culprit; bundled effects keep the base-keyed record (their code is Strand's). A driver reset (a panic under `poll`) counts as a loss too: the file that was running cost a device either way. Left open then for the owner (handoff.md item 7): each edit of a file that still loops forever is new code and can leak one more device, at most one per 30 s; capping that needed a rule design.md did not have. The owner later capped it at 3 lost devices per process (m4-owner-3). Tests: `strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::a_shader_file_that_hung_a_pass_is_never_run_again` (new uniforms, a new size and a new node not asked; an edit asked) and `a_hung_frame_records_its_inline_passes_as_failed` (now: new uniforms not asked; an edit asked).

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 7): `transition: crossfade` is gone; `none` names no mask.** The builtin schema's `SwapKind` offered `crossfade` (and the `transition:` prop's doc advertised it) since the schema became data (1ca21b8), but design.md lists only `transition: wipe(left) | disc | dissolve | pixelate`, no decision added a crossfade swap, and render's `transition::Kind::of` never drew one: `transition: crossfade` passed `strand check` and the LSP offered it, while the node snapped in, a removed one left no ghost, and on a `pages` it was worse, since `settle_pages` counted any `transition:` as a mask, turning off the directional slide with no mask to replace it (the same held for `transition: none`). Tests: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/checker.rs::transition_takes_the_design_masks_only` (the four masks and `none` check, `crossfade` is an error) and `crates/strand-render/tests/motion.rs::a_pages_with_transition_none_still_slides`, which fails without the `settle_pages` change.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 7): a helper that exited while idle is dropped, not signalled.** `Client::ensure_helper` sent every `try_wait` result but `Ok(None)` to `Helper::kill`, whose SIGSTOP, `/proc` descendant walk and group SIGKILL rest on the pid being "our child, not yet reaped". On `Ok(Some(_))` std had just reaped it with `waitpid`, so that pid (and its group's id, once the group is empty) could already name another process of the user. The check is now `Helper::running`: a live helper is kept, an exited one is only dropped (an idle helper runs no PAM conversation, so it left nothing to kill, and its orphans would have been re-parented anyway), and one whose state `try_wait` cannot read is still killed with its tree. `crates/strand-auth/src/client.rs::tests::an_exited_helper_is_dropped_without_signals` counts `kill` calls (a test-only counter): a zombie helper is reaped by the check with none.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 7): the fallback field ignores Return with nothing typed.** `LockFallback::key` turned Return or KP_Enter on an empty field into `Action::Submit(vec![])`, which `run/lock.rs` handed to the helper and PAM as the password "". With `pam_faillock` in the stack (authfail) each such Denied counts as a failed login, and Return is the key people press to wake a locked screen; the fallback shows exactly when something already went wrong, and unlike a config `lock` it has no setting to avoid this (swaylock's `--ignore-empty-password`). m4-lock-w2 left a faillock lockout to the stack owner for real attempts, and m4-lock-w1 already drops a submit while a check runs so nothing is double-counted; a keypress that typed nothing is not an attempt, so it is now `Action::None` and the field keeps its state (a refusal stays shown). An over-long field is still refused on Return without a check. A config `lock` decides for itself (`auth.submit` is called by its own handler); the client-level empty-password tests (`tests/protocol.rs`, `tests/pam.rs`, `vm_pam.rs`) are unchanged. `crates/strand-render/src/lock_fallback.rs::tests::return_on_an_empty_field_submits_nothing`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 7): a burst of file results is kept for its sources.** The image worker's `FileLoads` cleared every finished `svg`/`lottie` file result once 64 were held, meaning to drop results no source came back for (m4-effects-finish: "keeps at most 64 results that no source has taken"), but that also dropped results whose sources were still waiting: `files_arrived` marks every surface dirty and each new source sends its job in the same flatten, the worker runs them in microseconds while the loop takes milliseconds a frame, so more than 64 sources first drawn together had their results cleared and their files read and parsed again on the next flatten (converging, but repeating the IO each burst). Now `make_room` drops, once 64 are held, only results older than `FILE_RESULT_STALE` (1 s: a waiting source's surface flattens within a frame or so of the wake), and past 256 (`MAX_FILES_HELD`) the oldest, so the map stays bounded. `crates/strand-render/src/image.rs::tests::a_burst_of_file_results_is_kept_for_its_sources` (128 jobs finish before any is taken; each is taken without running again; fails with the old clear) and `::only_stale_or_surplus_file_results_are_dropped`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-audit (round 9): an offscreen group's cache entry pins the pixmaps its key names by address.** The offscreen group and backdrop keys hash an `image`'s pixmap, a GPU pass's result and a nested group's pixels by their `Arc` address (`flatten::hash_item`, `offscreen.rs`, `backdrop::key`), but an entry held only its output, and entries outlive their inputs (until the 4 MB budget or `IDLE_FREE`). Once an input was freed, glibc handed its block straight to the next pixmap of the same header size, so a new picture (album art, a GIF frame decoded again, each frame of a pointer-driven GPU pass inside a blurred parent) could hit an entry drawn from the old one, and stale pixels were drawn with no error. Each entry now keeps a `Weak` of every pixmap its key names (`offscreen::pins`): a `Weak` keeps the address allocated while the entry lives, so it cannot be reused, and a hit whose pin is dead (only a hash collision could do that) is a miss. This is backend.rs's `Uploads::id` guard in its cheapest form: a few dozen bytes per pinned header, no pixel buffer kept. Hashing content instead was rejected as a per-frame cost over every image's pixels. `offscreen::tests::a_freed_images_address_never_hits_a_stale_group` caches a blurred red image, frees it and makes a blue one at once: without the pins the blue pixmap took the red one's address (the test fails there); with them it never does, and the group is drawn again, blue.

Four changes, none of them changing a colour or a verdict: `material::from_seed` resolves all 49 roles through one shared `SchemeResolver` (`one_resolver_gives_every_getters_colour`) and keeps each thread's last eight palettes, keyed by 8-bit seed, variant, mode and clamped contrast, replaced oldest first (`a_kept_palette_is_the_one_solved_again`); `Motion::probe(at)` reads position, velocity and settling from one curve evaluation (`a_probe_is_peek_velocity_and_settled_at_once`); the contrast guard's memo hashes its colour-bit keys by word; and the swap's contrast play-through works each moment's root values out once for both passes and for the speed and settling checks, still charging `CHECK_WORK` exactly as before (`the_play_through_probes_each_moment_once_and_exactly`). ## m4-owner-3

The owner's remaining M4 decisions of 2026-10-10, integrated on `laptop/m4-close` from `laptop/m4-close-gpucap`, `laptop/m4-close-helper` and `laptop/m4-close-blend`. They answer handoff.md's open items 2, 6, 7, 8 and 9; code comments that cite m4-close-gpucap, m4-close-helper or m4-close-blend point here.

**2026-10-10 · m4-owner-3 (m4-close-gpucap, owner decision; closes handoff.md item 7): after 3 lost GPU devices in one strand process, the GPU stays off until strand restarts.** Before this, a lost device was asked for again every 30 s while demand lasted. Because the m4-audit round 5 rule only stops a shader file that lost a device until its file changes, editing a looping shader again and again could lose devices without limit. Only `GpuReply::Lost` counts toward the cap (`promote::LOST_CAP = 3`): a hang past `HUNG_AFTER`, a reset, or a panic the GPU thread answers as Lost. A device that fails to start (Unavailable) does not count, and it is still retried every 30 s. The count lives in the renderer's `Device`, not in a global. A strand process has one renderer, which survives reloads, so the count covers the whole process, and tests in the same binary do not share it. Once the GPU is off: no device is asked for again (every request path goes through `GpuState::want`), nothing is promoted, the host never starts a `Gpu`, and bundled effects use their CPU versions. A `shader` node draws nothing, and the CPU draws everything else. The status becomes `Unavailable { reason: GPU_OFF }` ("the GPU was turned off after 3 lost devices; restarting strand brings it back") and stays there. The host sends it whatever the frame shows (`Renderer::gpu_off()`, `StatusForward::check`), and logic turns it into one WARN and one `strand watch` notice. The cap only removes GPU paths, and lock surfaces never reach the GPU thread, so it cannot make the lock fail open. Tests: `crates/strand-render/src/promote.rs::tests::the_third_lost_device_turns_the_gpu_off` (no request even a day later); `crates/strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::the_gpu_is_off_after_three_lost_devices`, which runs the full retry-and-lose cycle with a zero retry wait (`set_gpu_retry`) so that only the cap keeps the device off, then checks no pass, no promotion, CPU pixels and ref `gpu_off.png`; and `crates/strand/src/run/gpu.rs::status_tests::the_gpu_turned_off_is_told_once_whatever_the_frame_shows`. design.md's Paint paragraph and architecture.md's GPU bullets record the cap and `Renderer::gpu_off`. `.text` on the branch alone: CPU-only unchanged, default +64 B.

**2026-10-10 · m4-owner-3 (m4-close-helper, owner decision; closes handoff.md item 9): a missing `strand-auth` keeps warn-and-lock, and `strand check` reports it.** A missing helper does not change `strand run`. It still warns at start, in its log and to `strand watch`, and still locks when asked: a lock that does not lock fails open, so it fails closed. But `strand check` now reports `check::lock_no_helper` as an error when the config has a `lock` and `strand_auth::default_helper` (the same lookup run uses: beside the executable, then /usr/libexec/strand, /usr/lib/strand, /usr/local/libexec/strand) finds no helper. The error names `cargo install --locked --path crates/strand-auth` and those folders. It is a check-time diagnostic in the binary's check.rs, not a compiler rule: whether a helper is installed is a fact about the machine, not the program, so the LSP and reload do not report it, and the lookup runs only when the config has a `lock`. It is one error, labelled at the first `lock`, and it covers the whole config: checking any one file of the config reports it, unlike problems that belong to other files, because the fault is the install's and a user who checks only the file they edit must still hear it (m4-close-helper review). The public `check_dir` always passes `default_helper`; tests pass their own lookup, and `check_dir_looks_up_the_real_helper` pins the public path to the real one. The README says a config with a `lock` needs both binaries: two `--path` installs (cargo takes one `--path` per install), or the single `cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/jakeb-grant/strand strand strand-auth`. Tests: `crates/strand/src/check.rs::tests::a_lock_without_the_helper_is_an_error`, `::check_dir_looks_up_the_real_helper`.

**2026-10-10 · m4-owner-3 (owner decision; closes handoff.md item 2): a hung frame on a presented (`GpuPresent`) surface stays bounded by the WSI's acquire timeout.** The owner accepts the bound as it is. It never reaches the lock: a lock surface is never lent or handed to the GPU thread (`crates/strand-surface/tests/session_lock.rs::a_lock_surface_is_never_handed_to_the_gpu`), each lock frame holds for the GPU at most `GPU_WAIT` (8 ms) before the CPU draws it (`crates/strand-render/tests/gpu.rs::a_readback_frame_the_gpu_never_answers_holds_at_most_gpu_wait`), a readback that never ends loses the device after `HUNG_AFTER` (10 s), and three lost devices turn the GPU off (above). No code changes.

The owner moved the presented measurement to M5: features.md's M5 list has an unticked box for it. Nothing changes in code until it is worked.

**2026-10-10 · m4-owner-3 (m4-close-blend, owner decision; closes handoff.md item 8): the 4K crossfade's blend is made cheaper, and it stays reported, not gated.** The owner chose "make the blend cheaper" and asked to keep item 8 open only if a 4K fade frame still costs more than a 60 Hz frame (16.7 ms) on the laptop. The crossfade's per-pixel blend now works in u16 lanes, which is exactly the old u32 formula (`255 * 256 + 128` fits in 16 bits), and a snapshot copies each row from its stride into fresh capacity instead of growing a reused buffer. No colour changes: `crates/strand-render/src/renderer/swap.rs::tests::the_blend_matches_the_wide_formula_exactly` checks the new blend against the wide formula, and `crates/strand-render/tests/theme_swap.rs::a_crossfade_on_a_padded_buffer_matches_the_packed_one` checks a padded wl_shm buffer (stride `w * 4 + 12`) row for row against the packed one, padding untouched. On the laptop (`theme_swap_bench.rs::a_4k_surface_crossfade_is_measured`, timing profile) a 3840×2160 fade's blend went from 10.5–20.5 ms to 3.6–5.1 ms per frame and its swap work from 4.2–6.0 ms to 2.9–4.4 ms, most of it the snapshot's 33 MB copy; the shell's three surfaces blend in 0.45–0.82 ms (was 1.8–3.5 ms; held to 4 ms). On the merged tree, run alone, the 4K case measured 3.38–3.42 ms of blending per fade frame (p95 4.0 ms) and 2.53–2.79 ms of swap work (medians, buffers of age 1 and 2). A 4K fade frame now fits well inside 16.7 ms, so item 8 is resolved; the 4K case keeps no gate, since GitHub's runners leave no headroom for one at 5 ms of swap work. `.text` on the branch alone: CPU-only +192 B, default +128 B.

Out of scope for M5 and for the freeze.
