**2026-10-11 · m5-inspect (wave 3): the outline and the flash are display items, and what they draw.** The shell's only inspector UI (m5-owner Q9) is drawn by appending items to a frame's display list after flattening (`strand-render/src/inspect/overlay.rs`), so the CPU raster and the GPU's lowering draw it with no code of their own, and a `GpuPresent` surface shows it as a CPU one does (`tests/inspect.rs::a_presented_surface_shows_the_outline_and_the_flash`, lavapipe). The outline is a 2 px ring (`#2196f3`) inside the node's drawn box, following its corner radii, under its transform and its ancestors' clip, so a scrolled-away or clipped node is outlined only where it shows; the box is the hit box without `hit: grow(n)`, which `HitBox` now records (`grow`), since the grown box is not what the user sees. The flash tints each frame's own content damage (`#00e676`, alpha 0.45 fading linearly to 0 over 300 ms, quantised to 1/255 so a fade step that changes no pixel repaints nothing); the overlay's own repaints (the fading tints, the outline moving) are never tinted, which is the "no feedback" rule, and a frame without a presentation time (an offline paint at time zero) tints nothing, so offline PNG tests show the outline only where they ask for it. A frame repaints the overlay's previous area and its new one only when what it draws changes (a signature of the items), so an idle outline costs nothing per frame. Off, the flash keeps no map (`HashMap::new()` allocates nothing) and wants no frames (`flash_off_wakes_nothing`). A lock surface is never picked, outlined or flashed, whatever the highlight names and whether the flash is on (`a_lock_surface_is_never_picked_or_outlined`): a lock's repaints (a typed character's) are drawn as they are.

**2026-10-11 · m5-inspect (wave 3): pick mode, and who owns what.** Pick mode lives on main: `Router::set_picking(true)` makes the router pass no pointer event to a handler (it still tracks the pointer, and turning picking on ends hovers, presses and drags as a leave would, so no handler is left mid-gesture), and the host feeds those events to `Renderer::pick_input`, which outlines the node under the pointer on whichever surface it is over and answers a left press with the surface and node. A pick does not end pick mode: each click sends a `picked` event, and pick mode ends when the client asks (`inspect.pick{on:false}`), disconnects, or another client takes it (the first hears `pick_ended`), when the surface it is over unmaps, or when a lock starts (main ends it and the outline, and logic tells the client `pick_ended`); `inspect.pick{on:true}` is refused while a lock is shown. `inspect.highlight` and `inspect.flash` belong to the client that set them the same way and end on its disconnect, so a crashed terminal leaves nothing drawn. All three are socket requests only: the D-Bus front end's methods are the CLI's, and a bus caller has no connection to own them or to hear events on (they answer as unknown there). `strand-dev inspect` turns pick mode off after one pick, so the shell has its input back while the user reads the pane (`p` picks again); it stays in line mode rather than raw mode (no termios dependency), so Escape is Escape then Enter, and Ctrl-C ends the client, whose disconnect ends pick mode. architecture.md's "Escape or Ctrl-C there sends `inspect.pick{on:false}`" is amended to say this. An `inspect.pick` answer means logic has told main, not that main has turned it on; the sway tests follow it with a `report` (a snapshot from main on the same channel) before clicking, and a user's click is never that fast.

**2026-10-11 · m5-inspect (wave 3): write-back's rules as built.** Write-back (m5-owner Q11) is `strand_dev::inspect::write`. A prop edit finds the innermost element whose span holds the node's `origin` span and the prop written directly in its block (not in a `when`, not the surface's); a token edit finds the entry in the `tokens <name>` block or the component's `tokens { }` that the token's provenance step names as its origin (`tokens base`, `component Toast`), and refuses any other origin (the built-in theme's `base`, a palette, an overlay: none is a literal in a file of the user's). The value replaced and the value written must each parse as one literal: a number (with its unit, or negated), a string, a colour or a boolean; a binding, an expression or a token reference is refused, since replacing it would change what the value means. The file must still hash (BLAKE3) to the hash in the running shell's answer; to make that possible for a token's file, `inspect.node` and `inspect.dump` now hash every file the program was compiled from, not only the files the nodes come from (`every_compiled_file_is_hashed_in_an_answer`). The write follows symlinks (the target is edited, the link stays), writes a temporary file beside the target with its mode, flushes it, and renames it over the target only if the target is still the same inode holding the hashed bytes, then flushes the directory; an editor's save renamed into place meanwhile is refused even if it saved the same bytes. A small window remains between that last check and the rename (POSIX has no compare-and-rename); closing it would need a lock the editors do not take. A target without write permission, or in a directory that cannot be written (a Nix store file), is refused with the reason and an offer to open it in `$EDITOR`, which the client asks about. The shell then reloads the saved file as it does any save, keeping state (`tests/m5/inspect.rs::a_written_back_edit_reloads_and_keeps_state`).

The end-to-end write-back test (`tests/m5/inspect.rs`) compiles strand-dev's `inspect/write.rs` by `#[path]` rather than depending on strand-dev: a strand-dev dev-dependency turned strand-compiler's `shaders` feature (naga) on in the CPU-only binary that budgets.rs builds as a test target, which measured +1,063 KB `.text` before it was taken out; strand's dev-dependencies gain only `blake3` 1.8.7 (strand-watch's and strand-theme's, with their features). strand-dev's dependencies gain `strand-core` (moved from its dev-dependencies) and `blake3` 1.8.7 (strand-compiler's version).

**2026-10-12 · m5-inspect (wave 3): size, over the 20 KB line, and why.** Measured with `scripts/size-report.sh` in the container, base `laptop/m5-w3` at `aa3053c` (CPU-only 18,555,351 B, GPU 22,473,111 B, the integrator's wave-2 figures exactly): CPU-only **18,590,359 B (+35,008 B)** against the 20 KB line; GPU **22,507,287 B (+34,176 B)** against 20 KB plus the GPU-only 19,520 B (39,520 B: within). Both stay under the gates (`TEXT_GATE_CPU` 18,874,368 B, `TEXT_GATE_GPU` 22,806,528 B; `budgets.rs::the_release_binary_code_stays_within_its_gate` passes, as does the design bar's memory budget, `the_design_bar_on_the_real_services_keeps_the_budget`, so the never-opened inspector costs no PSS a gate sees). Where the CPU-only bytes went, by symbol against the base: the overlay inlined into `Renderer::paint_frame` +9.3 KB; the input path moved, not grew (LTO now inlines `Router::route` into `Host::input`: `Host::input` +18.0 KB, `Router::route` −12.3 KB, `send_input` −7.4 KB, `click_away_from_others` +1.3 KB out of line, net about −0.2 KB); main's channel source matching four `ToMain` kinds (calloop's dispatcher +3.5 KB, `Sender<ToMain>::send` +3.8 KB now out of line); `Host::set_picking` 2.6 KB, `pick_input`, `set_hover`, `set_highlight` 2.1 KB; `Instance::identity` +3.9 KB out of line (it was inlined into `node_json`, −3.6 KB), `every_file` 1.1 KB; the four request arms, `picked`, `lock_guard` and the inspector's bookkeeping in `logic`/`Shell::handle` about 7.5 KB; the overlay's per-surface map (hashbrown 1.8 KB) and `RoundedRect`'s path (kurbo 1.7 KB); `report_request` −3.5 KB (LTO split it differently). The line was set for pick, outline and flash in render; the binary half (the IPC arms, main's dispatch, the host's pick forwarding, the lock guard) has no line of its own in m5-plan beyond the wave-2 arms' 3 KB, and is about 18 KB of the total. Nothing here runs per frame unless the inspector is on (`Inspect::idle` returns before any overlay work), and the input path is not slower (the router's early return while picking is one branch). Cuts considered: answering `inspect.pick` and the outline through one `ToMain::Inspect(..)` kind instead of three (about −1 KB of dispatch, not taken: architecture.md fixes the three messages); drawing the outline square instead of rounded (−1.7 KB, not taken: a rounded node outlined square misreports its shape). Under the owner's speed-first ruling the overrun is recorded rather than cut; the ledger charge (+35,008 B CPU-only, +34,176 B GPU) is the integrator's to enter.

**2026-10-12 · m5-inspect (wave 3): review round 1's fixes.** (1, inspect-r1-1) Write-back's `innermost_at` searched only an element's block, a surface's or component's body, `when`, `for` and an `if`'s `then` and plain `else`; an element in an `else if` branch or a `match` arm was never a candidate, so `set width` wrote the enclosing element's `width`. It now walks the whole `else if` chain and every arm (`ArmBody::Block` and `Single`) (`crates/strand-dev/tests/inspect.rs::a_node_in_else_if_or_a_match_arm_is_its_own_element`). (2, inspect-r1-2) `ToMain::PickMode(bool)` becomes `PickMode { on, seq }` and `PickEvent::Ended` becomes `Ended { seq }`: logic numbers every `PickMode` it sends; main keeps the last one's `seq` (`Forward::pick_seq`) and sends it back on an end; logic ignores an `Ended` whose `seq` is not its last. The socket and the `ToLogic` channel are separate sources, so main's end (a popup unmapped) could be read after a newer `inspect.pick{on:true}` had turned pick mode on again: logic dropped the new owner, told it `pick_ended`, and no `PickMode(false)` ever came, so main held every pointer event from the handlers. Tagging both messages was chosen over re-sending main the owner's state on every `Ended`, which would turn pick mode on again after a lock's end (`run/tests.rs::the_inspector_belongs_to_its_client`, `demo/host.rs::tests::pick_mode_follows_the_pointer_onto_a_popup_and_ends_with_it`). This is an interface change inside `strand` (the main↔logic messages), recorded in architecture.md's "M5 interfaces" with the reason. (3, inspect-r1-3) `strand-dev inspect`'s session is now `inspect::drive(path, Terminal { read_line, out, editor })`, which `run` calls with stdin, stdout and `$EDITOR`; a test drives it line by line against a scripted shell on a Unix socket: a pick ends pick mode before the pane is asked for and outlined, `r` resets and shows again, `f` toggles, events arriving while an answer is awaited are handled after it (`pick_ended`, after which Enter sends nothing; a `picked`), `e` opens the origin, and the `$EDITOR` offer takes the next line (`crates/strand-dev/tests/inspect_session.rs`). (4, inspect-r1-4) While picking, the router also holds another program's drag: `DragEnter`, `DragMotion` and `DragDrop` find no drop target (the offer is forgotten, so the surface manager declines it) and run no `on drop`; turning pick mode on forgets an offer already over a target (`crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::pick_mode_holds_drops_from_the_handlers`). (5, inspect-r1-5) `inspect.highlight` of a node is refused while a lock is shown, as `inspect.pick` is. An outline asked before the lock is no longer dropped silently: logic keeps its owner and node across the lock (main clears the outline while it lasts) and sends main `Highlight` again when the lock ends (or `None` if the node is gone), so the client is never left believing a node is outlined when nothing is. Restoring was chosen over a new `highlight_ended` event: it adds no concept to the protocol, and the client's request simply stays in force (`run/tests.rs::the_outline_hides_while_locked_and_returns_after`). (6, inspect-r1-6) The `$EDITOR` offer after a refused write-back opens the file at the edited value's own line (from the edit's span), so a token refusal lands on the token's definition, not the node's origin line (`inspect_session.rs`). (7, inspect-r1-7) The pick following the pointer onto a popup is tested through the host: the popup's node is outlined and picked with the popup's surface, the popup closing while the pointer is on the bar leaves pick mode on, and closing under the pointer ends it with the right `seq` (`demo/host.rs::tests::pick_mode_follows_the_pointer_onto_a_popup_and_ends_with_it`). (8, inspect-r1-8) architecture.md's thread table no longer says the three inspector commands are not served, and 0b's sentence says they are served on the socket and answered as unknown on D-Bus (`not_served`).

**2026-10-12 · m5-inspect (wave 3): review round 2's fixes.** (1, inspect-r2-1) A `pick_ended` that `strand-dev inspect`'s client set aside while it waited for `inspect.pick`'s answer ended pick mode on its side after the answer turned it on, though logic answers `inspect.pick` in the same pass that acts on it, so a `pick_ended` before the `ok` always ends the mode before; the client then held main in pick mode with Enter sending nothing. `Session::pick` now forgets the `pick_ended` events kept so far once the answer is in (`Connection::forget`); a refused `inspect.pick` keeps them, since the state did not change. The session test asserted the wrong reading with an ordering a real shell never sends; it now proves both: a `pick_ended` before the `ok` leaves pick mode on (Enter ends it), one after ends it (Enter sends nothing) (`crates/strand-dev/tests/inspect_session.rs::the_terminal_session_picks_shows_resets_flashes_and_offers_editor`). (2, inspect-r2-2) `PickEvent::Picked` gains `seq`, the `PickMode` main was in, and logic drops a pick whose `seq` is not its last, as it does an `Ended` (r1-2): a click main picked in one client's pick mode, read after another client's `inspect.pick` from the socket, reached the new owner as its own pick (`crates/strand/src/run/tests.rs::the_inspector_belongs_to_its_client`); architecture.md's `PickMode` paragraph says so. A pick from the same client's earlier mode, overtaken by its own `p`, is dropped too: the user clicks again. (3, inspect-r2-4) While picking, another program's drag kept no offer, and outside pick mode motion recomputes a target only for an offer it has, so a drag that entered during pick mode (strand-dev's one pick ends it) found no target until it left the surface and entered again. Pick mode now keeps the offer's surface with no target (on enter, motion and `set_picking(true)`), so the next motion after pick mode ends finds the target; a drop while picking still forgets it (`crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::a_drag_entered_while_picking_finds_its_target_after`, `::pick_mode_holds_drops_from_the_handlers` unchanged). (4, inspect-r2-5) Answers carry no id and come in order, so one that came after its request timed out (`WAIT`, 5 s; `inspect.node` waits on main's layout hop with no timeout on logic's side) was read as the next request's and shifted every later one. The connection counts answers still owed to timed-out requests and discards each when it comes, in `ask` and in `event` (`inspect_session.rs::a_late_answer_is_not_the_next_requests`); reconnecting was the other choice, but it would end pick mode, the outline and the flash, which belong to the connection. (5, inspect-r2-6) Deferred and recorded: design.md's Paint paragraph says a `shader` node that draws nothing (no device, or the GPU off after 3 lost devices) is explained by "the inspector and `strand report`"; `strand report` gives the GPU's status and reason (S-tools), but the inspector's node pane does not say why such a node draws nothing. m5-plan listed these "says why" lines in the node pane as optional, paid from the reserve, which wave 3 had already spent, so they were left out; the blur and tint half of design.md's "the inspector says why" is met by `strand watch` notices (m4-interaction-finish). features.md's Inspector box now records the deferral, and the integrator's handoff.md should carry it under deferred work (a pane line from main's GPU status on `inspect.node`'s layout hop, 2–5 KB by m5-plan's estimate).

**2026-10-12 · m5-inspect (wave 3): review round 3's fixes.** (1, inspect-r3-1) Round 2's item 4 rested on a false premise: answers carry no id, and they do not come in request order. Logic answers `inspect.pick`, `inspect.flash`, `inspect.highlight` and `reset` (and an `inspect.node` refusal) as it reads them, but it answers an `inspect.node` pane only once main's `SnapshotKind::Layout` hop is back (`inspector.nodes`, `layout_answered`). So while main stalls, the next request's answer comes before the late pane, and discarding "the next answer" threw away the real one: a flash that the shell had turned on was left off on the client, and a refused `p` or `r` read the late pane's `ok` as success. Matching answers by shape cannot fix this. A node refusal and another request's refusal look alike, and a pane whose snapshot main never answers would leave a count that is never paid. So a request that times out now starts a new connection (`Connection::ask`, `restart`). The old connection's late answers and events go with it, and the shell ends that connection's pick mode, outline and flash when it notices the hang-up. Its owner checks (`inspector_clients_gone`) leave alone whatever the new connection has taken over by then. Round 2 turned down reconnecting because it ends that state, so the session now asks for it again on the new connection (`Session::restore`): flashing if it was on, the outline on the node shown, and pick mode if it was on. A request that turns pick mode or flashing off counts as off on the client before it is sent, so a timeout never turns either back on. The pane is now stored before its outline is asked for, so a restore outlines the new node. If a restore request times out too, the rest stays off and the session says so. A failed write, or a socket that cannot be reached again, closes the connection and ends the client. The round-2 test sent the late pane before the flash's answer, the reverse of a real shell's order. It now sends the real order on two connections, a refused pick read as a refusal, and a reconnect that fails (`crates/strand-dev/tests/inspect_session.rs::a_late_answer_is_not_the_next_requests`). A session test times out `inspect.node` with flashing on and then shows that `f` turns flashing off with one press and that a refused `p` prints the refusal, not "picking" (`::a_timeout_starts_a_new_connection_and_keeps_the_session`, 5 s for the client's `WAIT`). Both fail on round 2's client. No protocol change: an id echoed in answers would be the cleaner fix, but it is a strand-core interface change, and the inspector is its only client that times out. (2, inspect-r3-2) Write-back decided "read-only" by `Permissions::readonly()`, which on Unix is only "no write bit at all". The rename that writes the edit needs write access to the directory only, so a `root:root 0644` file in the user's own config directory was replaced by a new file owned by the user. `write::replaceable` now refuses (with the `$EDITOR` offer, since `$EDITOR` writes in place or says why it cannot) when the file has no write bit, when another user owns it (the rewritten file would be ours, so root editing a user's file is refused too), when `access(W_OK)` fails, and when the file has a POSIX access ACL (`system.posix_acl_access`), which a new inode would not carry. The file's group is kept: the temporary file is given the original's gid when it was created with another one (the owner may chown to a group they are in), or the edit is refused. strand-dev takes `rustix` 1.1.5 (`fs`, `process`), the workspace's version (`crates/strand-dev/src/inspect/write.rs::tests::a_file_another_user_owns_is_not_replaceable`, which takes the uid as a parameter because the container cannot make a file another user owns; `crates/strand-dev/tests/inspect.rs::a_read_only_target_is_refused_offering_editor` unchanged). The group and ACL paths have no test: the container's user has one group and no `setfacl`.

## m5-ipc

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: what `get` answers.** `strand get <path>` reads what `set` writes: an exported `state`/`let` (or a field of one), a settings field, or a token with the token spelling (`'$accent'`, m5-owner Q10), the overlay included. The answer is `{"ok": true, "value", "text", "layer"}`: `value` is JSON where JSON has the kind (bool, plain number, text, list, record as an object) and otherwise the text `set` reads back (`"8px"`, `"#ff8800"`), so a script can hand it back to `set`; `text` is what the CLI prints; `layer` is a settings field's layer (`overlay`, `file`, `default`), a token's recorded origin (`overlay` while overlaid, else its tier), or null. `--json` prints the answer line. One shape for every path, rather than a per-kind answer, keeps one concept for scripts.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: `strand clear` and what it clears.** `strand clear '$accent'` / IPC `clear{path}` drops a token overlay; `strand clear file.settings.field` drops a settings field's runtime overlay (the notice's `[clear]` from the command line). Clearing what has no overlay answers `{"ok": true, "cleared": false}`, not an error, so a script can clear unconditionally; a path that cannot have an overlay (an exported state) is refused, naming the two kinds that can. *Amended 2026-10-11 (integrator decision d):* a token name the build does not have is refused with the closest name, word for word as `set` refuses it (`no token `$acent`; did you mean `$accent`?`), so a misspelled `clear` cannot answer `cleared: false` while the real overlay stays; `cleared: false` is for a known token without an overlay, and an overlay of a token the current build no longer defines is still cleared.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: `toggle` and `call`'s scope.** `toggle` flips a bool that `set` can write (an exported state or a settings field) and refuses any other type naming it ("`bar.label` is a text, not a bool"); service rw fields are not toggled in wave 1 (none of the builtin ones is a bool a user flips from a script that `set` does not already cover). `call` runs service-level actions only (Q13): an item action, a nested path or an exported `fn` is refused, an unknown service or action gets the closest name, arguments are text read by the parameter types as `set` reads values, missing defaulted parameters take the schema's default. Actions return nothing, so `call` prints nothing and `--json` prints `{"ok":true}`. The lock's `auth` actions are refused over IPC: a password is typed into the lock surface, never sent through a socket any process of the user can reach.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: `tokens.toml` and its writer.** The file is a flat TOML table of quoted token paths to text values (`"probe.c" = "#ff8800"`), the same text `strand set` takes, edited with `toml_edit` so a comment the user added survives a write; a hand-written number or bool is read too. A value its token's type does not read leaves the theme's value with one notice naming `strand clear`; a file that is not TOML is moved aside to `.tokens.toml.corrupt` with settings' `CorruptOverlay` notice, as settings' overlay is. architecture.md 0a says the file is "written on the persist IO thread"; strand-core's persist thread has no public raw-file write, and adding one is a strand-core interface change outside S-ipc, so the overlay has its own writer thread with the same discipline (newest text wins, temp file + fsync + rename + directory fsync, a write failure raised as a `WriteFailed` notice, a bounded wait at exit). *Amended 2026-10-11 (integrator decision b):* architecture.md 0a now says the overlay's own `strand-tokens` writer thread writes the file with that discipline, not the persist IO thread. A `tokens.toml` that is there but cannot be read (permissions, a directory, not UTF-8) is said once with `Unreadable` and never written over: `set` and `clear` on a token are refused ("could not be read; it is not written over") and read the file again, so fixing it by hand needs no restart and the overlays it held survive. Settings' overlay moves a *corrupt* file aside, which keeps its text; an unreadable one cannot be safely moved or merged, so refusing is the reading that loses nothing. An entry that is not a token's value is said once rather than dropped silently: a table (an unquoted dotted key, `radius.lg = "4px"`) is told to quote the path (`"radius.lg" = ...`), an array or date is named; flattening the table instead would give two spellings of one key.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: `auth` stays refused over IPC (integrator decision c).** The review asked whether `call lock.auth` should be served; the integrator confirmed the refusal above as decided: a password never crosses a socket every process of the user can reach.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: the `.text` overrun cut without costing speed (integrator decision a).** The review measured S-ipc at +116 KB `.text` against its 35 KB budget (CPU-only: 17,961,815 B at f61acec, 18,077,847 B at the first S-ipc commit; `scripts/size-report.sh`, fat LTO as budgets.rs builds). Symbol diffs against f61acec showed little of it in the request match itself: the handlers were already separate functions, and LTO inlined them into `Shell::request` (+21.7 KB there). The cuts: every IPC command handler (`get`, `toggle`, `call`, `clear`, `set`, `reset`, `mock`) is `#[cold] #[inline(never)]`, so `Shell::request` is a dispatch again (−19.8 KB there, the bodies counted once beside it); `value_json` inserts a record's fields one by one, so `collect` into `serde_json::Map` no longer pulls a ~5.1 KB stable sort of `(String, Json)`; the overlay's state keeps its handful of entries in sorted vectors instead of `BTreeMap<String, String>`, `BTreeMap<String, Option<PropValue>>` and a `BTreeSet` (each map's node code was 6–9 KB); every new `suggest` call (an unknown token, service or action) passes a `Vec<&str>`, one instantiation (~3.7 KB) rather than one per iterator; the file's read is a `#[cold]` function of its own, the memo keeping only the loaded check. After, with this round's fixes in: CPU-only 18,048,919 B (+87,104 over f61acec; −28,928 against the first commit), GPU 21,946,583 B (−28,928 against 21,975,511). Nothing on a frame or swap path changed: the handlers run once per IPC request, the memo's lookup is a binary search over a few entries. What remains is mostly the commands' own code (`call` resolution and its messages ~14 KB, `get` 5.3 KB, `clear` 3.6 KB, `toggle` 2.5 KB), the overlay layer (file read ~5.7 KB, writer thread ~3.7 KB, `toml_edit`'s writer 2.2 KB) and `instantiate::show` (~14 KB with `show_expr` and `paint`), which `get` uses for a token's text; it is kept, because `strand get '$shadow.lg'` printing Rust `Debug` would be a worse CLI for 14 KB, and it is not on any hot path. The remaining ~52 KB over budget is left for the owner to rebudget or to ask for further cuts; none of the remaining ones is free of a cost to users or speed. `scripts/container/run.sh` now passes `SIZE_REPORT_*` into the container, so `run.sh scripts/size-report.sh` honours them as the script's own re-exec already did.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: which saves the overlay shadows.** The "overlay wins" notice is raised when a committed build (a new program) changes the file's value of an overlaid token, once per change; a reload that leaves that token alone, or a re-evaluation of the same program, says nothing. It reuses settings' `SettingsNotice { issue: Shadowed }` with the overlay file as its file, so the reload overlay's `[clear]`, `strand watch`'s notices and `clear_settings_overlay` work unchanged; no second notice type. Overlay values are read for the token kinds a value can be written for on the command line (colour, length, percent, angle, duration, text, bool); others (paints, shadows, fonts) are refused, listing the kinds an overlay takes. When the shell runs without a state directory (the fallback storage), token overlays live in memory for the session.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: `clear` drops an entry that is not a value, and a file read again applies at once (review round 2).** The notice for a `tokens.toml` entry that is not text, a number or a bool advises `strand clear '$key'`, but `clear` only looked at the overlays it had read, so the advice answered `cleared: false` (or, for a key no token has, `no token`) and the entry came back every boot. Rather than drop the advice, `clear` now also removes such an entry from the file (`cleared: true`), and the instance counts the entry as something to clear before it asks the build for the token, so `strand clear '$list'` works on a key that is not a token too; once it is gone, an unknown name is refused again. A comment directly above the removed key goes with it, as toml_edit attaches it to that key. Separately, a `clear` that reads a file which could not be read before now builds the token table again even when it clears nothing, so the overlays the file holds apply (and `get` reports them) at once, as "fixing it by hand needs no restart" promises; before, only `set` did. Tests: token_overlay.rs `clear_drops_an_entry_that_is_not_a_value`, `a_fixed_overlay_file_applies_at_a_clear_that_clears_nothing`.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc: a hand edit of `tokens.toml` while the shell runs is read, not written over (review round 3).** The overlay read the file once at boot and every `set` or `clear` serialized that boot-time document, so a hand edit made while the shell ran was overwritten by the next write: an overlay removed by hand came back, an entry or comment added by hand was lost, and a file recreated after a corrupt one was moved aside was replaced, which broke "a comment the user added survives a write" and "fixing it by hand needs no restart" for any edit after boot. Settings' overlay edits read the current file on each edit (`edit_toml`), and token overlays now match them: the overlay remembers the text it last read or queued, and `set` and `clear` read the file again first when it holds anything else (or is gone, or cannot be read), replacing the in-memory overlays with the file's. They then apply the edit and build the table again, so a hand-removed overlay drops and a hand-added one applies at that step. This is one small read per `set`/`clear` on the logic thread (a CLI command, never a frame). The comparison is by content, not mtime and length, so a same-second edit that keeps the length is still caught. While a queued write has not landed, the file is not compared, so a hand edit made in those few milliseconds can still be overwritten; this is accepted rather than waiting on the writer. Edits are not watched between commands, so a hand edit applies at the next `set`, `clear` or boot, as before. Test: token_overlay.rs `a_hand_edit_while_running_is_not_written_over` (fails without the fix: the boot-time overlay is written back).

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2): the D-Bus front end as built.** `strand_services::ipc_bus` serves one object, `/`, with the interface `io.github.jakeb_grant.Strand` (the attribute's literal, held equal to `DBUS_NAME` by `the_interface_is_the_one_name`). Its methods are the scripting commands, typed: `Get(s path)`, `Set(s path, s value)`, `Toggle(s path)`, `Clear(s path)`, `Reset(s path)`, `Call(s target, as args)` and `Reload(b hard)`, each answering the socket's answer object as JSON text (`{"ok":true,"value":…}`), so a script reads one shape whichever way it asked; a refusal is `org.freedesktop.DBus.Error.Failed` carrying the socket's `error` word for word (an empty required field is refused there, in the socket `parse`'s words, without reaching the logic loop). Watching is the signal `Changed(s event, s data)`: every event a `strand watch` client gets, `event` its kind (so a match rule can take only `reload`s) and `data` the whole event as JSON; there is no `Watch` method, and the channel's `watch` stays answered as unknown. Typed methods were chosen over one `Request(s json)` method because D-Bus clients (`busctl`, `gdbus`, introspection) then see each command and its arguments; the cost is in the size paragraph below. The inspector's commands, `report` and `export` are the socket's only: their clients are the CLI's and `strand-dev inspect`. The front end is a task on the shared services runtime (`Services::spawn_task`), on a session-bus connection of its own (as the notification server's), so the name goes with the connection; the object is served before the name is asked for with `DoNotQueue`, so a call arriving the moment the name appears is answered. A second instance that finds the name owned logs once ("another instance owns io.github.jakeb_grant.Strand on the session bus; this one runs without it", a warning as the socket's is) and ends the task; it does not queue for the name or take it over when the first exits, as a second instance does not take over the socket. No session bus is an info line. The logic loop starts it once the real services exist, so not under `STRAND_MOCK`, whose mock host runs no services runtime; its event sink joins `Live::events_to`'s (both hear every event). The sink clones each event onto an unbounded channel unless the front end is gone; events are a reload's, a fault's or a notice's, never per frame. Tests: `ipc_bus.rs`'s four (methods to requests and back, refusals, empty fields, `Changed`, a second front end `Taken`, no bus, a closed loop refused), `tests/m5/dbus_ipc.rs` (`get_set_toggle_call_and_changed_over_dbus`, `a_second_instance_runs_without_the_name`) and budgets.rs's desktops, which now wait for the name beside the tray's and the notification server's, so the design bar's PSS and idle window are measured with it owned: PSS 36,665 kB in the container, the idle window and the minute tick's one burst unchanged.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2): a bus `reload` waits for its load.** architecture.md said `Job::Reload`'s client "becomes a `Caller`-like handle". The load still names its clients by `u64` id (`Loaded::clients`, the compiler worker's file, unchanged): a reload from the request channel gets an id of its own with the top bit set (`BUS_RELOAD`; the socket numbers its clients up from 1), kept in `Shell::bus_reloads` with its `Reply` until that load's event answers it through `Shell::reloaded`, which answers a socket client as before. A shell without a compiler worker answers "this shell does not reload" at once, as to the socket. A reply still waiting when the shell ends is dropped, which refuses it. Test: `run/tests.rs::saves_reload_live_with_state_kept` (a channel `reload` answered with its load's `reload` event).

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2): the inspector's three arms.** `inspect.node{id}`, `inspect.dump{surface?}` and `reset{node}` are served in `run/request/inspect.rs` over S-inspect's library. `parse` sends `inspect.node`, `inspect.dump` and a `reset` with a `node` and no `path` to `parse_m5`; M4's readings stay (a `reset` with both resets the path, one with neither "needs a `path`"). Answers add `"ok": true` to the library's object: `{"ok", "node", "files"}`, `{"ok", "nodes", "files"}`, and `{"ok": true, "reset": n}` with the cells changed. A ref that does not read as `index.generation` is refused saying what one is; one naming no node is "no node `12.0`". `inspect.dump{surface}` passes the node to `Instance::dump` as m5-inspect decided; a node that is not a surface root dumps its subtree rather than being refused, since the library reads it the same way and refusing would cost a check for no user gain. A subtree reset leaves the reload overlay's kept rows as they are (their `[reset]` resets a cell already at its default, which is harmless). *Amended 2026-10-11 (review round 2, item 2):* a subtree reset now drops the kept rows of the cells it reset, as `reset{path}` does. Tests: `run/tests.rs::saves_reload_live_with_state_kept` (the dump's root and tree order, one surface's dump, one node's pane, a reset subtree that shows the new default) and the refusals there and in strand-core's `malformed_requests_say_what_they_lack`.

The arms' figure is not the arms' own code: it is S-inspect's library becoming reachable. The wave-1 merged figure did not contain that library: it was dead code there (nothing called `dump`, `inspect_node`, `reset_subtree` or `provenance`), and LTO dropped it; S-inspect's 73.7 KB was measured with the arms wired temporarily, and the integrator's w1 paragraph read the merged figure as S-ipc and S-inspect "overlapping", which this measurement corrects: the library is charged for the first time now. In this build its share is `node_json` 29.0 KB, the reset subtree 7.8 KB (inlined into its arm), `TokenTable::provenance` 5.1 KB, `dump` 4.5 KB, `secrets` 2.5 KB and the rest; the arms' own code (dispatch, ref reading, answers) is about 2.2 KB, matching m5-inspect's 2,186 B. Cuts considered: answering a closed loop without building a JSON refusal (taken, −192 B); one `Request(s json)` method taking the socket's line instead of seven typed methods (about −18 KB, not taken: it would make the D-Bus interface a JSON tunnel that `busctl` and introspection cannot show, the reason the front end exists); dropping `Reset` (about −2.3 KB, not taken: the overlay's `[reset]` from a script is a command the socket has). Under the owner's speed-first policy this is recorded rather than cut further; the ledger consequence is the integrator's: the CPU-only gate's headroom is now 160,553 B (95,017 B above its 64 KiB reserve) for wave 2's remaining lines (S-palette 10 KB, S-tools 48 KB with report, plugins 8 KB, the inspector's render half 20 KB, xdg-activation 20 KB: 106,000 B), so either the reserve, those lines or the gate needs the integrator's and the owner's decision (the GPU gate keeps about 195 KB of headroom).

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2, review round 1, item 2): a cell kept at boot reaches a D-Bus listener once.** With the D-Bus sink present in every real run, a persisted cell kept over a changed default at boot reached it twice when no `strand watch` client was connected: as the boot's `notices` event (sent whenever the sink exists), and again in the next reload event's `kept_over_default`, which splices in `Shell::unheard` (kept while the socket had no watcher) for the socket's sake. The reload event now records how many of its kept entries came from `unheard`; the sink gets the event without them, and so does a bus `reload`'s answer, so every D-Bus client hears each kept cell once, while the socket's watchers and a socket `strand reload` still get them in the reload event (they missed the boot's). The copy is made only when such cells exist and a sink is present, which is once per boot at most. Test: `run/tests.rs::a_cell_kept_at_boot_reaches_the_event_sink_once` (fails without the change: the sink's reload event named `bar.hits` again). *Amended 2026-10-11 (review round 2, item 1):* reversed the other way round; the sink now hears the cell in the reload event, not at boot.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2, review round 1, item 3): spec.md does not yet name the D-Bus methods and signal; proposed text for S-docs.** spec.md section 13 names the bus name and path, and its compatibility covers commands only where that section names them, so the typed methods and `Changed` have no user-facing promise. spec.md is S-docs' file, so it is not edited here; the proposed bullet, to follow "The D-Bus name" in section 13: "- **Over D-Bus**, the interface's methods are the scripting commands: `Get(s path)`, `Set(s path, s value)`, `Toggle(s path)`, `Clear(s path)`, `Reset(s path)`, `Call(s target, as args)` and `Reload(b hard)`. Each returns the socket's answer as JSON text (`{"ok": true, …}`); a refusal is the error `org.freedesktop.DBus.Error.Failed` whose message is the socket's `error`. `Reload` returns once its load is committed, with its event. Watching is the signal `Changed(s event, s data)`: every event `strand watch --json` prints, `event` its kind (`reload`, `fault`, `notices`) and `data` the event as JSON. `report`, `export` and the inspector's commands are served over the socket only." The owner of the gap is S-docs (or the integrator at the M5 freeze, if S-docs has closed); it should land before M5 closes, and before any change such as item 1's choice (b), which would then need spec.md's text changed with it.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2, review round 2, item 1): a cell kept at boot reaches a D-Bus listener where a late `strand watch` hears it.** Round 1 sent the boot's kept cells to the event sink as a `notices` event at boot and stripped them from the next reload event for the sink and a bus `Reload`'s answer. On D-Bus that boot event is effectively lost: it is emitted right after `RequestName`, so only a match rule that existed before the shell started hears it, and every later subscriber and every `busctl call … Reload` then never learned the cell, while a `strand watch` and a socket `strand reload` at the same moment did. That broke the front end's contract (`Changed` carries every event a `strand watch` client gets; methods answer the socket's answer). The sink now follows the socket's rule: with a socket watcher connected, the `notices` event (cells and texts) goes to both as before; with none (at boot), the kept cells wait in `Shell::unheard` and the next reload event carries them, unchanged, to the socket's watchers, the sink and every `reload` caller, socket or bus. The sink still gets that moment's other notice texts at once (without the kept cells' own prose, with `kept_over_default` empty), so a D-Bus listener loses no lowering notice it heard before; each kept cell reaches it once. The reload event no longer records how many entries came from `unheard`, and `BUS_RELOAD` is no longer re-exported from `run/request`. Test: `run/tests.rs::a_cell_kept_at_boot_reaches_the_event_sink_as_a_late_watcher_hears_it` (replaces round 1's test): after the boot, a bus `Reload`'s answer, a late socket watcher's reload event and the sink's reload event each name `bar.hits`, and nothing sent to the sink before names it; it fails without the change (the bus answer's `kept_over_default` was empty).

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2, review round 2, item 2): a subtree reset drops the overlay's kept rows of the cells it reset.** `reset{node}` called only `Instance::reset_subtree`, which returns a count, so the reload overlay kept saying a reset cell was "kept (default changed)" while the bar showed its default and the inspector's badge (pruned by the instance) said otherwise; `reset{path}` drops the row (`Overlay::forget_cell`). Changing `reset_subtree` to return the paths it reset would change S-inspect's interface in architecture.md (0a), so the arm finds them in the strand crate instead: when the overlay has any row with a `[reset]` (`Overlay::has_resets`), it reads the `kept` badges the nodes under the node show (`Instance::dump(Some(node))`'s cells) before and after the reset, and drops the rows of the cells kept before and not after (`Overlay::forget_cells`, one refresh). The reset changes no cell outside the subtree, so a cell that was kept and no longer is was reset by it. The dump runs only on this cold command, and only when such a row exists. Should S-inspect later return the reset paths from `reset_subtree`, the arm can use them and drop the two dumps; that would be an architecture.md change, not proposed here because the strand-side reading is exact. Test: `run/tests.rs::saves_reload_live_with_state_kept` (the kept row for `n` is shown, and gone once `reset{node}` sets `n` to 7; it times out without the change). *Amended 2026-10-11 (review round 3, item 1):* the reading was not exact; the arm now drops the rows of every non-persisted cell under the node, from one dump before the reset.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2, review round 3, item 1): a subtree reset drops the kept row of a cell changed since it was kept.** Round 2 found the reset cells by comparing the `kept` badges under the node before and after the reset, but the badge holds only while a cell still has the exact value it kept, and the overlay's row stays after the user changes the cell (rows go only when forgotten or replaced). So a kept `n = 1`, clicked to 2, was reset to its default 7 by `reset{node}` and its "kept (default changed) [reset]" row stayed, while `reset{path}` drops it in the same case. The arm now takes, from one `Instance::dump(Some(node))` before the reset (still only when the overlay has a `[reset]` row), the paths of every cell the nodes under it show except the persisted ones, which `reset_subtree` leaves alone, and drops their rows (`Overlay::forget_cells`). Every such cell is at its default after the reset, so a kept-over-default row for it is stale whether or not the reset changed it. S-inspect's interface is unchanged; `reset_subtree` returning its paths would still be the exact source, should that interface change later. Test: `run/tests.rs::saves_reload_live_with_state_kept` now clicks `n` from its kept 1 to 2 (the row stays) before `reset{node}` and waits for the row to go; it times out without the change.

**2026-10-11 · m5-ipc (wave 2, review round 3, item 2): a boot-kept cell reset or set over IPC leaves the next reload event.** Since round 2, `Shell::unheard` is how the D-Bus `Changed` signal and a bus `Reload` answer hear the cells kept over a changed default at boot, but nothing removed a cell from it, so after `Reset("bar.hits")` (socket or bus) the next reload event still listed `bar.hits` in `kept_over_default` with its old value, while the overlay row was gone and the cell was at its default. `Shell::forget_unheard(path)` now drops the cell (or the cell a field path is under) from `unheard`; `reset{path}`, `set` on a state path (not a token) and `toggle` call it when they succeed. The paths match because both are spelled `module.name` (`Instance::reset` and the export lookup take the persisted path the kept record names). A change made from inside the shell (a click) does not remove the cell: the reload event then reports what was kept at boot, which is how a socket watcher connected at boot would have heard it; making the event check current values would need the inspector's kept set, which a hard reload clears, so it would drop cells still kept. Test: `run/tests.rs::a_boot_kept_cell_reset_or_set_over_ipc_is_not_reported_kept` (two persisted cells kept at boot, one reset and one set to its default over the socket, then a bus `Reload` whose answer's `kept_over_default` is empty; it listed both without the change).

**2026-10-11 · m5-integration-w1 (integrator): the `file` output host renders on the logic thread after the diff and writes on a thread of its own.** architecture.md put the host "on the main side", which no channel supports (`Update` is consumed on logic, main gets only `SceneDiff`s and the inspector's `ToMain` variants) and which would have sent failures the long way back to `Shell::broadcast`; m5-tools said only "off the logic thread". Outcomes come back over a channel the logic loop polls, so a failure is a notice and a `strand watch` event through `Shell::broadcast`. No main-side channel is added. The render cost sits beside the other-mode memo in the bench's both-modes case, after the diff and held to the same 5 ms. architecture.md's Threads table gains the writer thread and the token overlay's `strand-tokens` writer, which 0a named and `overlay.rs` spawns but the table lacked; the Logic row lists the M5 commands as 0a does. The other coherence fixes made with these: architecture.md's 0a `Instance` inspection block names the landed `inspect_node`, `dump`, `node_ref` and `parse_node_ref` with their answer shape and corrects the return types of `identity`, `reset_subtree` and `source_hash`; its token-overlay text states `clear`'s rule as m5-ipc amended it (a name with no token, no overlay and no file entry is refused; an overlay or entry the build lacks is cleared; a known token without one answers `cleared: false`).

## m5-palette

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette: the hue roles' canonical colours and how they are derived.** design.md and m5-tools fix the rule (the canonical hue, `blend::harmonize`d toward the accent, at most 15°, then Material tone 80 dark / 40 light; a bright is its base ± 0.08 OKLCH L) but not the canonical colours. They are the sRGB primaries and secondaries with orange between red and yellow: red `#ff0000`, orange `#ff8000`, yellow `#ffff00`, green `#00ff00`, cyan `#00ffff`, blue `#0000ff`, magenta `#ff00ff` (`palette.rs`, `BASE_HUES`). These are the colours the names mean everywhere else, so no second table of Strand-picked "nice" hues exists; the chroma comes from them too: `harmonize` keeps the canonical colour's chroma and tone and turns its hue, and `Hct::set_tone` then solves the tone at that chroma or the most the gamut allows there, which is Material's own custom-colour recipe (a harmonised colour's tonal palette at tone 80/40). A bright's lightness is clamped to 0–1 and gamut-mapped, as every derived role is. One function, `palette::fill_hues`, serves both paths: `Partial::fill` after the accent is known (so importers without hues, the persisted file of an older schema and `from_text` derive the same way), and `material::from_seed`, which fills the 49 roles from the dynamic scheme and the hues from its primary (`mc_role` is now `Option<McRole>`, `None` for a hue; `material.rs` is touched only for this, since a role table that must be total cannot skip the new roles). Given hues are kept as given (gamut-mapped and opaque, like any given role), and the contrast guard does not touch them, since they are in no pair. Tests: `crates/strand-theme/tests/palette.rs` (`hues_are_harmonised_toward_the_accent_in_light_and_dark`: each derived hue within 1.5° of the turn `harmonize` gives and so within 15° of its canonical hue, at tone 80/40, every bright its base's step, all 62 roles in gamut and opaque with the pairs at 3:1, over seven seeds, three variants, light and dark and the derivation table; `given_hues_are_never_changed`).

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette: extras and identity live beside the tokens, not among them.** architecture.md has `TokenTable` reserve `palette` "for extras and identity (read only by templates for now)". Inserting them as tokens (`palette.mauve` among `tokens`) would make every extra a palette root: the render thread springs every plain colour of a new table that differs (renderer/swap.rs), freezes every token each frame of a swap, and Catppuccin alone brings 26, so a swap's per-frame work would grow by half again for values no prop may read. So `TokenTable` gains a field, `palette: Vec<(String, PropValue)>`, written wholesale by `Palette::insert_into`: `name` and `source` as text (`source` only when the palette has one), `dark` as a bool, then the extras as colours in source order; `palette_value(name)` reads one entry. It is part of the table's equality, so a palette whose extras or name change still changes the table (and an output's memo), but `lookup`, `freeze`, the swap and the contrast guard never see it. A template's `$palette.<name>` reads `palette_value`, in the current or the other mode's table (S-tools). `strand_scene::tokens` names the reservation (`PALETTE_SEGMENT`, `is_palette_path`) and the hue roots (`HUE_ROOTS`, which `Role`'s test holds equal to the 13 hue names). architecture.md's strand-scene bullet now says so. The hue roles, by contrast, are ordinary palette roots: props read `$red`, so they spring in a swap like any role (13 more roots, about a quarter more of the swap's colour work).

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette: palette equality, names and the persisted file.** `Palette`'s equality now includes its extras and its own name (the source label stays out, as before), so `ThemeHost::remember_palette` re-persists a palette whose extras changed and nothing reading the palette misses such a change. `Palette::name()` is the scheme's own name, else the source string (`Option<&str>`, `None` only for a palette built from parts with no source). `to_text` writes `source`, then `name` (only the palette's own name, never the fallback, so a file read back keeps the distinction) after `dark`, the 62 role lines, then `extra <name> #rrggbbaa` lines; `from_text` reads them, and a file without them derives the hues and has no extras (`the_persisted_text_round_trips_extras_and_name`, which also builds an older file by dropping those lines). The importers' identity: Catppuccin is `Catppuccin Mocha` (`Macchiato`, `Frappé`, `Latte`); a base16/base24 scheme's `name:`, else the legacy `scheme:`; matugen and W3C files have none, so their name is the source string; `material(…)` likewise.

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette: what each importer keeps as extras, and in what order.** Catppuccin: its 26 names in the flavour table's order. base16/base24: every slot present, in the file's order (amended by m5-palette's review round 2; this said slot order), named lower-case (`base0d`); the scheme's existing role mapping is unchanged (`08` is still `error`, `0D` the accent, `16` `inverse_accent`) and `08`–`0E` and `12`–`17` now also fill the hue roles. matugen: every colour key of the mode, a role's included (`source_color`, `primary`), named by the key alone (amended by m5-palette's review round 3; this left the roles out). W3C: every colour token (a `$type` other than `color` is skipped, aliases are followed), named by its group path, a role's token included (`color.accent` is both `$accent` and `$palette.color.accent`), and a token whose path names a hue (`color.red`) fills that hue role as it would any role. `material(seed:)`, `material(image:)` and the built-in palette: `source_color`, the seed (8-bit, as Material reads it). Names: each segment lower-cased with every character other than an ASCII letter, digit or `_` made `_` (an empty segment is `_`), segments joined by `.`, and a *first* segment `name`, `source` or `dark` given a trailing `_`, since `$palette.dark.bg` would otherwise sit under the identity's bool. Two source colours that come to the same name are an import error naming both (`` `color.Brand` and `color.brand` are both `$palette.color.brand` ``), as m5-tools' first extras paragraph had it; the owner-approved paragraph is silent, and keeping one silently would drop a source colour, which "every importer keeps each colour" forbids. *Source order:* serde_json is built without `preserve_order`, so its maps are sorted; turning the feature on would reorder every JSON object the workspace writes (IPC answers, the inspector's dump) for this one need. matugen and W3C extras are instead ordered by a small scan of the already-parsed file's object keys (`import::key_order`, every key path in document order), walked with binary searches into the importer's path-sorted list (serde_json's maps iterate sorted), so no sort or second map is instantiated. Tests: `catppuccin_keeps_its_26_colours_and_its_name`, `base16_and_base24_keep_every_slot_and_map_their_hues`, `matugen_and_w3c_keep_their_colours_in_source_order` (keys out of alphabetical order, the `name_` rename, the collision error), `the_seed_is_the_material_palettes_extra`; themes.rs's `matugen_output_fills_the_palette` now also round-trips `source_color`.

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette: the reserved names in the checker and the schema.** The hue names reach the checker through the builtin schema's `palette { }` block, which gains the 13 names with their docs (`strand-compiler/src/schema/builtin.schema`, outside the one `check/tokens.rs` line m5-plan gives this stream, but the only place palette roles are declared to the checker): a prop may then read `$red`, and a token set defining `red` without `override` is the existing `check::override_needed` ("`$red` is a palette role"), while `override green: …` is allowed as for any role. The `palette` segment is a new code, `check::reserved_token`, raised for any entry of a token set (plain, `override`, or inside a group such as `palette { glow: … }`) whose path is under it, in `validate_set` before the override rules, so `override palette.name` cannot read as overriding nothing. Test: `crates/strand-compiler/tests/negative/reserved_token.strand` in `checker.rs::negative_corpus` (snapshot `checker__negative@reserved_token.snap`). `instantiate.rs::the_design_shells_run_on_the_mock`'s token snapshot gains the 13 hue roots.

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette: the `json` and `base24` writers' details.** `export::json(&Palette, &TokenTable)` writes `name`, `source` (`null` when absent), `dark`, `roles` (the 62 in schema order, each the table's resolved colour, so an overlay shows, else the palette's), `tokens` (every path of the table, plain and derived, sorted, each resolved in the global scope at `TimeContext::default()`; the roles are among them, so "every token path is present" holds without exceptions) and `extras` (source order). The value rules are m5-tools' "template expressions and formats" (a duration in milliseconds, numbers at most 3 decimals, `-0` written `0`, a colour gamut-mapped then `#rrggbb` or `#rrggbbaa`); the JSON is streamed by a small hand-written writer (`Json`'s `open`/`item`/`close`, keys written in the order the code emits them, so no value tree) with two-space indentation (serde_json's maps would sort the roles), strings escaped by serde_json (amended by m5-palette's review round 2; this said an ordered tree, which 431b7a6 replaced). `export::base24` writes base24's slot keys as tinted-theming spells them (`base0A`, upper-case hex digit) with lower-case `"#rrggbb"` values, the name YAML-escaped (falling back to `strand` for a palette with neither name nor source), and passes a `base16:`/`base24:` source's own slots through unless the slot's role is overlaid (`OVERLAY_ORIGIN`); `BASE24_SLOTS` is the slot table. *Round trip finding:* m5-tools asserts `fg_variant` among the roles that survive export and re-import for "any palette (the built-in one, `catppuccin:mocha`, a `material(seed:)`)", and those hold; for `catppuccin:latte` they do not, because the importer reads `base02` (Latte's `surface1`) as `surface_variant` and Latte's `subtext0` is under 3:1 on it, so the contrast guard moves `fg_variant` on the way back in. That is the format's loss, like `accent`; the test asserts it for Latte rather than hiding it. Tests: `crates/strand-theme/tests/export.rs` (`export_json_golden_from_catppuccin_mocha`, golden `tests/export/catppuccin-mocha.json` with one token of every kind and a `null` one, `STRAND_BLESS=1` rewrites it; `a_base24_scheme_passes_through_byte_for_byte`; `any_palette_round_trips_through_base24`; `overlays_reach_both_writers`: `strand set $fg #ffffff` reaches `base05` and `base06` of a base16 scheme's export, and `json`'s roles and derived tokens).

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette: size, measured: about 55 KB against the 10 KB line, over with the reasons below.** Measured with `scripts/size-report.sh` (fat LTO, as budgets.rs builds) against `laptop/m5-w2`'s head `3e833c9` built the same way in the container: CPU-only 18,076,567 → 18,132,695 B (**Δ +56,128 B**) and GPU 21,974,103 → 22,030,231 B (**Δ +56,128 B**), both with `export::json` and `export::base24` wired into `main` temporarily through `black_box` (not committed; S-tools' CLI and IPC request will call them, so unwired they would be stripped and the figure would hide them), the wiring itself about 1 KB of that. Both builds stay under their gates (18,350,080 and 22,282,240 B). The first commit measured +77.7 KB with the writers unwired: two instantiations of a stable sort of `(Vec<String>, Color)` (about 28 KB, for source order) went when extras were ordered by walking the document's key order instead; wired, that was +71.4 KB, and merging the table's two already-sorted key lists in place of a `BTreeSet` collect (about 5 KB of `&String` sort), a JSON writer that streams in place of a value tree and binary searches in place of a path map brought it to the figure above. Where the rest sits (symbol deltas): the writers about 13 KB (`json` 7.8 KB, `base24` 2.6 KB, the JSON writer's helpers, `quoted`, `hex`); the importers' extras about 17 KB (`import`'s Catppuccin path +4.7 KB, `extras_in_order` 5.4 KB with its name-collision map and messages, `key_order` 2.8 KB, `w3c` +2 KB, matugen's collector 2 KB, `snake_case`/`extra_name`); the hues about 4.5 KB (`fill_hues` 2.6 KB with `harmonize` and HCT, `from_seed` +0.6 KB, `Partial::fill` +0.5 KB); the table's palette entries about 8 KB in strand-scene (`TokenTable`'s derived `Debug` of the new field 2.3 KB, drop glue and moves of the larger table, `insert_into` +1.8 KB) and +2.3 KB inlined into `Instance::from_build`. m5-tools' estimate (hues and extras 4–6 KB, export 3–4 KB) did not count the source-order recovery, the collision error or JSON written without a serde map. Nothing here is on a frame path: the importers run when a palette is evaluated, the writers once per export, and the swap gains only the 13 hue roots as springing colours (the extras are held apart for exactly that reason). Cuts that remain would cost behaviour: dropping source order for matugen and W3C extras (−8 KB; the owner-approved design says source order), a linear name-collision check (−2 to −3 KB, quadratic on a large W3C file), or a hand-written `Debug` for the table (−2 KB). Under the owner's speed-first policy (m5-speed-policy) this stream reports the overrun rather than making those cuts; the 61,001 B review-fix reserve (55,625 B on the GPU build) would cover it, which is the integrator's and owner's call.

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette (review round 1): the identity's names are reserved as groups too, and the copies of the role list are tied by tests.** `extra_name` gives a trailing `_` to a *first* segment `name`, `source` or `dark` whether it names a colour or a W3C group, so a group `dark` holding `surface` is `$palette.dark_.surface`. spec.md 9.5 and the owner-approved m5-tools paragraph named only a colour; reading `$palette.dark.surface` would put a member under the identity's bool, so the code's reading is the only one that keeps both names readable, and spec.md 9.5 now says so (a later segment is never renamed: `color.name` stays). This widens the reserved names, adds no concept. Two tests had been missing: `insert_into_writes_the_identity_then_the_extras_in_order` reads `TokenTable::palette` through `palette_value` after `Palette::insert_into` (Catppuccin with name and source, latte's `dark` false, matugen's name falling back to its source string, a palette with neither giving `dark` alone, the extras in source order after the identity), since the writers' tests read the Palette directly and strand-scene's test fills the vector by hand; and `the_schema_palette_block_is_the_role_list` (strand-compiler tests/theme.rs) asserts the builtin schema's `palette { }` block, which the checker reads, has exactly `Role::ALL`'s names, so a misspelt hue there no longer passes. `Schema::palette_roles`' comment said declaration order; the token map is sorted, so it says name order and the test compares sorted lists. Both tests were checked failing against the mutation they guard (`self.name` for `self.name()`, `bright_magneta`).

**2026-10-11 · m5-palette (review round 2): base16/base24 extras follow the file, and the writers paragraph matches the code.** spec.md 9.5 promises every importer's colours "in source order", and the extras paragraph above had decided slot order for base16/base24 without amending the spec, so the spec wins: `yaml_pairs` now returns the file's `key: value` pairs in order (a `Vec`, a repeated key read last as YAML loaders do, through `yaml_get`) in place of a `BTreeMap`, and `base16` pushes each slot (`base` and two hex digits under `0x18`, either case) where the file first names it, with the colour the roles read. **2026-10-11 · m5-palette (review round 3): matugen keeps its roles' colours as extras, and matugen 3's layout has an extras test.** spec.md 9.5 says "An importer also keeps every colour of its source", and the owner-approved m5-tools paragraph says "Every importer keeps each colour of its source"; the exclusion of the 49 M3 names came from m5-tools' superseded list and was restated in this stream's extras paragraph without amending the spec, so the spec wins. matugen now does what W3C and base16 already did: a key that names a role fills it and is kept as `$palette.<key>` too, so `$palette.primary` and `$palette.surface_container` read for a matugen file as they do for a W3C one, and a custom colour `green` fills the hue and stays `$palette.green`. themes.rs's `matugen_output_fills_the_palette` compared the import to the seed palette whole; it now expects the seed's `source_color` plus the 49 names as extras and the roles as before. matugen 3's `colors.<role>.<mode>` branch had no extras test, and `extras_in_order` skips a found path missing from `key_order` silently, so a wrong prefix there would have dropped every extra unnoticed: `matugen_and_w3c_keep_their_colours_in_source_order` now reads a matugen 3 file with keys out of alphabetical order, a `default` value and per-mode colours. Both checked failing: the round-2 code fails the expected extras (and `insert_into_writes_the_identity_then_the_extras_in_order`), and the branch's prefix changed to `["colors", mode]` fails the matugen 3 case.

**2026-10-11 · m5-fixups: `strand new`'s grim references are made, on the frozen-clock mock, in `acceptance.rs`.** The owner deferred the PNGs to the integrator, whose call is to make them (rendering lands with offline PNG tests). S-tools left them out because "its clock and window title make its pixels change by the minute" (m5-tools, wave 3), but the acceptance mock (`STRAND_MOCK=acceptance`) already freezes the clock at 09:41 UTC and gives a fixed focused window. `acceptance.rs::the_new_shell_checks_and_runs_on_two_outputs` runs the built binary's `strand new` into an empty directory, `strand check` on it, then `strand run` on m5-plan's two outputs (2560x1440 at 1, 1920x1080 at 1.25), and compares each bar with `tests/refs/acceptance/new_shell_headless{1,2}.png` through the file's usual `settled_ref` and `STRAND_UPDATE_REFS=1` bless flow (read, and stable over two more runs). The test lives in `acceptance.rs`, not m5-plan's `tests/m5/new.rs`, because that binary holds the reference machinery (`Img`, tolerances, the bless flow) and the two-output desk; a second copy in the `m5` binary would add a second reference store for one bar. The references equal `hello_bar_headless{1,2}.png` byte for byte, as they should: the template is design.md's hello bar with a comment. `report.rs` keeps its own two-output desk (scale 2) for the report's sections. handoff owner item 6 is answered and m5-integration-w2's "left to the owner to confirm" no longer holds.

**2026-10-11 · m5-fixups: a config service's `rw` field is writable from the language.** spec.md 5.6 and 8.1 say `name: type rw = Property` is writable, and `services/custom.rs` writes it, but the checker refused every write: `rw_root` reached `ExprKind::Def` for `ppd` and asked `writable_place`, which accepts only `state` and settings. The arm is added in `rw_root` only (a `Def` of `DefKind::Service` is the write's root, as `ExprKind::Service` is), not in `writable_place`, so a config service's field without `rw` (which reaches `writable_place` through the user-record path) and a write of the whole service stay `check::read_only`. The checker's fix alone would have lowered the write as `PlaceRoot::Def`, a store into a slot the service does not have; `place_parts` now takes a config service's `Def` as `PlaceRoot::Service(name)`, so the VM writes it through the service host by name, as `audio.sink.volume` is, and the write edge (`WriteTarget::Service`) matches the read edge reads already recorded under that name. Proved by `checker.rs::a_config_services_rw_field_is_writable` (`=`, `+=` and `<->` check and lower to the service's field; the read-only field and the whole service refused) and `services.rs::a_config_services_rw_field_is_written_to_the_bus` (an `on change` assigns `ppd.profile`; dbusmock's power-profiles-daemon holds the new profile, the bar shows it, and assigning back sets the bus again). Guide level 5 no longer calls it a checker bug, and its control centre sets the profile on click.

**2026-10-11 · m5-fixups: a drop counts its rows without every copy of the dragged item, by an identity the compiler sends in `Prop::Drag`.** A dock is a `bar`, so each monitor draws every pin, and a drop handed to another monitor's dock counted that dock's own icon for the dragged pin (m5-docs round 3): one place on. Of m5-docs' two proposals, render's is taken: `drop_index` already owns `at`'s meaning, and logic's alternative (`drop_args` lowering `at`) would need the target's rows, which the logic thread does not mirror. The scene has no key per node, so the instance now always sends `Prop::Drag` as a `List` whose last item is `List [Text(identity)]`: an FNV-1a hash, in hex, of the value's drag type and of its identity (`Value::identity`: a keyed record's key, else the value) as it shows. FNV rather than `DefaultHasher` so the identity, and the snippet snapshot that prints it, are the same on every toolchain; a nested `Text` rather than a `Number` (an `f32`, 24 bits) or a bare `Text` (which `drag_export` would read as a file or the text). `strand_scene::drag_identity` reads it, `drag_type` and `drag_export` ignore it. `drop_index` leaves out every live row (the source's excepted, already out) that is or holds a `drag:` source of the dragged one's identity; a per-item target that is itself a copy keeps its own place, so a pin dropped on its own copy stays put. A copy unmounted from a windowed `list` is not seen (render has only the mounted rows). Equal values are one item by design: `pins.move(p.app, at)` keys by value too. architecture.md's drag-and-drop bullet takes the proposed wording ("`at` a global row index, with the dragged source and every copy of the dragged item left out") and the identity's shape; spec.md 6.7 says what `at` counts. Proved by `input.rs::a_drop_on_another_surface_leaves_out_its_copy_of_the_item` (before, past and at the end of the other surface's copy), `instantiate.rs::drag_sources_and_drop_targets_deliver_typed_values` (one identity per pin), and the guide's `the_guide_dock_drops_where_the_pointer_is`, whose last drop is now exact; level 5's prose says the pin lands where it is let go on either dock.

**2026-10-11 · m5-fixups: `key=value` documents skip `#` comments and lose single quotes, as os-release(5) writes them.** `Document::parse` read a file as pairs only when every non-blank line was a pair, and stripped only double quotes, so `/etc/os-release` with a comment line (openSUSE Tumbleweed) read whole into every field, and `PRETTY_NAME='Foo'` kept its quotes. A line whose first non-blank character is `#` is now not a line of the pairs; a value in double quotes loses them and the four escapes os-release(5) allows (`\"`, `\\`, `\$`, `` \` ``), one in single quotes loses them and keeps everything between. A file of a bare word and comments (hostname(5)) is still text, read whole with its comments: dropping `#` lines from plain text would change other text files (a Markdown heading). Proved by `strand-services`' `custom::tests::pairs_skip_comments_and_lose_their_quotes`; the guide's `the_guide_states_the_pairs_rule` (renamed from `…_limit`) now asserts the commented os-release sample reads as pairs, and level 5's prose states the rule rather than the limit.

**2026-10-11 · m5-fixups: the tray `open()` doc says what it does.** `tray.schema` (and builtin.schema's stub) said "Opens it as a popup"; `open()` tells the app and sets `item.menu.opened`, a DBusMenu's menu needs a `popup` bound to `opened`, and only an item without one shows its own (m5-docs, round 3 of wave 1). Both docs now say so; LSP hover reads them.

**2026-10-11 · m5-fixups: `strand report`'s percentiles are over drawn frames; "discarded" is left to `wp_presentation`.** S-tools recorded every `paint` and took the percentiles over all of them, calling a paint that damaged nothing "discarded". That paint costs next to nothing, so a surface whose diffs often change nothing showed percentiles below what a frame on screen costs, and "discarded" is the compositor's word for a frame it did not show (`FrameClock`, architecture.md), which a hardware-lab reader would take it for. By design.md's question, one word for two things adds a concept; so the percentiles are over the frames drawn among the last 600 paints (zero before the first), and the counts are `drawn` and `unchanged` (`FrameSummary { p50, p95, p99, drawn, unchanged }`, the JSON's `frames.drawn`/`frames.unchanged`, the text "p50 … over N drawn (M unchanged)", or "none drawn (M unchanged)"). The ring still holds the last 600 paints, so the window is the one m5-plan names. Whether the compositor then showed a frame is not measured here; `report` is new in wave 3 and unfrozen, so the keys change now. Proved by `renderer::summary::tests::{percentiles_are_over_the_drawn_frames_of_the_last_600_paints, one_frame_is_every_percentile}` and `report.rs`'s text test; architecture.md and m5-plan's report line follow.

**2026-10-11 · m5-fixups: `tests/m5/plugin.rs` builds its examples with the cargo running it.** A filtered `cargo test -p strand --test m5` builds no examples, so `plugin.rs` failed until `cargo build -p strand --examples` ran (both wave-2 merges built them by hand). S-plugins chose "never by a nested cargo"; this reverses it, since a filtered run is how a stream and the integrator run the suite. `example()` now first calls `build_examples` once per test process (a `OnceLock`): `$CARGO build --offline --quiet --profile <the test's> --manifest-path crates/strand/Cargo.toml --target-dir <the test's> --example plugin_hello --example plugin_bare`, with `--no-default-features` when the test was built without `gpu`. The profile and target directory come from `CARGO_BIN_EXE_strand`'s path (`debug` is the `dev` profile, whose settings `test` shares here, so nothing is built twice). Up to date it is a fingerprint check, and it runs beside the outer cargo without waiting on its lock. Checked in the container: with `target/container/debug/examples/` removed, and again after touching `plugin_hello.rs`, `cargo test -p strand --test m5 -- plugin` builds them and passes (6).

**2026-10-11 · m5-fixups: base16's `base02` keeps feeding three roles; m5-tools' round-trip claim narrows.** The importer reads `base02` into `surface_high`, `surface_variant` and `outline_variant`, and the exporter writes it from `surface_high`; Latte's `subtext0` is under 3:1 on `surface1` read back as `surface_variant`, so the import's contrast guard moves `fg_variant` (m5-palette, `export.rs` asserts it). The importer stays: `base02` is base16's only colour between the background and the comments, so the three roles' nearest reading is it, and changing it would change how every imported scheme looks to make one round trip exact. The guard is the import's legibility promise, and a palette that fails it on the way in is the format's loss, as `accent` is. So m5-tools' "(b) any palette … `fg_variant` … equal" means any palette whose `fg_variant` keeps 3:1 on its `surface_variant`; the built-in palette, `catppuccin:mocha` and `material(seed:)` do, Latte does not.
