**2026-10-12 · m5-fixups, review round 1: a drop leaves out the dragged row in its own list and one copy in another, by an identity equal exactly when the values are.** The review found the "every copy" rule wrong for a list holding equal items: `state items = ["a", "b", "a", "c"]`, the first `a` dragged to the end, had both `a` rows left out, so `at` was 2 and `items.move(it, 2)` (which takes the *first* equal item out, `vm/exec.rs` `move`) gave [b, a, a, c] for [b, a, c, a]; and the identity hashed `identity().show()`, which is lossy (`["a, b"]` and `["a", "b"]` both show "a, b", a `fn` field shows "fn", a node "node"), so values the language calls unequal could collide. Both are fixed; this amends the earlier entry's "every copy" and withdraws its "Equal values are one item by design", which holds for keyed lists only. `drop_index` now leaves out one row per list: in the list that holds the source, the row that is or holds it (equal items beside it are other rows, which `move` leaves in place, as before M5); in any other list (the same pins on another monitor's dock), its *first* row holding a `drag:` source of the dragged identity, the first because `move` takes the first equal item out; a per-item target is never the one left out (dropped on its own copy, the item stays). The identity is now FNV-1a over the drag type and a tagged, length-prefixed encoding of the value's identity (`mount.rs::identity_bytes`) that is equal exactly when `builtins::equal` is: numbers by value whatever their unit, records by type and fields, lists by items, and a `fn` or an element by which one it is (the language compares those by reference, so their identity is the `Rc`'s address and, for values holding one, is stable within a run only; the snippet snapshot has none). The snippet snapshot's one identity changes accordingly. spec.md 6.7 and architecture.md's drag-and-drop bullet say what `at` counts. With duplicates, `move` by value still cannot tell which equal item was dragged (dragging the second `a` moves the first), which is the handler's choice, not the drop's; a keyed list has no duplicates. Proved by `crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::equal_items_in_one_list_are_counted_apart` ([a, b, a, c] on two surfaces: the first `a` to the end at 3, the second between the first and `b` at 1, the first handed to the other surface's end at 3; it gave 2 before) and `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::a_drag_identity_is_the_values_equality` (equal lists share an identity, `["a, b"]` and `["a", "b"]` do not; equal before); `a_drop_on_another_surface_leaves_out_its_copy_of_the_item` and the guide's `the_guide_dock_drops_where_the_pointer_is` still pass.

**2026-10-12 · m5-fixups, review round 1: `tests/m5/plugin.rs` runs a nested cargo only when an example is missing or stale.** The earlier entry's "up to date it is a fingerprint check" was checked for a filtered `-p strand --test m5` only. In `cargo test --workspace` (CI, `run.sh ci`) features unify with every member's dev-dependencies (strand-services' `tokio` `test-util` and `rustix` `shm`, strand-fake-wayland's `wayland-protocols` `server`), while the nested `cargo build --manifest-path crates/strand/Cargo.toml` selects strand alone, so it would resolve those crates and everything above them under other hashes, rebuild them inside the running test process while the binary's other tests ran, and re-uplift the examples. `build_examples` now runs no cargo when both examples are fresh: built, and newer than every source their dep-info (`examples/<name>.d`, the workspace sources cargo built them from) names. A package or workspace run has just built them, so it never builds; a filtered run builds them when they are missing or a source changed since, as the earlier entry intended. The nested build also passes this build's `speed-bench`/`faults`/`gpu` features, so a `--features speed-bench --test m5` run does not build the examples without them. Checked in the container: a filtered run with no examples builds them and passes (6); run again it builds nothing (the examples' mtimes unchanged, 0.36 s); after touching `plugin_hello.rs` it rebuilds them and passes.

**2026-10-12 · m5-fixups, review round 1: `strand set` writes the config's own service's `rw` fields.** The language fix made `ppd.profile = …` work, but `set.rs` sent a path to the service host only when `services::is_service_path` (the served schema: builtins and plugin files) matched, so `strand set ppd.profile power-saver` fell to `Instance::set_text` and answered "nothing is exported as `ppd.profile`", although spec.md 13 and `strand help` name "an `rw` service field". `set.rs` now asks `services::config_service` (the program's `services`, by declared name) after the exported and builtin checks, and writes through `services::set_field_text`, which is `set_text_with` with the service's record and its type table passed in (the program's types for a config service, the served schema's for the rest; `set_text_with` resolves and calls it), through the VM's own host by name, as the handler's write goes. The same parse applies: the leaf must be `rw`, a signed number steps from the current value. spec.md 13 names the config's own services among the `rw` fields. Proved by `crates/strand/tests/services.rs::a_config_services_rw_field_is_written_to_the_bus`, which now ends with `strand set ppd.profile power-saver` (the bar turns green and dbusmock's daemon holds "power-saver"; without the fix the CLI exits with "nothing is exported as `ppd.profile`").

**2026-10-12 · m5-fixups, review round 2: a drop leaves out the dragged item's own row only in the list it is an item of, and the compiler marks every element holding a `for`.** Review found that round 1's "the row that is or holds the source" took any ancestor of the source: on a kanban board (`row { on drop(c: Card, at: int) {…} for col in board { column { for c in col.cards { box { drag: c } } } } }`), a card dragged out of `doing` and let go past the middle of `done` had the `doing` column left out of the board's rows, so `at` was 2 for 3; and another monitor's board left out its `doing` column too, because `copy` searched each row's whole subtree. At aa3053c only the source node itself was left out, so this was a regression of 9c2d07c. A source belongs to the list it is an item of, which render can tell only if it knows where a nested list starts, and render's tree marked `for` rows only on `on drop` targets (`Prop::DropRows`), so a plain column was indistinguishable from a wrapper (`box { image { drag: p } }`, whose row does hold the item). The compiler now sets `Prop::DropRows` on every element whose direct child is a `for`, `on drop` or not (one `Bool` per such element; the design-shell and snippet snapshots gain `drop_rows=true` on those nodes and nothing else), and `drop_index` counts a node as list `n`'s item row only when no `list` or `DropRows` element lies between it and `n` (`row_in`); a copy is a row holding a source of the dragged identity as `n`'s item, and the search does not descend into a nested list. A wrapper still has its row left out, a nested list's column is counted. This changes `Prop::DropRows`' meaning from "an `on drop` target whose direct child is a `for`" to "an element whose direct child is a `for`": architecture.md's drag bullet and the prop's doc take that text (render reads it only on drop targets and as this boundary), and spec.md 6.7 says a row of an outer list holding the item's list is counted. The same round brings the two stale statements of round 1's withdrawn rule in line, handoff.md's S-fixups paragraph and `strand_scene::drag_identity`'s doc, which said every copy of the dragged item is left out; both now say one row per list, the own row or another list's first copy. Proved by `crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::a_drop_on_an_outer_list_counts_the_row_holding_the_item` (two boards of three columns; past `done` at 3 within the board and on the other surface's board, between `doing` and `done` at 2; it gave 2 for 3 before) and `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::every_element_holding_a_for_marks_its_rows`; the dock, equal-item and copy tests still pass.

**2026-10-12 · m5-fixups, review round 3: an element holding a `for` is a nested list only for its rows (`Prop::NotRow`).** Review found that round 2 made every element with a direct `for` child a list boundary, so a list item's wrapper that holds a decorative `for` of its own beside a nested `drag:` source was taken as a nested list: on a dock with per-window dots (`row { on drop(p: Pin, at: int) { pins.move(p.app, at) } for p in pins key p.app { col { for w in p.windows { box { size: 4 } } image p.icon { drag: p } } } }`), `row_in(dock, image)` stopped at the item `col` and `copy` would not look into it, so neither the dragged pin's own row nor another monitor's copy was left out and a pin let go past the middle of pin 1 was at 2 for 1. This contradicted round 2's "a wrapper still has its row left out" and spec.md 6.7's "without its own row". Render cannot tell a `for`'s rows from the element's other children (the icon is a direct child of the `col` as the dots are); the compiler can. So it marks each child of a `DropRows` element that is not one of its `for`'s rows `Prop::NotRow` (a new compiler-set `Bool` in `strand-scene`, `Snap`; the emitter flags a `for`'s keyed fragment `rows`, and a node created under a `DropRows` parent with no such fragment between them is content, whether it is mounted at once, through an `if` or through a component), and `drop_index` treats a `list` or `DropRows` element as the source's list only when the path's child under it is not `NotRow`; `copy` searches a nested list's `NotRow` children only. Marking the content rather than the rows was chosen because content beside a `for` is rare and rows are many: one prop per header or icon, none per row, and the design-shell and snippet snapshots gain `not_row=true` on those nodes only. A kanban column's cards stay its rows, so round 2's board result holds. This adds a prop to the scene protocol: architecture.md's drag bullet gains `Prop::NotRow` and the instance-interface bullet, which still said "`Prop::DropRows` on a target with a direct `for` child" (review finding fixups-r3-2), now says every element with a direct `for` child, `on drop` or not, plus `NotRow` on its other children. A target's own content (a column's header) is still counted among its rows when it is the drop target, as m4-interaction-finish set; `NotRow` could leave it out, which is left for its own decision. Proved by `crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::a_dock_item_holding_a_for_beside_its_icon_is_the_icons_row` (pin 0 past the middle of pin 1 at 1 on its own dock and on the other monitor's; 2 before the fix) and `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::content_beside_a_for_is_marked_not_a_row`; the board, dock, equal-item and copy tests still pass.

## m5-platform

S-platform's wave-3 work on `laptop/m5-platform` (docs/m5-plan.md, "S-platform"): xdg-activation for notification actions and app launches, and the handler input context's route. Code comments that cite m5-platform point here.

**2026-10-11 · m5-platform: the press serial is joined in the binary's host, not returned by strand-render's router.** architecture.md had the router return each press's serial beside its `NodeEvent`. `Intent::Event` is matched at 30 sites in four crates, and the router never sees a serial: strand-surface does (`manager/seat.rs`). So strand-surface tells its host each press's serial before the press itself (`SurfaceHost::press_serial`, a new hook with an empty default, so no other host changes), and the binary's `Forward` (`demo/host.rs`), which already turns intents into `ToLogic`, joins the last one to the node events that press causes: a button's press or release, a key press or repeat, a click away. A scroll, a drag, a key release and a settled intent carry none. The route's outcome is architecture.md's (`ToLogic::Event { input }`), with one concept fewer in the renderer; architecture.md says so (crates/strand/src/demo/host.rs::tests::a_press_serial_rides_the_events_it_causes).

**2026-10-11 · m5-platform: `Instance::event_with` beside `Instance::event`, and one process-wide invocation counter.** architecture.md had `Instance::event` gain an `input` parameter. It has about 90 callers, nearly all tests and synthetic events with no press, so `event` stays and passes `None`, and `event_with(node, event, args, input)` is the one the shell's `ToLogic::Event` arm calls. Handler invocations are numbered from one `AtomicU64` for the process rather than per `Instance`: a reload builds a new instance while the old one's actions may still wait behind a token, and a per-instance counter would start again at 1 and queue the new instance's first handler behind an unrelated old one. The VM sets the running stretch's `ActionCtx` in a thread-local guard (`vm::action_ctx()`), clearing the press at the first `await` and keeping the number across them (crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::actions_know_whether_input_called_them).

**2026-10-11 · m5-platform: `State::activation_token` takes a callback; the token source is an `Arc<dyn Fn(u32, u32) -> TokenFuture>`.** architecture.md wrote `activation_token(surface, serial) -> async Option<String>`. The main thread runs calloop with no executor, so the strand-surface call takes `done: impl FnOnce(Option<String>)`, called with `None` before it returns when the compositor has no `xdg_activation_v1` and after 5 s at the latest for a token never answered. The binary's `token_source` (run/mod.rs) queues a `TokenAsk { surface, serial, answer }` for main and wakes it with a `calloop::ping` (first a calloop channel; see "the `.text`" below), and main's ping source calls `activation_token` for each with `answer.send` as `done`; a main thread gone drops the queue and the answers in it, which the waiters hear as `None` (crates/strand/src/run/tests.rs::the_token_source_asks_main_and_hears_its_answer, crates/strand-surface/tests/fake.rs::no_activation_protocol_means_no_token_and_no_wait).

**2026-10-11 · m5-platform: which actions want a token is a service's declaration, and a service reads it from `Cx`.** A service lists the actions that raise an app in `Service::ACTIVATION` (`#[service(activation = &["invoke", "activate"])]` in the macro; empty by default), so `DynService::action` asks a token only for those, and only when the handler had a press and a token source is set. A delivered action's token is `Cx::activation_token()`, set by each `recv` from the message the action came in (the run's channel carries `(Msg, Option<String>)`). notifications declares `invoke` and `activate` and sends `ActivationToken(id, token)` before `ActionInvoked` (nothing when there is no token), and answers spec 1.2; apps declares `launch`. The ordering queue (`strand_services::activation::Order`, one for every service on the logic thread, keyed by invocation) holds an invocation's later actions, to any service, behind its wait on the shared runtime, so logic never blocks (crates/strand-services/src/activation.rs::tests, crates/strand-services/tests/notifications.rs::activation_token_precedes_action_invoked, ::invoke_then_dismiss_keeps_order_while_waiting_for_a_token).

**2026-10-11 · m5-platform: inherited tokens are removed on the `Command`, not in `restore_in_child`.** m5-plan had `restore_in_child` strip the inherited `XDG_ACTIVATION_TOKEN` and `DESKTOP_STARTUP_ID`. `restore_in_child` runs between `fork` and `exec`, where `unsetenv` is not async-signal-safe (it may take the environment lock another thread held at the fork). So `strand_services::child::activation_env(cmd, token)` sets both variables to the press's token or removes both, on the `Command` before it spawns, beside `restore_in_child` at every site that starts a program: app launches (`apps::spawn_launched`, which `spawn_detached` now calls with no token), `exec` sources (`custom.rs`) and the editor (`overlay.rs`). The two variables carry the same token, as the xdg-activation spec asks for toolkits that read the startup-notification one (crates/strand-services/src/child.rs::tests::a_launch_carries_its_token_and_never_an_inherited_one, crates/strand-services/tests/apps.rs::a_launch_carries_the_token_and_not_an_inherited_one).

**2026-10-11 · m5-platform: the compositor matrix checks focus, on sway and niri here.** `a_launched_app_is_activated_with_its_token` (compositor_matrix.rs; m5-plan named it `a_launched_window_gets_focus_with_the_token`) runs `strand run` with a one-button launcher shell and a desktop entry whose `Exec` is the test binary's own `activation_helper`, clicks the button with the virtual pointer, and checks the app got a token in both variables and not the stale one strand was started with. Since sway focuses a new window anyway (m5-infra spike 3), the helper's window then loses the focus to another window, activates with a token nobody issued (the focus stays), then with its launch token (the focus comes back). The compositor's policy is set to focus where it has one and put back on drop: sway's `focus_on_window_activation focus`, Hyprland's `misc:focus_on_activate` (through `hyprctl keyword`; the result is logged, not asserted, since a Lua config may refuse `keyword`); niri focuses on a valid token by default. `MATRIX_FILTER=a_launched_app_is_activated_with_its_token scripts/container/matrix.sh` passed on sway 1.12 and niri; Hyprland was skipped (no KMS card here; CI runs it), and labwc skips it as it skips the other IPC tests (`live()`), since the test reads the focus from the compositor's IPC. Compositors without `xdg_activation_v1` skip it with a message.

**2026-10-11 · m5-platform: the `.text`, over its 20 KB line.** `scripts/size-report.sh` on `laptop/m5-platform` measures CPU-only 18,605,207 B and GPU 22,524,823 B, against 18,555,351 B and 22,473,111 B at `aa3053c` (the gate re-base's own figures, rebuilt here for the symbol comparison): **+49,856 B and +51,712 B**, against m5-plan's 20,000 B line, so 29,856 B (GPU 31,712 B) over it, and inside both re-based gates (`TEXT_GATE_CPU` 18,874,368 B, 269,161 B left; `TEXT_GATE_GPU` 22,806,528 B, 281,705 B left). The first build measured +60,736 B and +62,400 B; two cuts took 10,880 B with nothing dropped: the token asks reach main through a queue and a `calloop::ping` instead of a calloop channel of their own (a `Channel<T>` source's generic dispatcher was about 11 KB; the ping source is shared code), and notifications sends `ActivationToken` and `ActionInvoked` from one function. By the symbol comparison, what remains is spread, with no one bloated item: the two `xdg_activation_v1` interfaces' Wayland dispatch and requests (wayland-client and wayland-protocols, about 8.3 KB), `State::activation_token` inlined into the ping source's dispatcher (about 7.3 KB), the ordering queue, its wait and the one-shot (about 6.5 KB with tokio's timeout), the token beside each service's messages and the `ActionCtx` through `DynService::action` and `Client::act_with`, monomorphised per service (about 9 KB net), the launch environment (`Command::env`/`env_remove`'s map insert taken out of line, plus `activation_env`, about 3.6 KB net), and the binary's press join and token source (about 6 KB). The 8–20 KB estimate counted the Dispatch impls and the queue but not the per-service monomorphisation or calloop's inlining; under the owner's 2026-10-11 ruling ("those size overruns still exist and are fine", m5-integration-w2) it is recorded, not cut further, and the integrator's next re-base charges it. (These figures are `79f5c96`'s, before the review rounds; "the `.text` after review" below has the branch's.)

**2026-10-12 · m5-platform: review round 1.** Five confirmed findings, each fixed with a test that fails without it. (1) A `file` element's `run:` command (`run/outputs.rs`'s `run_once`) was the one program strand starts without `child::activation_env`, so it inherited the token strand was started with; it now goes through it, and architecture.md lists it (crates/strand/src/run/outputs.rs::tests::a_run_never_inherits_strands_activation_token, which runs a copy of the test binary started with both variables set). It still does not call `restore_in_child` (THP), which predates this stream; left for its owner. (2) Each held action's 200 ms ran from when the queue reached it, so N token-wanting actions in one invocation could hold the rest about N × 200 ms; each step now carries a deadline taken at submit and waits with `timeout_at`, so they wait together and the bound holds for the whole invocation (crates/strand-services/src/activation.rs::tests::token_waits_of_one_invocation_overlap). (3) An unanswered token was given up only when a later one was asked, not after 5 s as architecture.md and this file's callback decision say; each request now arms a calloop timer that gives it up (`done(None)`, the object destroyed) after `FORGET_AFTER`, removed when the answer comes. strand-fake-wayland gains `Cmd::HoldTokens` to stand for a compositor that never answers (crates/strand-surface/tests/fake.rs::an_unanswered_token_is_given_up_on_its_own). (4) Every click away carried the last press of ours, including the one strand-surface sends for a popup's `done` (the user clicked another client), whose serial is stale; `Forward` now marks a press fresh when `press_serial` tells it and spends that on the next input event, and a click away carries a press only when fresh (the catcher's), so a dismiss handler raised by the compositor asks no token with an old serial (crates/strand/src/demo/host.rs::tests::only_a_click_away_that_is_a_press_carries_one). (5) A held action was sent on the channel of the run in place when it was submitted, so a run that ended or was stopped (a reload's `stop_now`) during the wait lost it, after `act_with` had said `Ok`. Delivery from the shared runtime still sends directly (no extra hop for a launch), but under a per-run `stopped` lock that `stop` sets; an action that finds its run stopped or its channel closed goes back to the logic thread (`ClientInner::bounced`, with a services wake), and the next pump sends it through `with_run`, which starts a run for it as `act` does; one the old run still holds (its `Ended` not pumped yet) waits for the next pump, and `act_with` sends anything handed back before a new action, so order holds. Only a body waiting out its retry backoff refuses it, logged as a warning, as `act` refuses it then (crates/strand-services/tests/contract.rs::an_action_held_for_its_token_reaches_the_run_up_when_it_goes).

**2026-10-12 · m5-platform: review round 2.** Two confirmed findings in round 1's hand-back of held actions, each fixed with a test that fails without it. (1) An action of the same invocation submitted after its held action's run was stopped took the new run, queued behind the held one, and when the wait ended went straight to the new run while the held one was still on its way back through the logic thread, so `n.invoke("default"); await x; n.dismiss()` could close the notification before `ActionInvoked`: round 1's "order holds" was not true. Now a delivery from a token wait goes to `ClientInner::bounced` whenever that queue is not empty, not only when its own run is gone, and `redeliver` sends the queue to the run under the queue's lock, so a delivery racing it on the shared runtime waits and goes after (lock order: the queue, then the run's `stopped`; runs stop only on the logic thread) (crates/strand-services/tests/contract.rs::a_later_action_on_a_new_run_does_not_overtake_a_held_one). (2) Round 1's `deliver` always returned true, so a plain `Client::act` (no token wait) to a run whose body had ended, its `Ended` not yet pumped, returned `Ok` and the action went to the hand-back queue, where a failed body's retry backoff then dropped it with a warning; before, the caller got `not running`. `Deliver` now takes a flag saying whether it runs later from a token wait: sent at once on the logic thread, it never hands back and returns false for a run that cannot take it, so `act` reports the error again; only actions that already returned `Ok` while they waited are handed back (and those still drop with a warning in a backoff, as round 1 recorded) (crates/strand-services/tests/contract.rs::a_plain_action_to_an_ended_body_is_refused_not_lost). architecture.md's "Handler input context" says both.

**2026-10-12 · m5-platform: review round 3 — one hand-back queue for every service, joined by every action while it holds anything.** Two confirmed findings in round 2's hand-back, both fixed with a test that fails on round 2's code. (1) The rule that a later action never overtakes a held one was kept only on the token-wait path: an action sent at once checked no queue and relied on `act_with`'s `redeliver` having emptied it, but the drain on the shared runtime can hand a held action back (its run stopped) after that `redeliver` and before `Order::submit` finds its Line done, so `n.invoke("default"); await x; n.dismiss()` across a stop could still close the notification first. Now an action sent at once also joins the queue at the back while it holds anything, under the queue's lock, and the wake that came with the hand-back sends both on in order at the next pump; only with the queue empty does a run that cannot take it make `act` return `not running`, as round 2 kept (this amends round 2's (2): an action sent at once may now return `Ok` and wait in the queue, and if its service's body is then in its retry backoff it drops with a warning like any handed-back action; order wins over that error, which the queue's emptiness makes rare) (crates/strand-services/tests/contract.rs::an_action_sent_at_once_waits_behind_a_handed_back_one, which holds the window open with a handed-back action whose body ended unpumped). (2) The queue was per service (`ClientInner::bounced`) while the ordering line is per invocation across services, so a held `invoke` handed back to notifications' queue let the line's next step, `mpris.pause()`, go to mpris' live run at once, and `pump` redelivered member by member rather than in submit order. The queue is now the registry's (`Registry::bounced`): one `VecDeque` of `(member key, type-erased (Msg<S>, token))` in hand-back order, which every service's deliveries join; `Services::pump` sends it on after the services' envelopes (`Registry::redeliver`: for the front entry's service, `Member::ready_run` starts or finds its run off the lock, then under the lock every front entry for that service goes to it, and so on; an entry its run cannot take yet stops the queue for the next pump; a service taken away or in its backoff drops its entry with a warning), and `act_with` does the same before its own action. architecture.md's "Handler input context" says it (crates/strand-services/tests/contract.rs::a_held_action_handed_back_keeps_another_services_action_behind_it, with a second test service `Other`).

**2026-10-12 · m5-platform: the `.text` after review (rounds 1–3).** "The `.text`" above was measured at `79f5c96`, and rounds 1 and 2 added code without measuring again. `scripts/size-report.sh` with round 3 in place measures CPU-only 18,649,623 B and GPU 22,569,943 B: **+94,272 B and +96,832 B** against `aa3053c`, 74,272 B (GPU 76,832 B) over m5-plan's 20,000 B line and inside both gates (224,745 B and 236,585 B left; before, 269,161 B and 281,705 B). A CPU-only build at round 2's tip (`a5b9a8d`) measured 18,670,039 B: rounds 1–2 added +64,832 B over `79f5c96`, and round 3's one registry-wide hand-back queue took 20,416 B of that back (−19,249 B in strand-services, −1,071 B in tokio's), since round 2's `bounced`, `redeliver` and their `act_with` closure were monomorphised for every service. What rounds 1–2 still cost is the per-request calloop `Timer` sources and `give_up_token` (calloop's `DispatcherInner<Timer, …>` instances for `State`, about 1–1.3 KB each), the per-run `stopped` lock and the hand-back closures per service (`act_with::{closure#3}`, about 0.8–1 KB per service), the press freshness in `Forward` and `run_once`'s launch environment; no `79f5c96` symbol list was kept, so that rest is not split further. Under the owner's ruling (speed beats size; overruns are fine with a recorded reason) nothing is cut: the review fixes are correctness (no lost or reordered action, no stale token), and m5-plan's ledger charges the branch's figure for the integrator's re-base.

**2026-10-12 · m5-integration-w3 (integrator sweep): canvas paint order is pinned by a PNG test; the drop limit is in spec.md (sweep-11, sweep-9).** The guide's level 5 hedged that how `c.fill` and `c.stroke` combine with the shapes after them "is not yet pinned down by a test", and spec.md says nothing about canvas, so the freeze would have shipped it untested. The rule is the one `strand-render/src/canvas.rs` has had since M4 (its module comment): shapes add to one path; `fill` (non-zero) or `stroke` paints the shapes since the last paint and starts a new path, so a paint never reaches a later shape nor one an earlier paint took; a shape with no paint after it draws nothing; `fill` with no path paints the whole box, `stroke` with none draws nothing; later paints cover earlier ones. An offline PNG test now pins each clause, and the guide states the rule instead of the hedge (crates/strand-render/tests/canvas.rs::a_paint_takes_the_shapes_since_the_last_paint, ref `canvas_paint_order.png`). spec.md 6.7, about to be frozen, said a drop's `at` in another list leaves out "that list's first copy" of the item, which `drop_index` cannot do for a copy outside a windowed `list`'s mounted rows (m5-fixups). ## m6-services

S-services' M6 wave-1 hardening on `laptop/m6-services`: the four service limits handoff.md listed (remote media art, 802.1X joins and the inline join, a notification's time of day, `StepVolume`). Code comments that cite m6-services point here.

**2026-10-12 · m6-services: remote media art is fetched, with ureq over rustls.** `media.art` was null for `https://` art (Spotify, browsers; wave4-a2 left fetching "for when a shell needs it"), and design.md's `image media.art { fit: cover; filter: blur(30) }` backdrop wants it. `http://` is fetched too: design.md says nothing either way, MPRIS players send it, and the picture is checked like any other. A fetch never runs on the media body's loop, the logic thread or a frame: the body asks for it on the services runtime's blocking pool and goes on answering players and actions (`remote_art_is_fetched_cached_and_never_stalls_the_player` presses play/pause during a 4 s fetch). It reads at most 8 MiB (a refused `Content-Length` before the body, a body limit after), within 10 s end to end, redirects (at most 4) included, and keeps the bytes only if their signature is PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP (remote SVG is not taken). They are written as a content-addressed, pinned file beside the notifications' and tray's pictures (`pixmap::write_file`, which `write_png` now calls), so `art` is a path and the renderer decodes it at the drawn size on its image worker as any local picture; a panic in the fetch is a failed fetch. The body's `art::Cache` keeps the last 16 URLs' files (LRU by when each was last shown; the evicted file goes with its last handle), runs two fetches at once at most, and remembers the last 64 failures for 5 minutes, so a URL that is not a picture, is missing or times out costs one request however often a player repeats it, and `art` stays null (the shell's `?? "audio-x-generic"` shows). The client is `ureq` 3.4.2 (blocking, no async stack beside tokio; `rustls-no-provider`, no gzip, cookies or JSON) with `rustls` 0.23.45 on `ring` (no OpenSSL, no cmake) and the system's certificates through `rustls-native-certs` 0.8.4, read once on the first fetch (`SSL_CERT_FILE`/`SSL_CERT_DIR` honoured; webpki-roots not compiled in). reqwest or hyper would bring hyper, h2 and tower for one GET. Tests run a local HTTP server and a local HTTPS server with a test CA (`tests/fixtures/art-tls`, P-256, valid to 2126); nothing reaches the internet (crates/strand-services/src/art.rs::tests, crates/strand-services/tests/media.rs::remote_art_is_fetched_cached_and_never_stalls_the_player).

**2026-10-12 · m6-services: 802.1X and WEP join through a saved profile; a join is a task.** An enterprise (802.1X) network's login (EAP method, identity, certificates) is not something `connect_with(password)` can carry, and design.md has no prompt for it, so the reading closest to "does it remove a concept, or add one?" is: such a network joins with `ap.connect()` when NetworkManager has a profile saved for it (made in the system's network settings), which is activated as any saved profile is; `connect_with(password)` on it, and `connect()` on one without a profile, fail at once with an error that says which (`failed(ssid, error)`), and NetworkManager is asked to add nothing. WEP is treated the same: its saved profile joins, an unsaved one is refused ("WEP is not offered here"). A personal network (PSK or SAE) is unchanged; a key management offering both a password and 802.1X joins by password, Enhanced Open (OWE) counts as open, and an open network given a password is refused. The access point's kind is read from its flags before anything is asked, and the saved profile is looked up first. The join was also awaited inside the body's loop: up to 5 s per settings call and 25 s for the activation, during which the radio switch, NetworkManager's signals (the state other joins are followed by) and other joins waited. It now runs as a task with what the last read knew (the Wi-Fi devices and access points), its answer applied by the loop; an active connection that ended before its join's answer came is remembered (the last 32, only while a join is asked) so the answer settles at once, and an answer from a NetworkManager that has since restarted is a failure ("NetworkManager stopped"). python-dbusmock answers one call at a time, so the inline wait is shown against a NetworkManager of the test's own in zbus whose `ListConnections` takes 4 s (crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::{enterprise_and_wep_networks_join_only_through_a_saved_profile, a_slow_join_does_not_hold_up_the_radio}, crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::{enterprise_and_wep_networks_join_only_through_a_saved_profile, a_join_answered_after_its_connection_ended_is_settled_from_the_signal}).

**2026-10-12 · m6-services: `Date` gains `hour` and `minute`; `Notification.time` and `clock.now` fill them (spec.md 14).** `Notification.time` was a `Date` with no time of day, so a notification centre could not show "12:04" (wave4-a2's known gap: "the language track adds a time of day to `Date` (or a `received_at`), and the field follows"). The builtin `Date` record, whose doc already said "a date and time of day", gets two fields, `hour: int?` and `minute: int?`: an addition to a builtin schema entry, which spec.md 14's compatibility policy allows. They are optional, so `Date(year: …, month: …, day: …, weekday: …)` still builds; a separate `received_at` would add a second notion of a moment for one field. `Notification.time` and `clock.now` ("the current date and time") carry the hour and minute; `clock.today` and a calendar's days carry none, so design.md's `when d.date == clock.today` holds on today's cell as before. `format` formats the time of day when there is one (`n.time.format("%H:%M")`) and, without one, refuses a time pattern as before; `add` keeps it; `month_start` is a date. Filling them is a change to what two existing fields hold, so it is not covered by "additive" alone; it is made as a bug fix under spec.md 14, the same footing spec.md 6.7 gives the windowed-list drop limit (m5-integration-w3, sweep-9). spec.md 14 holds a builtin entry to its documented meaning, and the documented meaning was already a moment: `clock.now` is "the current date and time", `Notification.time` is "when it arrived", and their type is "a date and time of day". A value with the time of day cut off fell short of that meaning; the change makes the values what the schema said they were. What it changes for a program: `n.time == clock.today` and `clock.now == clock.today` were true on the same day and are now false (one has a time of day, the other has none), so a 1.0 shell that compared a moment with a date to mean "same day" now gets false. That shell relied on the defect (the documentation called the two different things), and a grep of every `.strand` file, guide page, design.md block and fixture finds no such comparison (the only `== clock.today` in tree is design.md's calendar `d.date == clock.today`, two dates, unchanged); comparing the day is `n.time.format("%F") == clock.today.format("%F")`. The alternative that changes no existing value, keeping `time` and `now` date-only and adding a `received_at` beside `time` (and a second `now`), was not taken: it adds a concept (two fields for one moment, one of them wrong by its own documentation) rather than removing one, and would leave `clock.now` documented as a time it never carried (review services-r1-2 corrected this paragraph's earlier "nothing is removed or changed in meaning"). Seconds are left out: `clock.now` is tracked on the minute, and a second-exact `now` would wake a shell reading it every second (crates/strand-compiler/src/vm/clock.rs::tests::a_date_can_have_a_time_of_day, crates/strand-services/tests/notifications.rs::the_server_serves_the_spec_and_the_store).

**2026-10-12 · m6-services: `StepVolume` is removed, not wired.** design.md steps the volume by assignment only: `audio.sink.volume -= dy * 0.05` in a handler and `strand set audio.sink.volume +5%` over IPC (example (d)). Both reach the audio thread as `SetVolume` (the VM's compound assignment, and `services::set_text` resolving the relative form against `ServiceHost`'s optimistic cell, which makes quick steps compound; wave4-audio), and design.md names no step action, so wiring `StepVolume` would add a second way to do what assignment does. It is removed with what only it used: the echo tracker's pending write (`Echoes::pending`, `base`), the core sync issued after every volume write and its sequence (`wait`, `synced`), and the tests of the step base; the echo readback every write uses is unchanged, and `writes_land_where_wpctl_reads_them` now clamps with `SetVolume` (crates/strand-services/tests/audio.rs::writes_land_where_wpctl_reads_them, crates/strand-services/src/audio/thread.rs::tests).

**2026-10-12 · m6-services (review round 1): what the fixes changed.** (services-r1-1) A join is a task, so it no longer waited for the one before it: two joins of one unsaved network (a double click) both found no saved profile and both called `AddAndActivateConnection`, leaving NetworkManager two profiles (`Home`, `Home 1`) and ending the first activation with a `failed` while the network came up. The body now asks one join per network name at a time (`network::Asked`): a join asked again with the same password while it is asked is a repeat and dropped (it is compared by a fingerprint, so the password is not kept); with another password it waits for the answer, the last one asked winning, and is then asked, so it finds the profile the first saved, as the inline await did. That bounds the join tasks to one per network name, plus one waiting join each (crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::two_joins_of_one_network_add_one_profile, crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::a_network_is_asked_one_join_at_a_time). (services-r1-4) When NetworkManager's owner changes, the joins still asking are stopped (`JoinSet::shutdown`) and each reported as `failed(ssid, "NetworkManager stopped")`, with the joins followed; before, a task between calls sent its next call (`ActivateConnection`, `AddAndActivateConnection`) to the well-known name, so the new NetworkManager activated a network while the service reported the join as failed and did not follow it. With the tasks stopped, the per-generation check on an answer is gone (crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::a_join_stops_when_networkmanager_is_replaced). (services-r1-2) The `Date` paragraph above no longer says nothing changed in meaning: filling `hour` and `minute` for `clock.now` and `Notification.time` is recorded there as a spec.md 14 bug fix, with what it changes for a program and why `received_at` was not taken. (services-r1-3) Fetched art is on `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, a tmpfs, so its files are memory outside the process's PSS that neither `strand report` nor the budgets see, and 16 files of up to 8 MiB was up to 128 MiB. `art::Cache` now also holds its files to `art::KEPT_BYTES` (16 MiB, two of the largest pictures) together, dropping the least recently shown first but never the URL shown last or the newest; usual covers (100 KB to 2 MB) still fill all 16 places. `MAX_BYTES` stays 8 MiB so a lossless cover still shows; re-encoding to a smaller size was not taken, since it would decode on the services side what the renderer already decodes at the drawn size (crates/strand-services/src/art.rs::tests::the_cache_is_bounded_by_its_bytes_and_keeps_what_is_shown). `art::fetch` returns `art::Art { file, bytes }` for this (architecture.md follows). (services-r1-7) The first half is refuted by the review itself: `media`'s `signal()` reports a change for every player `PropertiesChanged`, identical metadata included, so `shown()` and `Cache::start` run on every resend and the "no retry storm" assertion does depend on the failure memory. The second half holds and is fixed: a picture sent chunked with no `Content-Length`, 1 MiB over `MAX_BYTES` (under ureq's own default limit), is refused by the read limit, and one within it is taken (crates/strand-services/src/art.rs::tests::https_art_is_fetched_checked_and_kept_as_a_file).

**2026-10-12 · m6-services (review round 1, services-r1-8): built, tested and measured; remote art overruns both `.text` gates, recorded for the integrator and the owner.** The tree is built and its lock file updated (`ureq` 3.4.2 with `ureq-proto`, `rustls` 0.23.45, `ring` 0.17.14, `rustls-webpki` 0.103.15, `rustls-native-certs` 0.8.4); the ureq calls compile as written. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean, and `strand-services` (lib, `network`, `media`, `notifications`, `audio`) and `strand-compiler` pass in the container, as does `strand-dev`'s reference-currency test. `scripts/size-report.sh` on this tree measures CPU-only `.text` 19,633,431 B (+922,304 B over 18,711,127 B at `361296e`) and GPU 23,550,935 B (+920,640 B over 22,630,295 B): 759,063 B and 744,407 B over the gates (18,874,368 and 22,806,528 B), so `crates/strand/tests/budgets.rs::the_release_binary_code_stays_within_its_gate` fails on this branch until the gate is re-based or the stack changes. The HTTPS stack is about 778 KB of it, by crate (CPU build): `rustls` 286,712 B, `ring` 257,889 B (88,835 B of Rust and 169,054 B of its C and assembly), `ureq` 108,788 B, `webpki` 49,728 B, `http` 29,988 B, `rustls_pki_types` 17,212 B, `ureq_proto` 12,387 B, `rustls_native_certs` 8,659 B, and under 8 KB of `httparse`, `base64`, `log`, `zeroize` and the rest; the remainder is this stream's own code (the join task's `ask` future, `art`, the media body's fetch) and the generic instantiations it brings. Nothing cheaper was found inside this choice: `ureq` turns on `rustls`'s `logging` and `tls12` itself (`cargo tree -e features -i rustls`), so dropping them from strand-services' line measured the same 19,633,431 B, and the TLS crates are already at opt-level `z` (ring's handshake crypto left at its default). Under the owner's policy (speed beats size; the gates are regression tripwires and an overrun is fine with its reason) the reason is: design.md's media backdrop (`image media.art { fit: cover; filter: blur(30) }`) needs the art Spotify and browsers send, which is `https://`, and a TLS client with certificate checking is the smallest correct way to read it in-process; none of it runs on the frame, reload or logic path. The alternatives, for the owner rather than this stream: (a) accept and re-base both gates by the measured figures (the integrator's, in `budgets.rs`); (b) fetch remote art with the system's `curl` on the blocking pool, close to zero `.text` but a runtime dependency strand does not have today and a process per cover; (c) put remote art behind a default-on cargo feature, so a size-sensitive build drops it; (d) plain `http://` art only, which loses the players that matter. The features.md boxes stay unticked until the integrator has merged and re-run the budgets.

**2026-10-12 · m6-services (review round 2): `secure` matches the join rules, a repeat during the activation is dropped, skipped tracks' fetches do not hold up the shown art, and the shown art's file outlives its body.** (services-r2-1) Round 1's join rules contradicted the `secure` flag the schema tells a shell to gate its password field on ("It needs a password"): `secure` was true for any RSN flag, so an Enhanced Open (OWE) network and every 802.1X one said they needed a password, and `connect_with` on them was then refused; and an unsaved WEP network's `connect()`, which reached NetworkManager's secret agent before (as the schema's `connect()` doc still says), was refused before NetworkManager was asked. Of the two ways out (a new `AccessPoint` field telling a password network from a profile-only one, or `secure` holding what its doc says), the second removes a concept rather than adding one: `secure` is now true exactly where `connect_with(password)` joins, a personal (WPA, WPA2, WPA3) or WEP network, and false for open, Enhanced Open and 802.1X networks. That changes what an existing builtin field holds for OWE and 802.1X networks, so it is made as a bug fix under spec.md 14, as the `Date` paragraph above is: the field's documented meaning was already "It needs a password", and the values now are what it said (a shell that drew a lock from `secure` no longer draws one on an 802.1X network; the schema never promised "encrypted"). WEP, rather than being refused, joins as a personal network does: `connect()` on an unsaved one asks NetworkManager, whose secret agent asks for the key, and `connect_with(key)` carries it (`key-mgmt` `none`, `wep-key0`, `wep-key-type` 1 for a 5- or 13-character or 10- or 26-hex-digit key, else 2, a passphrase), which is what made `secure` true for it honest; round 1's "WEP is not offered here" is withdrawn. An enterprise network still joins only through its saved profile. The schema's `secure`, `connect()` and `connect_with` docs say this (docs/reference follows); an addition-free doc change to a frozen builtin entry, allowed as above (crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::secure_is_exactly_the_networks_a_password_joins, crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::enterprise_networks_join_only_through_a_saved_profile, renamed from `enterprise_and_wep_…`). (services-r2-2) `network::Asked` dropped a repeat only while its task waited for NetworkManager's answer; once `ActivateConnection` or `AddAndActivateConnection` answered (quickly), the join moved to the followed activations and a second click activated the network again, ending the first activation with a `failed` ("the Wi-Fi device disconnected") while the network came up, so round 1's double-click claim held only inside the ask window. A followed activation now keeps its password's fingerprint, and a join of a network being activated with the same password is a repeat and dropped; with another password (a corrected one, or `connect()` after `connect_with`) it is asked, and the activation it replaces is followed no more, so its end is not a failure while the new one's is (crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::a_repeat_while_the_join_is_activating_is_dropped, crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::a_repeat_of_a_join_activating_is_dropped). (services-r2-3) `art::Cache::start` is asked only for the URL shown, so with two slots the fetches of two skipped tracks on stalled hosts held the shown track's art back for up to `art::TIMEOUT` (10 s). A blocking ureq call cannot be cancelled, so a skipped track's fetch runs on (its file kept for a skip back); `art::IN_FLIGHT` is raised to 6, and what it bounds is restated: the threads stalled hosts may hold, not a queue the shown art waits in, which it now does only after six skips within 10 s, each across a stalled host (crates/strand-services/src/art.rs::tests::stalled_fetches_of_skipped_tracks_do_not_hold_up_the_shown_art). Per-phase timeouts or a cancellable reader were not taken: neither frees a thread stalled in a connect sooner than the global timeout does without an async client. (services-r2-4) A fetched cover's file was pinned only by the media body's `art::Cache`, while the store's `art` holds just its path and keeps publishing it after the body ends (a restart after an error, or the stop when nothing reads `media`); the cache going removed the file, so an `image media.art` built meanwhile read a missing file and drew nothing (`??` does not apply to a non-null path). The body now takes the cache the last body left and leaves its own, the shown file only and no fetch counted as running, however it ends (`media::Kept`, a drop guard over a process-wide slot), so the published path names a file that is there and the next body shows it without fetching it again; at most one cover (8 MiB at most) stays on the tmpfs while `media` is stopped. Clearing `art` when the body ends was not taken: a stopped run's update is not applied (crates/strand-services/tests/media.rs::remote_art_is_fetched_cached_and_never_stalls_the_player, crates/strand-services/src/art.rs::tests::the_cache_left_to_the_next_body_keeps_only_the_shown_file).

**2026-10-12 · m6-services (review round 3): a body's running fetches go to the next body, the cache it leaves is its runtime's, and a new password merges into a saved profile.** (services-r3-1) Round 2's `Cache::keep_shown` cleared `fetching` when a media body ended, but its fetches were `spawn_blocking` tasks in the body's `JoinSet`, which dropping cannot cancel: they ran on for up to `art::TIMEOUT`, their ends were thrown away, and the next body, counting none of them, fetched the same URL again beside the first (the body does end inside 10 s: `STOP_GRACE` is 5 s, and a bus error restarts it), so `IN_FLIGHT`, the threads stalled hosts may hold, did not hold across bodies, and a failure that ended after its body was never remembered. Of the two ways out the finding names, the fetches are handed over: they are detached blocking tasks that report `(url, result)` on a channel left with the cache (`media::Left`), `keep_shown` keeps `fetching`, and the next body applies their ends as its own, so a URL being fetched is not fetched beside itself and a failure lands in `failed`. A picture that comes in while no body runs is not kept (only the shown file is kept while `media` is stopped, as round 2 bounded it): the fetch sees the body flag down and sends no file, and the next body calls `art::Cache::abandon(url)`, which stops counting it without recording a failure, so it may be fetched once more if shown (crates/strand-services/src/media.rs::tests::fetches_running_when_a_body_ends_are_counted_by_the_next, crates/strand-services/src/art.rs::tests::the_cache_left_to_the_next_body_keeps_only_the_shown_file). (services-r3-2) The slot was a process-wide static, so in a process with more than one services runtime (tests/media.rs runs four tests in parallel) one runtime's body ending replaced, or took, another's cache, dropping its pinned file and making round 2's assertions racy. It is now a thread-local: every services runtime is one `strand-services` thread (`client::Shared`), the media body runs on it and its `Kept` drops there, so the slot is the runtime's and the shell's single runtime behaves as before; what a thread left goes with the thread. Serialising the tests would have hidden the sharing rather than removed it (crates/strand-services/src/media.rs::tests::another_runtime_s_body_does_not_take_what_this_one_left). (services-r3-3) A password given for a saved profile replaced its whole `802-11-wireless-security` section with `key-mgmt` and the key, so a shared-key WEP profile (new in round 2, which stopped refusing WEP) lost `auth-alg: shared` and its `wep-tx-keyidx` and failed authentication from then on, and a saved WPA profile lost `proto`, `pmf` and its secret flags (from before round 2). The new secret is now merged into the section the profile has (`network::merged_security`): its other keys stay, `key-mgmt` and `psk` (or the WEP key and `wep-key-type`) are written, and a WEP key goes at the profile's transmit index (`wep-key<wep-tx-keyidx>`), the key NetworkManager sends with. A section of the other kind (a WEP profile given a WPA password, or the other way) has nothing that applies and is replaced as before (crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::a_new_key_keeps_the_saved_profile_s_security_settings, crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::a_new_password_keeps_the_saved_profile_s_security_settings). The schema's `connect_with` doc (the password is "saved in its connection") still says what happens; no spec change.

## m6-edges

**2026-10-12 · m6-edges (M6 wave 1, S-edges): a drop's `at` is exact in a windowed `list`, by logic, and spec.md 6.7's limit is removed under spec.md 14.** spec.md 6.7 defines `at` as the place among the target's rows counted without the dragged item (in another list, without its first copy), and named a limit of the implementation: render has only a windowed list's mounted rows, so a copy scrolled out above them was counted and `at` was one too high (m5-fixups, m5-integration-w3). Of the two fixes the stream was offered, logic's is taken: render keeps owning `at`'s meaning over the rows it can see (the kanban, per-item target and dock rules stay where they are), and only the rows before the mounted window, which logic holds and render does not, are judged by logic. The other fix (logic sending render each row's identity and place) would put the whole list's identities on every list change for a correction needed only at a drop. So `strand_render::NodeEvent::Drop` gains `hidden: Option<HiddenRows { list, before }>`: `drop_index` sends it when the drop is a `drag:` source of another list (in its own list the source's row is mounted and is the one left out) on a list with `row_first > 0`, and the mounted copy it left out, if any, is not before the pointer (if it is, a copy above the window would have been the first and left out in its place: the same count). Before the pointer is judged by the copy's middle against the pointer when it is laid out, as the pointer is placed among the other rows, and by its place among them only when it is not: a copy just past the pointer sits in the gap the pointer's index names, so its place alone would call it before (m6-edges review, edges-r1-6). `run::NodeEvent::Drop` carries `hidden` to the logic thread, and `drop_args` asks `Instance::drop_at`, which makes `at` one less when one of the list's first `before` items is a copy by render's own test: a row holding a `drag:` value of the dragged value's typed identity (`strand_scene::drag_identity`, the type's name and then a keyed record's key or the value). A row not mounted has no `drag:` value, so logic reads off the mounted rows what one of each row's own `drag:` values (render's walk; review round 2, below) is of its item: the item, its key or one of its fields, the one that fits every mounted row, and judges the hidden items by it. So a `Tile` or a text dropped on rows of another type keyed by the same text is no copy, nor is anything among rows with no `drag:`, as render finds none among the mounted rows either; the first draft's untyped identity made `at` depend on the scroll position there (edges-r1-4). What still differs: rows whose `drag:` value is not one of those of the item (or not the same one for every mounted row) are never copies to logic, where render can find a copy among them while mounted; for these `at` stays one too high when the copy is above the window, as before M6. `before` is render's `row_first`, so the count matches what render counted even if logic's window has moved since. spec.md 6.7 now says `at` holds in a windowed list too, and keeps the narrower limit just described as one of the implementation (that narrower limit was removed in turn by the integrator's sweep, m6-integration-w1 sweep-1, which evaluates a hidden row's `drag:` values from its item); this is a bug fix under spec.md 14 (no syntax or schema entry changes, and the meaning is the one 6.7 already stated), which the limit's own text named it. Proved by `crates/strand-compiler/tests/render.rs::a_drop_on_a_scrolled_windowed_list_is_exact` (two monitors' docks compiled, rendered and routed; `p5` from DP-1 let go between DP-2's `p42` and `p43`, DP-2 scrolled to row 40: render's 43 with rows 0..40 hidden, 42 after `drop_at`, and the pins land in that order), `crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::a_drop_on_a_windowed_list_names_the_rows_it_could_not_see` (a `list` target: a copy above the window, one mounted before the pointer, one past it, and the source's own list) and `::a_per_item_drop_on_a_windowed_list_names_the_rows_it_could_not_see` (per-item targets: either side of a row's middle, a copy before the pointer, one just past it, and the drop on the item's own copy), `crates/strand/src/run/lists.rs::tests::a_drop_leaves_out_a_copy_render_could_not_see` and `::a_hidden_copy_is_one_by_renders_test` (pins, apps' texts, `Tile`s and installed `App`s keyed by the same texts, and rows with no `drag:`), `crates/strand/src/run/tests.rs::a_drop_reaches_its_handler_with_the_hidden_rows_judged` (`ToLogic::Event` through the logic thread to `on drop`) and `crates/strand/src/demo/host.rs::tests::drops_are_forwarded_to_logic`; the cross-monitor dock tests (`input.rs::a_drop_on_another_surface_leaves_out_its_copy_of_the_item`, `crates/strand-dev/tests/guide.rs::the_guide_dock_drops_where_the_pointer_is`) are unchanged. architecture.md's drag-and-drop bullet records the interface change, proposed for the owner's review.

**2026-10-12 · m6-edges: inspector write-back swaps the file in with `renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` and checks what it took out.** M5's write-back checked the target's inode and hash, then renamed the new text over it; an editor's save between the two was lost (POSIX has no compare-and-rename). Linux's exchange closes that window without a lock editors would not take: the rewritten file is exchanged with the target, then the file now at the temporary name (what was in place at the instant of the swap) must be the one hashed, same inode and same hash. If it is not (a save renamed into place, or the file written in place, at any moment before the check), the two are exchanged back and the edit is refused as `Changed`, so the editor's file is in place again, the same inode, and our file is removed only when it is still exactly ours (inode and text). If the file was saved again before the swap back (a new file renamed over the edit, or the edit written into), what the swap back brings out is that latest save: it is exchanged once more so the latest save is in place, the save before it is kept at the temporary name, and the refusal (`Io`) says so (each such exchange checked by what it brings out: review round 2, below). If the swap back fails, the refusal says what the file holds then and where the editor's save is kept. Nothing is removed that was not checked. The temporary name is each write's own (`.{name}.strand-dev-{pid}-{n}`, `n` counting this process's writes, a name left by another process passed over), so a version kept at one never blocks a later write of the file (the first draft's fixed name made every later write fail with `EEXIST`, edges-r1-2). Where the filesystem has no exchange (`EINVAL`, or `ENOSYS` before Linux 3.15) the M5 way is kept, the check just before a plain rename; it is chosen per write, silently (strand-dev has no logger, and the user can do nothing about it). What remains: an editor that already holds the file open and writes into it between the check of the file swapped out and its removal writes into the file being removed; recorded in handoff.md's known limits. The test hook is `write_with(edit, Swap::{Auto, Exchange, Rename}, hook)`, `hook` called at `Moment::Before` (the new text written, nothing swapped), `Moment::Window` (after the last look at the file before it is replaced: with the exchange, the file swapped out and not yet checked, at its temporary name; with the plain rename, the file checked and not yet renamed over) and `Moment::Back` (the file swapped out found changed, not yet swapped back). The first draft's hook ran before the swap only, which is also before M5's check, so its in-place test passed on the plain checked rename too; decisions.md's claim that it ran "in M5's order, the window between its check and its rename" was wrong (edges-r1-1). Proved by `crates/strand-dev/tests/inspect.rs::a_save_after_the_check_is_swapped_back_and_kept` (an editor's descriptor writes the file at `Window`: the exchange keeps it, the same inode, and the plain rename loses it, the window the exchange closes), `::a_second_save_before_the_swap_back_is_kept_in_place` (a save at `Window` and another at `Back`, renamed or written in place: the latest in place, the one before it kept and named, and the next write of the file goes through), `::a_swap_back_that_fails_says_the_edit_is_in_place` (the directory made read-only at `Back`) and `::a_rename_into_place_between_hash_and_write_is_refused` (both ways). architecture.md's `strand-dev` bullet and handoff.md's known limits follow.

## m6-lock

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: PAM's conversation reaches the lock as it happens; two additive `auth` fields, no new concept in the language.** m4-audit (round 3) deferred streaming PAM's texts: on a stack with `pam_fprintd` ahead of `pam_unix` the lock never showed "Place your finger", the password never reached `pam_unix` inside the client's 30 s, and the fallback met the same wall. The fix keeps design.md's lock as it is (a `lock` that calls `auth.submit`, a helper, fails closed) and changes only what the helper and the `auth` service carry. The helper's protocol (version 2; the client refuses a version-1 hello) is a conversation: the client sends `BEGIN`, the helper runs `pam_authenticate` and sends each `PAM_TEXT_INFO`/`PAM_ERROR_MSG` as an `INFO` frame and each `PAM_PROMPT_ECHO_OFF` as a `PROMPT` frame the moment PAM's callback gets them, waits for the client's `SUBMIT` for each prompt, and ends with the `VERDICT`. `PAM_PROMPT_ECHO_ON` still fails the conversation closed (a password field cannot answer it). The `auth` service gains `message: text` (PAM's latest text, cleared when PAM next asks for a password and while no lock is shown) and `prompt: text` (the hidden prompt PAM waits on, "" otherwise); `busy`, `failed` and `submit` keep their meaning, `submit` now answering the prompt PAM waits on or the next one it asks. That is additive schema growth, which spec.md section 14 allows in 1.x ("builtin schema entries … are only added, never removed or changed in meaning"): every 1.x program keeps its meaning, a lock that reads neither field behaves as before on a password-only stack, and spec.md 5.1 gains two sentences saying so. Rejected: a lock-level prompt element or an `on message` event (a new concept where a field does), and a style field for errors (PAM's own texts already say which they are). Each hidden prompt takes one password, as `login` does; `Client::submit`, which the fallback field and the tests use, answers every prompt of its conversation with its one password, as the helper always did.

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: deadlines count only while a password waits for PAM or is with it.** One 30 s bound on the whole exchange cannot hold a module that waits on the user. The client now has no deadline while no password is waiting or with PAM (PAM may wait on a reader for as long as its module likes); once the helper has a password it must send a frame within the timeout (30 s, `AuthConfig::timeout`) of the last one or of the answer, so a module that keeps talking stays alive; and a password must be answered (the next prompt or the verdict) within `LIMIT_FACTOR` (3) timeouts, 90 s by default, of being sent, including the wait for PAM's prompt: room for `pam_fprintd`'s default 30 s ahead of `pam_unix`, which the task's "type a password while fprintd waits" needs. A frame once begun comes whole within the timeout. The cost: a module that hangs before PAM asks for anything, with a password typed, now takes up to 90 s rather than 30 s to show the fallback (whose own check goes through the same stack anyway); `tests/pam.rs::a_hanging_module_times_out_and_its_processes_are_killed` measures that limit and its bound is 10 s for a 1 s timeout. A dropped `Answers` (the lock ended, the store stopped) ends a conversation with no password in it (`AuthError::Cancelled`, the helper killed with its tree); one with a password runs to its verdict, which still reaches the sinks (m4-audit's "a check outlives its store").

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: the store keeps a conversation open only while a lock is shown, and never loops.** A fingerprint must work before any key, so PAM's conversation must run before a submit; but a conversation outside a lock would hold the fingerprint reader (fprintd claims a device for one client) while the user runs `sudo`. The binary tells the store through `auth::LockSignal` (`AuthConfig::lock`, set in `LockScreen::see` after the lock session's generation is bumped, and cleared at the unlock): while it is set the store begins a conversation (when the lock shows, or when the store starts under one), and begins the next after one a password was given to that did not unlock. One that ended with no password in it (a `pam_faillock` lockout ending at `preauth`, a helper that died while waiting, no helper at all) is begun again only by the next submit, so a stack that fails at once costs one conversation per key press, never a loop; and a failure in it is logged, not a fault: only a check with a password in it goes to the `FailureSink` (the fallback) and sets `failed`. A refusal with no password (the lockout) leaves `failed` as it was and its text in `message`. The conversation's session tag is read when it begins, so a finger's unlock for a lock session that has ended is dropped like a password's. Without a signal (tests, an embedder) each submit begins its own conversation, as before. `busy` is true from a submit until PAM answers that password: through a fingerprint module's wait when typed early, and false again when PAM asks another prompt (a one-time code). A password PAM cannot take (a NUL, longer than 511 bytes; `strand_auth::refusal`) is refused by the store before it is queued, by the client before it is sent, and by the helper.

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: the helper's fault points strike when a password arrives, and the tests that used `pam_permit` ask for one.** `auth_crash`, `auth_hang`, `auth_garbage` and `auth_stdio` used to fire on a `SUBMIT`; a `SUBMIT` now answers a prompt, so they fire there, inside the conversation callback, before PAM sees the password: the lock VM's fault matrix (a password typed into the config's lock, then the fault) is unchanged. A `pam_permit` stack never prompts, so the tier-A tests of the fault points and of `auth_stdio` now use a stack whose `pam_exec expose_authtok` accepts any password (`tests/pam.rs`'s `prompting`). The fallback field keeps `Client::submit` and shows no PAM text (strand-render's `lock_fallback` draws no text, and the fallback is the field that depends on least); its password goes through the same stack, so a fingerprint stack delays it by the reader's wait (`fingerprint_stack_in_the_fallback`).

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: the fingerprint is emulated in the lock VM with `pam_echo` and a waiting `pam_exec`.** fprintd needs a reader and a D-Bus daemon the VM has neither of; what the lock must handle is its shape: a `PAM_TEXT_INFO` text, then a silent wait that succeeds on a finger, ahead of `pam_unix`. `scripts/lockvm/scenarios/fingerprint.sh` installs that stack (`auth optional pam_echo.so file=…` saying "Place your finger on the fingerprint reader", `auth sufficient pam_exec.so` waiting 5 s for a file the tests touch, then the image's `common-auth`), runs `vm_pam.rs::pam_fingerprint_then_password` with the shipping helper against real `pam_unix` and strand's `fingerprint_*` tests on headless sway, and puts the image's stack back; `strand_lock.sh` skips the `fingerprint_*` tests, which need the stack. The text comes from its own `pam_echo` line, not from `pam_exec`'s `stdout` option, so the text and the wait stay apart, as pam_fprintd's are, and the test does not depend on how `pam_exec` buffers its program's output. README's PAM section drops its password-only advice and says what a fingerprint stack still costs (a password typed during the reader's wait waits for it; after a wrong password PAM starts over with the reader); handoff.md's known limit says the same.

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: what ran, and its `.text`.** In the container: `cargo test -p strand-auth --features faults` (the client's conversation tests against fake helpers, the real helper's against private stacks with `pam_echo` and a waiting `pam_exec`), `cargo test -p strand-services --test auth`, strand's `run::lock` unit tests, strand-surface's `session_lock`, strand-dev's `ladder` and `spec`, and clippy on the workspace and with the `faults` features. In the lock VM, `scripts/lockvm/scenarios/all.sh` printed LOCK VM SCENARIOS PASSED: session_lock 9, strand_lock 31 (the four `fingerprint_*` tests skipped there), faillock 1, fingerprint 1 + 4, pam 1 + 1. `scripts/size-report.sh` measures CPU-only 18,735,127 B and GPU 22,654,295 B, +24,000 B each over M5's close (18,711,127 B and 22,630,295 B), inside both gates (18,874,368 B and 22,806,528 B): the client's conversation loop, the store's event channel and the watch.

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: the review's fixes (lock-r1-1 to lock-r1-5).** (1) `docs/reference/services.md` is regenerated (`cargo run -p strand-dev -- reference`): the `auth` section lists `message` and `prompt` and the new texts of `busy` and `submit`, so `reference::tests::the_reference_is_current` passes again; the stream had run only strand-dev's `ladder` and `spec`. (2) The store compares a running conversation's session tag with the current one. When the signal says a lock is shown and the conversation running was begun for a lock session that has ended (the binary ended a lock and showed the next before the store saw the `false`, which a `watch` may coalesce away, or the old conversation was still being killed), its answers are dropped, `busy`, `message` and `prompt` are cleared, and when it ends the new lock's conversation begins, whatever it ended with; a stale conversation's `failed` is not applied, and its unlock (which the binary drops) does not count as one. Before, such a lock showed no "Place your finger" and the finger did nothing until a password was typed. (3) What a conversation says (`message`, `prompt`, `busy` from a prompt) shows only while the signal says a lock is shown and only for the session the conversation began in, so a conversation that runs on after the lock goes (a password was in it) no longer sets `auth.message` on the desktop, as auth.schema and spec.md 5.1 already said. Without a signal nothing changes. (4) The services test now proves the store ends a conversation when the lock goes: the fake reader counts the moment it gives up waiting, and the test waits past it. Removing the store's `r.answers = None` fails that assertion; the two new cases fail without (2) and (3). Those were mutation-checked by hand: each fix undone, the test fails. (5) A password submitted after a conversation's blocking task returned but before the store took its verdict went into an `Answers` nobody read, and was lost with no `failed`. `strand_auth::Answers::take_back` (architecture.md, as an interface addition) returns the password no prompt took. When a conversation ends, the store takes back a password that the conversation never saw (`answered` false) and begins the next conversation with it, as a fresh submit. A password submitted while a conversation is ending (its answers dropped) is held for the next one the same way, while a lock is shown. Outside a lock it is dropped as before, since a conversation there would hold the fingerprint reader. A password the conversation did see (one still waiting when the verdict came) is not resubmitted, so a stack that refuses at once cannot loop. The store-level window is too narrow to hit deterministically (the select between the task's join and the submit), so the test is the API's (`crates/strand-auth/tests/client.rs::a_password_sent_too_late_is_taken_back`). The lock VM's `scripts/lockvm/scenarios/all.sh` printed LOCK VM SCENARIOS PASSED on these changes.

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: the second review's fixes (lock-r2-1, lock-r2-3).** (lock-r2-1) Once `pam_fprintd` gave up (30 s, or its max-tries) PAM went on to `pam_unix`'s prompt and the conversation waited there with no deadline, and the store began a new one only after a refused password, so a lock left past the reader's wait (the idle lock, the most common one) never listened to the finger again, against design.md's "a finger unlocks". Of the two readings (record the limit and soften design.md, or have the reader listen again) the fix takes the second, since it keeps design.md's promise and adds no concept to the language: `auth::LockSignal` gains `wake()` (and `wakes()`, a count), which the binary's `LockScreen::input` calls for each key, pointer motion, button and axis event while a lock is shown (not focus changes). On a wake, when the conversation running waits on a prompt that came after a text and no password was given to it (the reader ahead of it gave up), the store ends it (its answers dropped, its helper killed, `prompt` cleared) and begins the next once it has, so "Place your finger" shows again and the reader listens. A stack with no text before its prompt (password only), a conversation whose reader still waits, one with a password in it (a one-time code's second prompt) and one from an ended lock session are left alone; with no input nothing begins, so nothing loops. Rejected: restarting when PAM prompts after only texts (a reader that fails at once would loop, and the prompt would never stay) and restarting on a timer (the same, slower). The cost, recorded in README and handoff.md: the wake is the first key of a password too, so a password typed on a lock whose reader gave up waits through the reader's wait again, as one typed at a fresh lock does; a user who wants the password at once keeps `pam_unix` alone, as README says. design.md's lock sentence adds that waking the lock has the reader listen again; spec.md 5.1 already says a module needing no password can unlock and is not changed (the language is frozen and this is behaviour, not syntax or schema). architecture.md names `wake`/`wakes` and the binary's call as an interface addition. (lock-r2-3) `UnlockToken`'s rustdoc names `Client::converse` beside `Client::submit`, and that `converse` mints one for a conversation no password was given to when the stack succeeds without one; architecture.md's `auth` paragraph says a refusal of a password or a check with one in it that could not be made sets `failed`, while one with no password in it (the lockout, a cancelled conversation) leaves it as it was, as the store does. Tests: `crates/strand-services/tests/auth.rs::auth_checks_through_the_helper_and_only_success_unlocks` (a reader that gives up is asked again only after a wake, a wake while it listens or at a textless prompt begins nothing; with the store's restart disabled it fails at "the reader asked again"), `crates/strand/src/run/lock.rs::tests::input_on_a_shown_lock_wakes_auth`, and in the lock VM `crates/strand/tests/lock.rs::fingerprint_a_woken_lock_listens_to_the_reader_again` (a key on a lock at the password prompt, then the finger, unlocks). The lock VM's `scripts/lockvm/scenarios/all.sh` printed LOCK VM SCENARIOS PASSED (session_lock 9, strand_lock 31, faillock 1, fingerprint 1 + 5, pam 1 + 1).

**2026-10-12 · m6-lock: the third review's fixes (lock-r3-1, lock-r3-2).** (lock-r3-1) lock-r2-1's wake restarted any conversation waiting on a password prompt that came after a text with no password given, so on a stack where a module that only speaks comes ahead of `pam_unix`, every key press, release and pointer motion killed the helper and began a conversation that said the same and asked again: a `pam_echo` banner for every user, and Arch's `system-auth`, whose `auth required pam_faillock.so preauth` (no `silent`) says "The account is locked …" during a lockout and, being `required` rather than `requisite`, goes on to `pam_unix`'s prompt. The "nothing loops" of lock-r2-1 held only with no input, and the earlier paragraph's "a `pam_faillock` lockout ending at `preauth`" holds only for `requisite` (the VM's `faillock` scenario); under `required` the lockout's conversation reaches the prompt and is now left alone, as below. Of the three remedies the review offered (restart only when the text's module then waited, once per prompt until a new text, rate-limit wakes) the fix takes the first, since it is what "the reader gave up" means and needs no counter or clock the user could notice: the client's callback timestamps each text and prompt, and a wake restarts only a conversation whose prompt came `auth::READER_WAIT` (2 s) or more after its first text. pam_fprintd waits 30 s by default (10 s as Ubuntu sets it) or until the finger has been tried, while texts from modules that do not wait reach the prompt in milliseconds, so 2 s separates them with room for a slow PAM; the VM's emulated reader waits 5 s and the services test's 3 s. A restarted conversation can be restarted again only after its own wait, so input drives at most one restart per reader wait. Measuring from the first text rather than the last keeps a reader that says "timed out" just before giving up restartable; measuring from it rather than from the conversation's start keeps a slow module ahead of a banner from counting as a wait. Rejected: once per prompt until a new text (an idle lock woken twice would not listen the second time, against design.md's promise) and a rate limit (still restarts a banner stack, only less often, and clears the prompt while the user types). `READER_WAIT` is an interface addition in architecture.md. Kept as a recorded limit rather than code: the limit is what turns a module that hangs with a password in it into the fallback (removing it while no prompt has come would leave the lock busy for ever on a hung module), and no frame tells a waiting reader from a hung one. README's PAM section now says to keep `timeout=` under 90 s and why, handoff.md's known limit says the same, and `crates/strand-auth/tests/client.rs::a_reader_wait_past_the_limit_times_out_a_password_typed_early` pins the behaviour the docs describe (a 5 s wait against a 4.5 s limit: the early password and `submit` both time out).
