The router now moves the pointer into the widget's laid-out box first (`InputScene::to_laid`, `Renderer::to_laid`: through the node's last hit box, so offsets, glides and transforms are undone the way hit testing applies them) and keeps the laid-out arithmetic (the knob's span) unchanged. Alternatives: give the router drawn rects instead of laid-out ones (every caller of `node_rect` would change, the drop-index code among them, which reads row boxes against each other and is not affected here), or forbid paint offsets above widgets (drops a feature). Pointer coordinates themselves were right: they are surface-local, and the popup's window-geometry overhang, its negative margin and bug 6's placement shift do not enter them; fractional scale only rounds the drawn box to physical pixels (under 0.4 logical px at 1.5). Proven at scales 1 and 1.5 (`crates/strand-render/tests/widgets.rs::widgets_moved_by_paint_offsets_read_the_pointer_where_drawn`).

**2026-10-14 · m6-owner-fixes: a hover popup takes its whole box while a press on it is held (owner-testing.md bug 15).** The owner's island folds, closes or stops following while a slider on it is dragged. Strand and the config both keep it on headless sway: a held press keeps `hover` latched on the pressed chain, the card the config folds on included, and keeps the popup open (spec.md 6.3), and sway's implicit grab sends every motion to the popup. Hyprland 0.56.2 keeps the pointer on the pressed surface only while some surface has keyboard focus and is mapped (`InputManager.cpp:412-413`, "focus held by buttons"); a `trigger: hover` popup never takes the keyboard, so on a workspace with no focused window the pointer leaves the popup as soon as it leaves its input region, which for a popup that draws nothing is the drawn card (m6-w2-surface). The leave ends the drag and the hover with no release ever seen. A client cannot keep a pointer the compositor takes; it can keep the region it sits in. So while a press that went down on such a popup is held its input region is the popup's whole box (`Painter::input_region` returns none, the surface manager's own region; the press marks the popup for the frame that commits it), and the island's region comes back on the release. This adds no concept: the region was always "what the popup is used through", and during a drag that is the popup. Alternatives: keep Strand's press across a leave (the release goes to another client, so the press would stick until some later release on the popup), or ask for a pointer grab (only `xdg_popup.grab`, which needs the opening press's serial and takes the keyboard, which spec.md 5.1 rules out for hover popups). Past the popup's box Hyprland still takes the pointer. Proven in `crates/strand-render/tests/boxes.rs::a_held_press_takes_the_hover_popups_whole_box`; Hyprland's behaviour needs the owner's run. A popup whose surface goes while the press is held (the compositor closed it mid-drag) is let go with it: `Router::detached` releases the press, so its chain hears `pressed` false at the next flush and the popup does not open again with its whole box as its region (review of the integration: the router dropped the press silently and the renderer kept the root pressed; crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::a_surface_that_goes_mid_press_is_not_left_pressed, which failed before).

**2026-10-14 · m6-owner-fixes: a popup that maps under a still pointer is hovered at once (owner-testing.md bug 12, B-d).** The owner's island opens its dashboard popup over the island (a negative margin) while the pointer rests there; `card.hover` read false until the pointer moved, while the popup stayed open (the router saw the pointer on its anchor). Headless sway 1.9 sends no `wl_pointer.enter` to a popup that maps, or whose input region grows, under a pointer that does not move: the pointer stays on the bar until the next motion (`crates/strand/tests/hover_popups.rs::a_hover_popup_mapped_under_a_still_pointer_is_hovered` failed so). Hyprland 0.56.2 re-picks once on map (`Popup.cpp` `onMap` calls `simulateMouseMovement`), but only against the region the popup's first commit carries, and never when the region grows later. The pointer's place is not in doubt, and spec.md 6.3 defines `hover` by where it is, so Strand works it out itself: after each frame a popup paints, if the pointer is still on a surface the popup opens from (directly or through popups), on the same output, and the popup now takes input there (its painted input region, or its box), the host takes the pointer onto the popup (`Host::rebase_pointer`): that surface hears a leave and the popup an enter at the same place, through the router as if the compositor had sent them. Until the compositor moves the pointer itself, its events for the old surface go to the popup moved by the two surfaces' origins (a motion off the popup ends it, with a leave of the popup and an enter of the old surface); its own leave of the old surface was already heard and is dropped, its enter of the popup becomes a motion, any other enter or leave ends it, and the popup closing gives the pointer back. A leave of the old surface with no enter of the popup by the end of the batch of events it came in (`Host::settle_rebase`, called after each dispatch of the main loop: a compositor sends the leave and enter of one motion together) means the pointer went to another client's surface: the rebase ends and the popup hears a leave, and the popup closing later gives the old surface nothing. Strand's own leave and enter are heard before the rebase starts (review of the integration: they went through the rebase themselves, so the old surface heard no leave, its item stayed hovered under the popup, and the rebase ended as it began, sending a click without a motion to the bar; crates/strand/src/demo/host.rs tests::a_popup_mapped_under_a_still_pointer_takes_it_from_the_bar and ::a_rebase_ends_when_the_compositor_takes_the_pointer_elsewhere, which failed before). Not while a button is held (the compositor keeps the pointer on the pressed surface), during a drag, or in pick mode. Alternatives: re-derive `hover` in the router from a cached position without moving events (the anchor would stay hovered and a click would go to the bar under the popup), or ask the compositor to re-pick (there is no request for it; a zero-length pointer warp needs pointer-constraints and focus). Nothing new in the language; spec.md 6.3 says it, for a pointer on a surface the popup opens from only (review of the integration: its sentence said any popup opening under a still pointer, and the island's `big` opening over its sibling `peek` under the pointer is not taken). Only there is the popup sure to be above the pointer's surface, a popup being stacked above the one it opens from; a sibling popup or another client's layer surface is stacked as the compositor chooses (creation order on wlroots, unverified on Hyprland), and taking the pointer onto a popup under it would hover what the pointer cannot reach. A sibling case, if the owner's island needs it, takes the stacking from the compositor first.

**2026-10-14 · m6-owner-fixes: `open:` opens a `trigger: hover` popup from code (owner-testing.md gap 21, G-b).** The owner's island needs a peek (a live activity) that hands over to the dashboard, a `trigger: hover` popup, and a hover popup took no `open:` (a load error, m6-w2-surface), so nothing but the pointer could open it. Taken: `open:` on a `trigger: hover` popup opens it from code and holds it. While its value is true the popup is open whatever the pointer does (at once, without its `delay`, closing another hover popup open from the same surface, as the pointer's would); once it is false the pointer holds it as any hover popup, so it stays while the pointer is on it or its element and closes after its `grace` otherwise. It is one way: `open: <-> x` on such a popup stays a load error (`check::hover_popup_open`, now about two-way only), since the pointer, not the program, closes it, and `p.open` reads whether it shows. The handover is `open: handing`, set when the pointer has rested on the peek's middle and cleared `on show`, and the pointer (taken onto the popup under it, B-d) holds it from there. This removes a rule rather than adding a concept: every surface already says whether it shows with `open:`, and a hover popup now does too, with the pointer as a second reason to show. Lowering: the compiler binds such a popup's `open:` (in its props or a `when`) to `Prop::Hold`, a scene prop never written in source like `watch` and `two_way`, and leaves `Prop::Open` to the router's writes (`NodeState::open`), so the router's open/write bookkeeping is untouched; `Router::observe` keeps the held set (architecture.md). Alternatives: an action on the popup id, `big.show()` (adds methods on node ids, which spec.md 8.3 keeps read-only, and leaves a shown popup with no state saying why); `open:` as an edge that only opens (the program would have to reset it to open again, and could not keep it open); `open:` OR the pointer with no grace once it lets go (the popup would close under a pointer resting on it in some orders). Proven in `crates/strand-render/tests/input.rs::open_on_a_hover_popup_opens_and_holds_it`, `crates/strand-compiler/tests/instantiate.rs::open_on_a_hover_popup_is_its_hold`, the checker's `a_hover_popup_takes_no_two_way_open`, and on headless sway `crates/strand/tests/hover_popups.rs::open_opens_a_hover_popup_from_code_and_holds_it`; spec.md 6.3, the schema's `trigger` doc (elements.md) and the guide's level 3 say so.

**2026-10-14 · m6-owner-fixes: `hit: none` (owner-testing.md gap 22, G-c).** The owner's island wants parts of a drawn element to let the pointer through (a hover popup's island whose card is larger than what should hold the pointer, a decoration over a control), and nothing per node could say so: a hover popup's input region was each drawing top-level element's whole box. Taken: `hit` takes the keyword `none` beside `grow(n)` (`enum HitKeyword { none }`, the shape of `radius: corners | RadiusKeyword`). A node with `hit: none` has no hit shape of its own, so a point inside it and outside its children hits what is below; its children keep theirs, and a hit on one still lists the node among its ancestors, so the node's `hover` and its handlers above the child work as before. On a `trigger: hover` popup that draws nothing, such a top-level element hands the input region to its children's boxes (recursively, until one without it). This extends a prop that already says how a node takes the pointer rather than adding one. Alternatives: `pointer: none` as CSS's `pointer-events` (a new prop, and CSS's version also stops the children unless they opt back in, which is the opposite of what the island needs); `input: false` on the popup only (covers the region case but not a decoration over a bar); a subtree-wide `hit: none` that also stops the children (then a card could not pass the pointer through its gaps while its controls take it, the owner's case; a subtree that should take nothing sets it on each node that would). Proven in `crates/strand-render/tests/boxes.rs::hit_none_takes_no_input_in_its_own_box`; spec.md 6.7 and the schema's `hit` doc (elements.md) say so.

**2026-10-14 · m6-owner-fixes (owner-testing.md gap 20): an action or write a builtin service cannot take is a service failure, never a runtime fault; `network`, `bluetooth` and `session` gain `available`.** What was a bug against the spec: spec.md 12 says service failures reach the program "as values (an action's error, an `Async`'s `.error`) and as service diagnostics; they never stop the shell", and 8.3 that "a failing action … never stops other handlers". But when a service's body could not run (no system bus, or one that does not answer: the body fails and waits out its retry backoff), `Client::with_run` refused the call and `DynService::action` and `write` returned that error to the VM, which faulted the handler's component in its red frame until a reload (the island bar's `on click: 'network' is not running`). And with the system bus disabled the idle body swallowed actions, so `session.lock()` neither did anything nor fired `session.failed`, which its docs promise for "no login session". The fix is at the service boundary, where what the failure means is known: an action that reaches no run is reported as that service reports the action failing, through a new `Service::refused(action, error) -> Option<Event>` (`#[service(refused = …)]`): `session.failed(action, error)`, `network.failed(ssid, error)` and `bluetooth.failed(address, error)`, the same events polkit's or BlueZ's refusals already arrive as, applied on the logic thread as the run's own event would be, and logged (the body's failure is already a service diagnostic). The idle body without a bus refuses its actions the same way. A write to a service that cannot run is dropped and logged, the field left as the service last reported it, as a write the rate guard held is when its run is gone. `DynService::action` and `write` now return an error only for what the program got wrong (an unknown action, a value of the wrong shape); `Client::act` keeps returning the refusal to Rust callers. What is new: a readable way to know a service can work before using it. Checked first: `session.can_*` are false without logind but also when logind forbids, `network.connected` is false offline, and `brightness.available` already says "a backlight was found". Alternatives weighed against design.md's "does it remove a concept, or add one?": (a) a generic `x.running` on every service adds a concept (a meta-field beside each service's own) whose meaning differs per service (a body running is not its daemon answering: `network` runs and reads "offline" without NetworkManager) and is noise on services that always run (`clock`, `cpu`); (b) a `services.running("network")` lookup adds a service and a stringly-typed name; (c) actions failing as values alone is needed but not enough, since a menu wants to hide its Wi-Fi toggle before it is clicked; (d) per-service `available`, the field `brightness` already has, adds no concept: `network.available` (NetworkManager or iwd answers), `bluetooth.available` (BlueZ answers with an adapter, so a laptop without one hides the menu) and `session.available` (logind answers). (d) with the fix is taken; `battery.present` already covers UPower's case, and services Strand serves itself (notifications, tray) or that have no daemon (cpu, clock) need none. spec.md 12, the schema docs and docs/reference say so (crates/strand-services/tests/session.rs::without_logind_session_is_unavailable_and_its_actions_fail_as_events, crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::an_unreachable_network_is_unavailable_and_fails_as_values, crates/strand-services/tests/contract.rs::errors_from_a_body_end_the_run_and_a_reader_restarts_it, strand `services::tests::a_service_that_cannot_run_fails_as_values_not_faults`, the `available` asserts in bluetooth.rs, network.rs and network_iwd.rs). `available` also goes false when a run that said true fails (review of the integration: a hung NetworkManager or a system bus connection ending left it true through the backoff, while every action was refused): the client sets a service's `available: bool` field to its default as a run fails (`Client::unavailable`), every other field keeping its last value, and the next run that answers says true again (crates/strand-services/tests/contract.rs::a_failed_run_is_not_available_while_it_backs_off, which failed before). And a caller outside the program hears the refusal (review of the integration: `DynService::action` returning Ok for a refused action made `strand call session.lock`, and its D-Bus front end, answer `{"ok": true}` while nothing locked, the refusal only logged for services with no failure event): `strand_services::catch_refusals` collects what `DynService::action` refused inside a closure, and `strand call` answers those as `session.lock: `lock`: why`; a handler is unchanged, hearing only the failure event. A per-call flag in `ActionCtx` was weighed and not taken, as it changes strand-core's struct every handler builds for one CLI path (strand `run::tests::strand_call_hears_an_action_the_service_could_not_take`, which failed before; the `catch_refusals` asserts in contract.rs::errors_from_a_body_end_the_run_and_a_reader_restarts_it). Nor is an action lost in a run that fails before reading it (review of the integration: a click on `session.lock()` just after the retry started a run still connecting to a system bus that does not answer went into that run's channel and was dropped with it, no `session.failed`): `Cx`'s `Drop` closes the queue and leaves its unread actions on the run, and the client refuses them as the run ends, with the run's error; writes and async calls left there end as before (the write dropped, the call's reply gone) (crates/strand-services/tests/contract.rs::an_action_a_failing_run_never_read_is_refused, which failed before).

**2026-10-14 · m6-owner-fixes (owner-testing.md gap 23): lists gain `index_of(test) -> int?`, `find`'s position.** The island bar stepped workspaces by scroll by comparing `id`s, because no list member gives an item's position, and an `id` is not the number `workspaces.focus(int)` takes on sway or niri. The name and shape follow the members already there: `find(test)`, `any(test)`, `all(test)` and `count(test)` all take a predicate named `test`, so `index_of(test)` is the same call answering "where" instead of "what", and `int?` because `find` is `T?` (null when no item passes). Alternatives: (a) `index_of(item)` by equality, as `contains(item)` is: it cannot find a record by a field (`w.focused`), which is the case found, and a predicate covers equality (`xs.index_of(x => x == "b")`); taking either would make one name mean two calls; (b) `position(test)` reads as geometry beside `.box` and layout; (c) `find_index(test)` names a second concept where one word does; (d) a `find` that also hands back the index, or `for (i, x) in`, adds a tuple or a new loop form. Indices count from 0 as `xs[i]` does, so `xs[(xs.index_of(t) ?? -1) + 1]?.focus()` steps to the next item, `null` past the end. It is not one of the `Async` transforms: on an `Async` list it is a load error, as `find` is (spec.md 8.6). spec.md 7.1 says so, and docs/reference/functions.md now lists a list's members under `[T]`, generated from the compiler's `list_members` (crates/strand-compiler/tests/checker.rs::index_of_is_an_optional_int_of_a_predicate, crates/strand-compiler/tests/vm.rs::index_of_finds_the_first_position).

**2026-10-15 · m6-owner-fixes: `attach:` keeps the margin on its side (owner-testing.md gap 26).** The island test bar grows its cards over its 32 px bar from the screen's edge with a negative top margin (gap 24), and could not use `attach: top` for their fillets: `attach:` made a popup's gap 0 whatever its margin, so the card opened below the bar, and it drew its concave ears itself (`Fillet` in `notch.strand`). A panel had the same rule (its margin on the attached edge forced to 0, m4-surface-w1), so a panel under a bar could not reach the screen's edge either. The owner-testing entry's likely direction, letting `attach:` name the screen's edge for a popup that covers its anchor, adds a second meaning to `attach:` and a rule for when it applies. The reading that removes a concept: `attach:` no longer places the box at all. It names the side the fillets go on (and a popup's side that touches its anchor, a panel's anchored edge, as before), and the margin on that side is kept like any margin: 0 while unset, so an attached surface still touches its anchor, the screen's edge or a bar's exclusive zone by default (a popup's unset gap is 0 rather than 6), a set positive one leaves a gap, and a negative one overlaps, so `attach: top; margin: -32, 0, 0` on the island's popup covers the bar and its fillets meet the screen's edge, where the box's top now is. Render needed no change: the fillets are drawn at the box's attached edge and the overhang past it is none, wherever placement puts the box. One behaviour changes for configs: a panel with `attach:` and a margin set on that side (`margin: 8` all round) now sits that far from the edge, where it was flush; the margin was written, and dropping it silently was the hidden rule. No config in the repository did that (the one `attach:` in a fixture has no margin). `placement::layer_config_with` drops its `flush`, and `popup_config` gives 0 for an unset margin with `attach:` instead of 0 always. The island's own `Ear`s on the bar stay its own: a `bar` takes no `attach:`, and its ears are not a surface's edge (crates/strand-surface/src/placement.rs::tests::an_attached_panel_is_anchored_to_its_edge_and_keeps_its_margin, ::an_attached_popup_touches_its_anchor_at_its_margin, crates/strand-surface/tests/sway.rs::an_attached_surface_keeps_its_margin_on_its_attached_side, crates/strand-surface/tests/render.rs::attached_surfaces_with_a_negative_margin_grow_out_of_the_screens_edge, all failing before; crates/strand-render/tests/fillet.rs::a_popup_attached_over_its_bar_draws_its_fillets_at_the_edge, reference `fillet_popup_over_bar`, which passes before too, render being unchanged).

**2026-10-15 · m6-owner-fixes (owner-testing.md bug 17): fade layers, a cached offscreen group per fading subtree, built only where its content costs more than the layer; the island card's raster is per-pixel cost, not content.** Bug 17's open half named a lever: a subtree whose only change in a frame is its opacity or offset is drawn once and composited. It reuses design.md's cached offscreen groups (item 2 of "Runtime changes these need"); no new concept reaches `.strand`. The flattener tags each opacity group's marker with its node and whether its opacity or paint offset is in flight (`Item::PushOpacity(f32, Option<Fade>)`). The raster keys a group by its items hashed from the top-left pixel of what they draw, quantised to 1/4096 px (`flatten::Shift`), so content moved by whole pixels keeps its key and a half-pixel phase at scale 1.5 gets a second one. It draws the cached layer as an image whose alpha is the group's opacity, which needs no group to composite. A layer is built only on a frame that repaints all of the group that shows, while its node is in flight or its key recurs, and a node whose last two layers were never drawn again builds no more until it rests. Groups under a transform or holding an offscreen group (blur, colour matrix, backdrop) are not layered. Translation-only subtrees, which have no opacity group, are not layered either: adding marker groups for them would change what the backdrop and GPU passes see. Damage is unchanged. Pixels match a re-raster within the PNG tolerance (2), not bit for bit, because the layer's pixels are 8-bit before they are blended. Where the group crosses a clip's antialiased edge as that clip springs between pixels, they can differ by up to 8 on that edge only. So `random_edits_match_full_repaint` turns layers off, and `tests/fade_layers.rs` holds the layered random edits to that tolerance. The measurement decided the policy. On vello_cpu's f32 fine stage, a layer's image costs about what flat fills, borders, plain text and images cost. The owner's dashboard panels (solid fills and text) rastered 3.14 ms a frame layered against 2.92 ms without, the builds included. With shadows and gradients in them, the same panels took 5.20 ms against 6.85 ms (median frame 3.89 against 5.67 ms). So a group is layered only when it holds a shadow, a gradient or paint-filled text, and the owner's config is drawn exactly as before. The island card's frames cost about 5 ns per damaged pixel offline (13 on headless sway) whatever is in them. The levers left are per-pixel: vello_cpu's u8 pipeline rasterised the same frames 2.9 to 3.7 times faster (island swell raster 1.63 to 0.45 ms), but it broke four exact-damage tests (incremental frames no longer match full repaints through clip edges, why the f32 pipeline was chosen), and drawing cells on several threads is against design.md's single-threaded vello_cpu. Both are for the owner to choose; neither is taken here. The 9 to 11 ms mounting frames are layout, not flattening. On such a frame the card's size springs start, so the surface is laid out at rest and again with the sizes in flight. Then the text the worker delivers mid-frame lays it out a third time. Each layout is a full taffy pass over 242 nodes, about 2 ms on the laptop's headless sway, and the same 2 to 2.9 ms is spent on every frame of the swell, because the card's size spring is at the surface's root, so `relayout_sized` falls back to the whole surface. Making taffy's tree persist between passes would fix both, but that is not cheap, so it is left open in bug 17.

**2026-10-15 · m6-owner-fixes (owner-testing.md gap 18): a builtin `outputs` service configures the monitors over wlr-output-management, applied and tested as whole configurations through actions, not written field by field.** The owner asked for a settings page for modes, scale, position and turning monitors on and off, "writable with apply and test". `zwlr_output_manager_v1` is what sway, Hyprland, niri and labwc implement, so the service speaks it alone, compositor-agnostic first as design.md asks; no IPC adapter is needed. *Name and shape.* It is `outputs` (records `Output`, `OutputMode`, `OutputChange`, enum `OutputTransform`), not a part of `screens`: `screens` lists the monitors that are on, in logical size, and mounts a `bar` on each, while a configuration page needs the monitors that are off too, their modes in hardware pixels and the compositor's own serial, and a `bar` must never mount on a monitor that is off. The protocol and every compositor's config call them outputs; `Output.name` is `Screen.name` while the monitor is on, so a config joins the two by name. Its fields follow the services' conventions: `all` keyed by `name`, `available` as gap 20 gave `network`, `bluetooth` and `session`, and `failed(action, error)` as `session.failed` is, with `action` as written. *Why actions and not `rw` fields.* The protocol applies a whole configuration atomically, and needs every head in it; arranging two monitors means moving both at once, a test must see the whole configuration, and a field written per step (a scale slider's `<->`) would modeset at every step and answer through echoes the compositor does not give (it may round a scale). So `outputs.apply(changes)` and `outputs.test(changes)` take a list of `OutputChange` records, built with the call syntax every record has (`OutputChange(name: o.name, scale: 1.5)`), each optional field null meaning "keep", and monitors not named keep theirs: one concept (a change) serves a single toggle and a full arrangement, and a page's draft is plain `state`. The answer is an event: `outputs.succeeded(action)` is new beside `failed`, since a test that passes must be heard (a page shows "this works" before applying, or keeps a revert timer only once applied). *What is refused before sending.* The protocol counts an unset or repeated head, a scale of 0 and a zero-sized custom mode as errors that end the client's connection, so the service checks them and answers `failed` itself: an unknown or repeated name, a scale below 1/256 (`wl_fixed` sends it as 0: found on sway, where 0.001 killed the connection) or above `wl_fixed`'s largest, a mode size not above 0, a refresh or place outside the protocol's integers. *Modes.* A change's mode is matched to the monitor's listed mode of that size nearest its rate within 0.5 Hz (a page shows `59.951` while a person writes `60`), the fastest for a rate of 0, else sent as a custom mode; a monitor turned on with no mode named shows its current mode, else its preferred, else its first. Modes are listed once each (monitors list a size and rate twice under different flags) and are plain data, so a `for` over them names its key (`key join("x", m.width, m.height, m.refresh)`); giving `OutputMode` a key field would make every `OutputMode(…)` built by hand name it. *Rotation.* `OutputTransform` uses the protocol's (and niri's) counter-clockwise names; sway's config and IPC count clockwise, so sway reports `rotate_90` as `270`. Renaming to clockwise would make the record disagree with what Hyprland and niri configs and the protocol say; the reference says which way it turns. *Cancelled.* A configuration the compositor cancels (the outputs changed under it) is made again from the new state, at most three times, then `failed`; configurations run one at a time in order, so two quick applies never race each other's serial. A lost connection empties `all`, clears `available` and answers each configuration not yet answered with `failed`; the run backs off and reconnects as every service does. On sway 1.9's headless backend nothing but adaptive sync is refused (a 40000 px mode and a scale of 1000 are accepted), and its `test` checks the state without committing it, so adaptive sync passes a test and fails to apply: the test bar records that a tested configuration may still fail, as the protocol says. The compositor matrix (niri, labwc, Hyprland) is not run here; its legs should list `outputs.all` against each compositor's own outputs and apply a scale change (crates/strand-services/tests/outputs.rs::outputs_lists_configures_and_tests_sways_heads, ::refused_configurations_arrive_as_failed, ::without_a_compositor_outputs_is_unavailable_and_fails_as_events, crates/strand-services/src/outputs.rs::tests::a_mode_is_the_listed_one_nearest_its_rate, crates/strand-compiler/tests/checker.rs::outputs_is_a_display_settings_page).

## m6-service-gaps

The service gaps the owner agreed to on 2026-10-15 after surveying their own quickshell config for capabilities (owner-testing.md gaps 28 to 35; the config shows what to support, never a design to copy). Code comments that cite m6-service-gaps point here.

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 28): leaving the network is a service-level `network.disconnect()`, not `ap.disconnect()`.** `access_points` is filled only while a list is open and only one Wi-Fi network is joined at a time, so a quick-settings tile reading only `network.ssid` must be able to leave it too. NetworkManager's `Device.Disconnect` (on the Wi-Fi device) and iwd's `Station.Disconnect` mean the same thing: leave, then join nothing on their own until a network is joined. It also stops a join in progress, which is not reported as a failure: iwd's `Aborted` answer to a join `disconnect()` stopped is dropped, and a join NetworkManager answers after the disconnect (its `AddAndActivateConnection` still in flight) is not followed and is deactivated once the disconnect has left (connectivity-r1-6, below). With nothing joined or being joined it fails, `failed("", "no Wi-Fi network is joined")` (crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::disconnect_leaves_the_joined_network, ::a_join_answered_during_a_disconnect_is_deactivated_once_left, crates/strand-services/tests/network_iwd.rs::iwd_says_what_it_is_joining_and_leaving_and_disconnects, crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::a_join_cancelled_by_disconnect_is_not_followed, crates/strand-services/src/network/iwd.rs::tests::an_aborted_join_after_disconnect_is_no_failure).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 28): the in-progress state is `network.connecting: text?` and `network.disconnecting: text?`.** They name the network and use the actions' own words, connect and disconnect. They come from the daemon (NetworkManager's ACTIVATING and DEACTIVATING Wi-Fi active connections; iwd's Station `State` with its `ConnectedNetwork`, and for a leave the network last joined once the station no longer names it), merged with the shell's own requests so a click shows at once, through one overlay both backends share (`network::Pending`, `overlay`; the daemon's own value wins). Over NetworkManager, `ssid`, `strength`, `frequency` and `security` now name only an ACTIVATED connection. Before, an activating connection already showed as joined, unlike iwd, where a connecting station names no `ssid`: a bug fix under spec.md 14, as a shell reading `ssid` sees a network it is not on (crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::only_an_activated_connection_is_joined, ::the_overlay_merges_the_shells_requests, crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::network_says_what_it_is_joining_and_leaving, crates/strand-services/src/network/iwd.rs::tests::the_station_says_what_is_in_progress, crates/strand-services/tests/network_iwd.rs::iwd_says_what_it_is_joining_and_leaving_and_disconnects).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 28): the joined network's details are `frequency: int?` in MHz and `security: WifiSecurity?`.** There is no `band` field: the band follows from the frequency, and the reference gives the ranges (one number, more information). `WifiSecurity { open, enhanced_open, wep, wpa, wpa2, wpa3, enterprise }` is a new builtin enum declared beside `OutputTransform`. Over NetworkManager it comes from the joined access point's flags (802.1X key management is `enterprise`, SAE alone `wpa3`, OWE `enhanced_open`, the privacy flag with no key management `wep`); a WPA3 transition access point reads `wpa2`, because the flags do not say which method was used. Over iwd it comes from `StationDiagnostic.GetDiagnostics` (`Frequency`, `Security`), read when the station becomes connected (joins and roams, and a network named while the station already says connected), falling back to the Network's `Type` with a null frequency where iwd serves no diagnostics. One deviation from the plan: the diagnostics are kept as a struct whose two fields are each optional (`iwd::Diagnostics`), not as `Option<(u32, String)>`, since an iwd may answer one key without the other (crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::the_joined_networks_security_is_named_from_its_flags, crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::network_tells_the_joined_networks_details, crates/strand-services/src/network/iwd.rs::tests::diagnostics_name_the_security, crates/strand-services/tests/network_iwd.rs::iwd_tells_the_joined_networks_details, crates/strand-compiler/tests/checker.rs::network_is_a_wifi_page).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 28): `network.address` comes from the kernel over rtnetlink.** The follower (`network::address`) dumps RTM_GETADDR and then reads the IPv4 and IPv6 address multicast groups. iwd does not know the address under systemd-networkd or dhcpcd (the owner's laptop), and does not publish it even with its own DHCP; networkd's D-Bus knows only its own links, and NetworkManager only its own. Every stack writes the address into the kernel, so one event-driven reader serves both backends with no polling. The rustix `net` feature is used; no new crate. The value is the IPv4 address (universe scope preferred, so `lo`'s 127.0.0.1 counts), else the global IPv6 one (non-temporary preferred), as text without a prefix, never IPv6 link-local, tentative, failed or deprecated. The interface is NetworkManager's default-route connection's device (wired too) or iwd's Wi-Fi interface. The value is null while not connected. It is a `#[store(stream)]` field, so the socket is open only while a visible reader shows it; a socket that fails is not opened again until `address` is watched anew, and a kernel that dropped messages (`ENOBUFS`) is dumped again. One deviation from the plan: `Follower::changed` returns `io::Result<Option<String>>`, so a socket error closes the follower (and clears the value) instead of looping on it (crates/strand-services/src/network/address.rs::tests::new_and_removed_addresses_are_followed, ::the_best_address_is_ipv4_then_global_ipv6, ::a_dump_is_parsed_across_messages, ::the_kernel_gives_lo_its_address, crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::network_tells_the_joined_networks_details, ::disconnect_leaves_the_joined_network, crates/strand-services/tests/network_iwd.rs::iwd_tells_the_joined_networks_details).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 28): an explicit `network.scan()` and `network.scanning: bool`, keeping the scan made when a reader opens the list.** That scan raises the flag too. NetworkManager has no scanning property, so the flag runs from an accepted `RequestScan` until the device's `LastScan` changes, or for at most 15 s (`SCAN_LIMIT`, NetworkManager before 1.12). Over iwd it is the Station's `Scanning`, so iwd's own scans show too, and the list is read again when a scan ends. A scan the daemon refuses because one runs or has just run (NetworkManager's `NotAllowed`, iwd's `Busy`) is no failure. With the radio off or no device, the scan fails, `failed("", "Wi-Fi is off")`. `network.failed`'s first argument is "" for an action that names no network: a scan, or a disconnect the service could not take, refused ones included. A switch of the radio NetworkManager accepted is taken as its state at once (its signal follows), so a scan asked right after switching off fails rather than reaching the daemon (crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::an_explicit_scan_raises_scanning_until_it_ends, ::an_unreachable_network_is_unavailable_and_fails_as_values, crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::a_scan_refusal_is_no_failure, crates/strand-services/tests/network_iwd.rs::an_explicit_scan_on_iwd_raises_scanning).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 29): nearby devices are `bluetooth.nearby: [BluetoothDevice]`, a stream field.** Discovery (`SetDiscoveryFilter` with `DuplicateData` off, then `StartDiscovery`) runs only while a visible reader reads the list, as Wi-Fi scanning does, and starts again when the adapter powers on or BlueZ comes back while it is read; a discovery BlueZ refuses is not asked again on every signal. BlueZ's per-client discovery sessions mean `StopDiscovery`, sent only for a discovery this body started (and when the body ends), never stops another program's. Only unpaired devices with a name are listed (anonymous BLE advertisers would flood a menu), sorted by name. Signals that change only `RSSI`, `TxPower`, `ManufacturerData`, `ServiceData`, `AdvertisingFlags` or `AdvertisingData` are dropped unread. The flag is `bluetooth.scanning` (the adapter's `Discovering`, another program's included): the same word as `network.scanning`, one concept across both services. The record is the same `BluetoothDevice` in both lists, as `workspaces.configured` reuses `Workspace` (crates/strand-services/tests/bluetooth.rs::bluetooth_finds_nearby_devices_only_while_read, crates/strand-services/src/bluetooth.rs::tests::nearby_lists_named_unpaired_devices_only_while_listing, ::advertisement_only_changes_are_ignored, crates/strand-compiler/tests/checker.rs::bluetooth_is_a_pairing_page).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 29): `d.pair()` pairs, trusts and connects as one action; `d.forget()` is `Adapter1.RemoveDevice`.** Pairing is how a nearby device is added; on a device already paired (`AlreadyExists`) it trusts and connects, and one already connected is no failure. Pairing may take a minute (a person answering the system's agent), a connect 30 s. Each runs as a task, so nothing waits on another, and every failure is `bluetooth.failed(address, error)` with BlueZ's own words ("Authentication Failed", "Page Timeout") or "timed out"; a device whose connect failed after pairing stays paired. An action on an address BlueZ does not list fails with "no such device". Strand registers no pairing agent. BlueZ then uses the system's agent if one runs (its PIN dialog keeps working), else pairs without one, which is enough for most headphones, mice, keyboards and phones; a device that insists on a PIN fails with BlueZ's error. Adding a Strand agent would add a passkey event and an answer action, which the owner did not ask for. This was put to the owner as a question and the recommended answer used; the owner may overrule it, and an agent can be added later, additively (crates/strand-services/tests/bluetooth.rs::pairing_a_nearby_device_pairs_trusts_and_connects_it, ::disconnecting_and_forgetting_a_paired_device, ::without_bluez_pair_and_forget_fail_as_events).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 29): each device's progress is `BluetoothDevice.connecting: bool` and `disconnecting: bool`, from the shell's own calls in flight.** BlueZ has no connecting property. `pair()`'s whole run (pair, trust, connect) shows as `connecting`, rather than as a third `pairing` state; this too was put to the owner as a question (their bar shows "Pairing..." apart from "Connecting...") and the recommended answer used, overrulable: a `pairing: bool` can be added additively. These are booleans on each item, while network's are names on the service: several devices can be busy at once, but only one Wi-Fi network. A connect another program makes is not shown (crates/strand-services/src/bluetooth.rs::tests::busy_devices_show_connecting_and_disconnecting, crates/strand-services/tests/bluetooth.rs::pairing_a_nearby_device_pairs_trusts_and_connects_it, ::disconnecting_and_forgetting_a_paired_device).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps: new members are appended after the existing ones.** In the Rust struct, the .schema text and the compiler's provisional stub alike, so field indexes (a `powered` or `wifi` write by index) and the stub drift test hold, and the growth is additive under spec.md 14 (crates/strand/src/services/mod.rs::tests::each_builtin_stub_has_its_service_schemas_members, ::service_schemas_extend_the_builtin_one, crates/strand-services/tests/bluetooth.rs::bluetooth_follows_bluez).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 28, review connectivity-r1-1): over NetworkManager, `AccessPoint.active` is the ACTIVATED connection's access point, as `ssid` is.** The list still marked every Wi-Fi active connection's access point, so while NetworkManager was activating or deactivating a network the menu showed it joined (and sorted it first) while `network.ssid` was null and `connecting` or `disconnecting` named it. iwd marks an access point active only while the station is connected. `active` and `ssid` now say the same thing on both backends; the schema says `active` is the network joined, not one being joined or left (crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::only_an_activated_connection_is_joined).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 28, review connectivity-r1-2): NetworkManager's `NotAllowed` answer to `RequestScan` is no failure only when its words say "not now".** NetworkManager uses one error name for two kinds of refusal and tells them apart only in the message. Before 1.22 it refused a scan running ("while already scanning"), one just run ("immediately following previous scan"), one its supplicant did not want then ("at this time"), and a device activating ("while unavailable or activating"). Since then it refuses only a device that cannot scan ("while unavailable": the hardware rfkill switch, a device not ready). Treating every `NotAllowed` as busy made `scan()` silently do nothing with the radio blocked in hardware while `WirelessEnabled` was true. Now the "not now" words, and "activating" while a Wi-Fi connection is activating, are no failure; "unavailable" otherwise is `failed("", "the Wi-Fi device is unavailable")`, as the radio off is; any other `NotAllowed` fails with NetworkManager's words. Matching message text was preferred to reading the device's `State` before every scan: NetworkManager's own reason is what decides, and the text is stable across its releases (crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::a_scan_refusal_is_no_failure).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 29, review connectivity-r1-3): a Bluetooth call repeating one in flight on its device is dropped, the call asked last is what the device shows, and a pairing past its limit is cancelled.** Each device action was its own task with no check, so a double click on Pair sent two `Pair` calls; BlueZ answers the second `org.bluez.Error.InProgress`, which surfaced as `bluetooth.failed` while the first went on. The busy state per device came from a map keyed by task, so with a connect and a disconnect both running, the device showed whichever the map yielded. Now `bluetooth::InFlight` numbers the calls in the order asked. A connect, pair, disconnect or forget repeating the same call on the device is dropped, as is a connect while a pair runs (the pair connects). A disconnect during a connect, or a connect during a disconnect, is asked, because the person changed their mind, and the device shows the call asked last; a forget shows nothing. This matches `network`, which drops a repeated join. A `Pair` not answered within its limit (a minute) is followed by `Device1.CancelPairing`, so BlueZ stops pairing and a retry is not refused as in progress (crates/strand-services/src/bluetooth.rs::tests::a_device_shows_its_last_call_and_repeats_are_dropped, ::a_pairing_that_times_out_is_cancelled, crates/strand-services/tests/bluetooth.rs::a_repeated_pair_or_connect_is_asked_once).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 28, review connectivity-r1-6): the joins a `disconnect()` stops are held until the disconnect answers, not dropped when it is asked.** A disconnect stopped joins (neither followed nor reported) before the daemon answered it. If the daemon refused it (polkit denying `Device.Disconnect`, a policy denying iwd's `Station.Disconnect`), the join went on unfollowed, and its later failure (a wrong password) was never reported. Over NetworkManager, the joins still asked and those activating are now held (`network::Stopped`, `Asked::stopping`) while the disconnect is in flight. Once it has left they are dropped, and an activation NetworkManager answered meanwhile is deactivated then; it may have started after the device was left, so deactivating it at once could race the leave. If the disconnect fails, the joins are followed again: their answers are awaited and their activations followed, and a join that ended or failed meanwhile is reported. Over iwd, each join records the disconnect that stopped it (`Join::stopped_by`). A failed disconnect lets those joins go on and reports a failure they answered meanwhile. The disconnect's own failure is still `failed(ssid, error)`. The integration tests for the deactivation path that were missing now exist (crates/strand-services/tests/network.rs::a_join_answered_during_a_disconnect_is_deactivated_once_left, ::a_join_a_refused_disconnect_stopped_is_still_followed, crates/strand-services/tests/network_iwd.rs::a_join_a_refused_disconnect_stopped_is_still_reported, crates/strand-services/src/network.rs::tests::a_join_cancelled_by_disconnect_is_not_followed, crates/strand-services/src/network/iwd.rs::tests::a_failed_disconnect_resumes_the_joins_it_stopped).

Meanwhile the device has nothing active, so `disconnect()` asked the first Wi-Fi device anyway (`Device.Disconnect`, or iwd's `Station.Disconnect`). NetworkManager refuses that with `NotActive` ("This device is not active"), iwd with `NotConnected`, and the refusal went down the failed-disconnect path: `network.failed` named the network and the join was resumed and went through, against the schema's "stops the one being joined". The test NetworkManager answered such a `Disconnect` Ok, so the test passed against behaviour the daemon does not have; it now refuses as NetworkManager does, and the fake iwd refuses `NotConnected` and `Busy` as iwd does. Now, with no Wi-Fi connection activated or activating (NetworkManager) or no network named by the station (iwd), the daemon is not asked: the joins not yet started are stopped by the service, and nothing is reported. Over NetworkManager, a join still asked is cancelled for good (`network::cancel_joins`), and the activation NetworkManager answers it with is deactivated, as for a join a disconnect left (decisions above); one answered but not yet seen activating is deactivated at once. Over iwd, each join carries a stop flag its task reads before `Forget` and before `Connect` (`iwd::drop_joins`), so it asks nothing more, and if iwd joins it all the same (its `Connect` already sent) the station is disconnected; the flag is raised too on the joins a disconnect stopped once that disconnect has left, so a join still forgetting its old password does not go on to join after the leave. Calling the device anyway and taking `NotActive` as left was not taken: the join would still go on, since nothing stops a call already in flight. A disconnect in flight now drops a repeat, as Bluetooth drops a repeated call on a device (review connectivity-r1-3); the first one's answer decides. **2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (owner-testing.md gap 30): the clipboard is two paths, not one.** An `input` copies, cuts and pastes on the main thread through strand-surface's existing `wl_data_device`, with the serial of the key press, so it works on every compositor, data control or not. The builtin `clipboard` service watches and sets the selection over data control on a thread of its own with its own Wayland connection, as `outputs` does. Neither depends on the other. Alternatives: one path through data control (an `input` would then need the service running and a compositor offering data control, which a plain text field should not), or one through `wl_data_device` (a handler's copy has no key serial and no keyboard focus, and the history needs to see other programs' copies without focus). Built: Render's Router asks with `Intent::Clipboard(ClipboardAsk)` and gets `InputEvent::Paste` back; the binary's `Forward` keeps the asks (beside the intents it maps) for `SurfaceHost::take_clipboard_asks`, which the seat drains right after the key reaches the host; dnd.rs's pipe reader and writer moved to `manager/pipes.rs` for both.

Without either, `clipboard.available` is false, `history` stays as last loaded and `clipboard.copy` or `e.copy()` fail as `clipboard.failed(action, error)` (spec.md 12's rule); there is no fallback through `wl_data_device` for a handler's copy, which would need keyboard focus and a press serial. **2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (owner's ruling): the history survives restarts.** It lives in `$XDG_STATE_HOME/strand/clipboard/` (else `~/.local/state/strand/clipboard/`, `PersistStore`'s rule): `history.json` (texts inline, ids, times) and `images/<id>-<time>.png|.jpg`, directory 0700 and files 0600, each written atomically (a synced temporary file renamed over, the directory synced) on the service's thread. A corrupt file is an empty history with a warning, replaced at the next change. `clipboard.clear()` empties the history and deletes the file and every image; the selection stays, being another program's. An image's path is never reused (the time in its name), not even after `clear`, so no renderer cache shows a stale picture.

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (owner question, answered with the recommended "yes"; the owner may overrule it): the history records while a program reads it anywhere.** Services stop 5 s after their last shown reader, so a history popup that is usually closed would miss most copies. A program that reads `clipboard.history` anywhere (a closed popup, a `let` only it reads) holds `clipboard` and the field from its top level for as long as it runs, as bars hold `screens`; a program that never reads it never records anything or writes clipboard data to disk. History is a `#[store(keyed, stream)]` field, recorded only while watched, and images are read only then. Built as `lower::Program::services_anywhere` (every scope's uses, `let`s and `fn`s resolved) and a one-entry table, `instantiate::HELD_ANYWHERE`, so the rule is a fact about named fields rather than a new syntax; a config's own `service clipboard` shadows it. Alternative: a `hold:` or `keep` marker in the language, which adds a concept for one service.

Like any Wayland client's, Strand's copies vanish when Strand exits; keeping other programs' selections after they exit (wl-clip-persist) and the primary selection (middle-click paste) are not built.

The run now sends a `wl_display.sync` after `get_data_device`; a selection told before its answer is the one found (`Ev::Selection { at_bind }`): it sets `text` and `holds_image` but is never recorded, and the run is ready (and runs queued actions) only once that answer came, so an action never races it. ""` a type error that reads as if it should work. The bool is `holds_image`; the current selection's picture is `history[0].image` once recorded. A property a player does not report counts as able, as `seek()` already treated `CanSeek`: a button that may work is never dimmed by a player's omission. `can_seek` also needs a track length above zero, and one predicate (`Player::can_seek`) serves both the field and a `position` write, so `when !media.can_seek` dims exactly the scrubber a write would not move; a seek with `CanControl` false is no longer sent (MPRIS: such a player takes no seek). MPRIS signals these properties, so the `PropertiesChanged` the service already follows carries them; an invalidated one is read again with the player's other properties (the existing whole re-read), so nothing is polled and no D-Bus traffic is added. `next()` and `previous()` are unchanged: MPRIS says a call the player cannot take does nothing.

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 34): the uptime and the kernel's release are `system.uptime` and `system.kernel`.** They go on `system`, which already holds the machine's facts beside the desktop's settings (`hostname`); a new service for two fields would add a concept where a field does. `kernel: text` is `/proc/sys/kernel/osrelease` (what `uname -r` prints), read once as the service starts, since it cannot change while the machine runs. `uptime: duration` is `/proc/uptime`'s first number (CLOCK_BOOTTIME, so time suspended counts, as `uptime` counts it) floored to whole minutes, so `dur(system.uptime)` reads `3 h 12 min` with the formatting a config already has. `system.boot: Date` was weighed and rejected: a `Date` has no difference, so showing time since boot would need a new function, where a `duration` needs none. It is a `#[store(stream)]` field: read only while a visible reader shows it, at once when one starts to, then by a timer set to the next whole minute of uptime plus 50 ms of slack (a timer waking early reads the old minute and is set again), so the logic thread is woken at most once a minute and never while nobody shows it; a minute is the precision a dashboard's uptime shows, and seconds would wake the logic thread every second for a number nobody watches tick. The timer is tokio's, on the monotonic clock, which stops while the machine sleeps: accepted that after a resume the value may lag by up to a minute (the next timer reads the right value). The idle loop without a session bus (`Bus::Disabled`) is now the same `select!` with the portal's follow left pending, so the uptime ticks there too.

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 33): a builtin `disk`, shaped like `memory`, with `all: [Filesystem]`.** The owner's dashboard shows how full the disks are. A new builtin `disk` follows `memory`'s shape for what most shells show, the root filesystem (`usage`, `used`, `total`), so `pct(disk.usage)` reads as `pct(memory.usage)` does, and adds `all`, a keyed list of `Filesystem` records (`path`, `device`, `usage`, `used`, `total`, `free`) for a page that lists every disk; `/` comes first so `disk.all[0]` is the root. `free` is included (as `df`'s "Avail", `f_bavail`), which `memory` does not have, because a filesystem's usage cannot be shown honestly without it: ext4 reserves 5% for root, so `used/total` understates a full disk; `usage` is `used/(used+free)`, as `df`'s "Use%" counts it, and `used` is the size less every free block. Listed: `/` always (an overlay root in a container too), then every mount of a block device (`/dev/…`) or a ZFS dataset, leaving out read-only images (`squashfs` snaps, `iso9660`, `udf`), network and FUSE filesystems (a `statvfs` on an NFS mount whose server went away hangs; they are not "this machine's disks"), mount points that are not directories (a container's bound `/etc/hosts`), mounts at or under an automount point (amended by review round 1, below), and a second mount of the same device and root (binds), while btrfs subvolumes, whose roots differ, stay listed; a later mount at the same point hides the earlier one. The mount table is `/proc/self/mountinfo`, read again at every sample, so mounts come and go without a watch. It samples every 10 s (disk usage moves slowly; `cpu`'s 1 s would be wasted work) only while a reader is visible, at start before `ready` and at once on becoming visible again. `statvfs` (rustix, no unsafe) runs on tokio's blocking pool, one sample at a time: a hung one holds no thread of the shared runtime, keeps the last values shown and queues nothing behind it. GPU statistics are not added: they stay a config's own command, as the plan says.

The record is `Filesystem` (no builtin type had the name). The new provisional stubs in the compiler's builtin schema go after `outputs`'s, so the ids of the records declared before them do not move.

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 35): the notification history is remembered across restarts, on by default, with `notifications.remember: bool rw` to turn it off.** The owner's notification centre keeps its history across restarts; `notifications.all` was memory-only. *Default (the owner's question, answered with the recommended reading; overrulable).* On by default, because a history that vanishes on every restart is the gap, and a person who opens a notification centre after logging in expects what arrived before. Notification bodies can hold sensitive text (codes, messages), weighed this way: the file is the user's alone (the persist store's directory is created 0700 under `$XDG_STATE_HOME/strand/persist`); a sender's `transient` hint (which the spec defines as "do not keep in history") is honoured, for remembering only: a transient notification still shows and stays in `all` for the run; `clear()` and `dismiss()` erase from disk too (the next save drops them); and one write, `notifications.remember = false`, erases the file at once and keeps the choice (`services:notifications.remember`, "0"), so it stays off across restarts until set true again. *Storage.* The persist store, `services:notifications.all`, JSON through serde_json (`{"version":1,"notifications":[…]}`, oldest first: app name and icon, summary, body, image, urgency, timeout, persistent, time), the newest `KEPT` (1,000), as many as memory keeps. A file that does not read (bad JSON, another version, or a broken persist header) is logged, starts empty and is replaced by the next save; it is read through a read-only store, so it is never set aside as a `.corrupt` copy (amended by review round 2, below). *Restoring.* A new run reads it off the runtime before it asks for the name (the plan said after; before, so no id is handed out before the restored ones are numbered), renumbered 1..=n with new ids above them; their old ids are not live, so a sender's `CloseNotification` or `replaces_id` of an old id is treated as closed. They come back without actions, because their senders' processes (or bus connections) are gone and could not hear an `ActionInvoked`; `n.activate()` on one only dismisses it, and closing one sends no `NotificationClosed`, since no sender knows its new id. They never appear as popups and emit no `received`. Images: only a sender's `image-path` is written, never the PNGs we wrote from `image-data` into `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` (gone after the run), and a path whose file no longer exists is dropped at restore (an icon name is kept). *Saving.* A change to `all` (an arrival, a close, `clear()`) schedules a save 1 s after the last change but no later than 5 s after the first unsaved one (amended by review round 1, below), off the runtime on the blocking pool; saves are numbered process-wide and the latest wins (as `Frecency::save_latest`), and a `SaveOnStop` drop guard queues the last pending save through the services' finalizer, so a stop or shutdown loses nothing within the 500 ms finalize limit. With no state directory (`notifications::Config { state: None }`, what tests use) nothing is read or written, `remember` reads false, and a new run starts with none, exactly as before. Tests never touch the real `$XDG_STATE_HOME`: every in-process test that starts `notifications` on a bus sets a temp dir or `state: None` (the notifications and dbus_idle tests; strand's in-process tests start it only without a bus, and its subprocess tests set `XDG_STATE_HOME`). A settings page binds it two-way like any `rw` field; the checker test uses a `segmented` (`value: <-> notifications.remember`), as Strand has no `toggle` element (the plan named one).

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 31): a builtin `keyboard` with `caps_lock`, `num_lock` and `layout: text?`.** The lock screen's Caps Lock warning and a bar's layout indicator need the keyboard's state, and nothing served it. One builtin carries the three, all stream fields, so nothing runs for one nobody shows. The sources, in order: (1) while one of Strand's surfaces has keyboard focus, that `wl_keyboard`'s locked or held `Lock` and `Mod2` modifiers and its keymap's name for the active group (xkbcommon), exact and event-driven; this is the lock screen's case, and is compositor-agnostic; (2) otherwise the lock keys come from the kernel's keyboard lights, `/sys/class/leds/*::capslock` and `*::numlock`, any keyboard's light on meaning on; (3) the layout, when no focused report names one, from the compositor adapters through the shared hub: Hyprland's `j/devices` (the `main` keyboard's `active_keymap`, else the first keyboard's) at connection and after a reload, then `activelayout` events; sway's `GET_INPUTS` (the first keyboard's) at connection, then `input` events with `xkb_layout` or `xkb_keymap`; niri's `KeyboardLayoutsChanged` and `KeyboardLayoutSwitched`. With several keyboards the last one switched wins. A layout is the keymap's description (`English (US)`), which xkb and all three compositors report alike; a config wanting short codes maps them with `match`. A devices or inputs reply the adapter cannot read leaves the layout null and degrades nothing: the layout is auxiliary. Hyprland's adapter makes one more request at connection and on each reload. sway 1.9 does emit `input` `xkb_layout` for a virtual keyboard's group change (`sways_layout_is_the_active_keyboards`). The lock's built-in fallback field is unchanged.

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (gap 31, polling the lights): the lock keys are read from the lights every 250 ms, only while needed.** A light's brightness raises no event (input-leds sets no `brightness_hw_changed`), and no compositor IPC reports the lock keys with events (Hyprland's `devices` has `capsLock` but no event; sway and niri say nothing), so with no Strand surface focused the only reading is a poll. The lights are read every 250 ms only while a visible reader shows `caps_lock` or `num_lock` and no focused report holds, once at once when that starts and when the focus leaves; a read that changes nothing sends nothing, so a steady state wakes only the services thread, never logic. Owner question ("is polling acceptable here?"), answered with the recommended reading: yes, as above; a focused surface such as the lock screen gets exact keyboard events with no polling. The owner may overrule it.

**2026-10-15 · m6-service-gaps (review round 1 of the small services): four confirmed findings fixed.** Each test named fails without its fix. Two readings were weighed: clearing the lock keys on every leave, or dropping them on the enter. The enter is the one place where they are known stale, and a destroyed surface's focus may end with no leave, so an enter drops that keyboard's lock keys and reports nothing; the protocol requires the compositor to send `modifiers` after `enter`, and that event reports. Until then what was reported stands, which is `None` after a real leave and the same keyboard's still current state when the enter ends a leave held or sent in the same dispatch (sway's late leave), so neither case reports a state that was never true (`crates/strand-surface/tests/fake.rs::an_enter_reports_the_lock_keys_of_now_not_of_the_last_focus`). (3, gap 35) The history's save waited 1 s after the last change with no upper bound, so a sender replacing a notification every half second (a progress bar) postponed it for as long as it kept updating, and a crash in that time lost every change since. A save now falls due 1 s after the last change but no later than `SAVE_WITHIN`, 5 s after the first change it holds, which keeps a burst to one write while bounding what a crash loses; the stop's finalizer save is unchanged, and the gap 35 paragraph's "a stop or shutdown loses nothing" holds for an orderly stop, a crash losing at most those 5 s (`crates/strand-services/src/notifications.rs::tests::a_history_changing_without_pause_is_saved_within_its_bound`).
