## ci-speed

**2026-10-15 · ci-speed: the inner loop tests what changed; the whole suite runs once per branch.** The owner saw agents spend much of their time in CI ("a little fix -> 18 min of CI -> another fix -> repeat"). About 850 agent transcripts show it: a full `run.sh ci` took about 26 min, the agents that ran it ran it twice on average and up to eight times, and CLAUDE.md asked for `cargo test --workspace` before every commit. CLAUDE.md's checks are now formatting, workspace clippy and `run.sh affected` before each commit: `scripts/container/affected.sh` tests the workspace crates with a changed file since the merge base with `main` (committed or not), the crates whose tests read `docs/` when docs changed, every crate when the root manifest, the lock file or `.cargo/` changed, and with `--deep` every crate depending on the changed ones; `--list` names them without running. `run.sh ci` runs once per branch, and after a failure at step N an agent fixes it, reruns that test and resumes with `CI_FROM=N`; the commit going to `main` still gets one whole run from step 1, the integration's. `scripts/container/test-affected.sh` checks its choices on stand-in diffs (`AFFECTED_FILES`), in `ci.sh`'s and GitHub's lint jobs.

**2026-10-15 · ci-speed: incremental debug builds, set once in the profile.** wave3-cleanup turned incremental compilation off in `.cargo/config.toml` to stop agents' differing settings from keeping several copies of each crate, not because incremental builds were slow. The setting is now `incremental = true` in `[profile.dev]` (the test profile inherits it), still one setting for every agent, and `.cargo/config.toml` no longer overrides it. It applies to the workspace's own crates only; dependencies are never incremental. Measured in the container: a one-line edit in `strand-services` rebuilt its tests in 18 to 38 s and then `strand`'s in 20 to 24 s without it, 5 to 6 s and 5 s with it. GitHub's jobs set `CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0`: they build from rust-cache, never from a previous edit, and incremental state would only grow their caches.

**2026-10-15 · ci-speed: sccache shares compiled dependencies between worktrees.** Every workflow agent starts in a fresh worktree and compiled every dependency again. The CI image now carries sccache 0.18.0 (a pinned release checked by its sha256, as tree-sitter is), and `run.sh` wraps rustc with it, its cache in the named volume `strand-sccache` (40 GB cap; `RUN_SCCACHE=0` turns it off). Paths under the checkout are hashed relative to it (`SCCACHE_BASEDIRS`), and `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` is now `target/container` relative to the container's working directory, the checkout: sccache hashes `CARGO_*` variables, and the absolute path made every Rust crate miss in another worktree (0 of 718 hits; 14 of 16 once relative). Incremental crates, proc macros and links are not cached. Local only: GitHub's jobs keep Swatinem/rust-cache, and compiled output is the same either way, so pixel references hold.

**2026-10-15 · ci-speed: a build alone uses every core.** `run.sh` set `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=6` so three worktrees could build at once (CLAUDE.md's limit). It now divides the machine's cores among the strand builds running (containers labelled `strand.build=1`), at least 4; `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` still overrides. Measured, a fresh worktree's clippy plus building every test: 445 s at 6 jobs without the cache, 290 s at 16, and 206 s at 16 with the cache warm from another worktree (623 of 718 Rust crates from it).

**2026-10-15 · ci-speed: `reload_latency` runs 15 rounds in a local `ci`.** The step is advisory on the laptop (a gate miss warns) and took 189 s on average and 442 s in the last run at 50 rounds; GitHub's timing job enforces the gate on 50. Locally it now runs 15 rounds, 50 under `STRAND_STRICT_TIMING=1`; a p95 over fewer rounds is noisier, which only moves an advisory warning. Measured with the m6-service-gaps fix (dependencies optimised in debug builds), the workspace test step's test execution went from 706 s to 326 s; `lottie.rs::the_file_is_read_on_the_image_worker` then failed once, as the faster worker could publish the file before the test saw its wake (the worker sends, then wakes): the test now waits for the wake too, 0 failures in 40 runs. `renderer::tests::a_poisoned_slot_keeps_no_stand_ins` failed the same way on GitHub (its crashed request answered within flattening's `ESTIMATE_WAIT`) and turns that wait off, as `crashing_requests_are_not_retried` does.

## popup-slide

**2026-10-15 · popup-slide (owner-testing.md bug 19): a popup asks the compositor to slide it only on an axis where it does not fit its output.** Every positioner asked for `slide_x | slide_y` beside its flip, as a fallback for what the manager could not know. Hyprland 0.56 slides into the output's box shrunk by 4 px on each side (`CXDGPositionerRules::getPosition`, `constraint.expand(-4)`), so a popup that fits but touches an edge is moved 4 px in: the island's card, lifted over its bar to y 0 by a negative margin, opened 4 px below the screen's edge. The manager already moves the box inside its output along the anchor's edge (`popup_shift`, bug 6), so it knows where the box lands; `popup_slides` now asks for a slide on an axis only where that box passes the output, and on both while the output is not known (a posed parent, an output not yet described). The flip stays asked for. A layer surface's popups are constrained to the whole output on wlroots compositors and Hyprland alike (Hyprland's `CPopup::reposition` takes the reserved area off only for a window's popups), so another client's exclusive zone is no reason to keep the slide.

## seam-snap

**2026-10-15 · seam-snap (owner-testing.md bug 20): a box moving in flight is drawn with each edge rounded from where it falls.** A paint offset in flight (a spring's way to its rest, a FLIP glide) was rounded on its own and added to the box layout had snapped, and each ancestor's offset was rounded apart too. Edges that meet exactly then missed by a pixel: the island's card is a body springing its `x` and width beside an ear springing its `x` to the body's right edge, and round(x) + round(width) is not round(x + width). Layout now keeps each box's residue (`Boxes::residues`: how far its edges lay from where it snapped them, only for boxes that have one), flattening carries the offsets in flight down the tree unrounded (`Inherited::flight`, the offsets at rest stay in `offset`), and a box with anything in flight is drawn from its snapped edges moved by the residue plus the flight, rounded half up (`flatten::node::drawn_span`). So both edges land where an exact layout of the moving boxes would snap them, and boxes that meet stay joined. The rest holds: nothing in flight draws exactly the laid-out box as before; content laid out still while its card grows around it stays still (its exact edge plus the card's flight is constant); a spring's tail within half a pixel of its rest draws its rest. A box's drawn width may differ from its laid-out width by a pixel while it moves, which its clip and background follow. A subtree relaid alone (only sizes moved) takes residues relative to its root's snapped box, as its rects already are.

**2026-10-15 · seam-snap: the full shell's PSS ceiling is 104 MB (106,496 kB), from 86 MB; its 76 MB target stays.** GitHub's budgets job failed `the_full_shell_on_the_real_services_is_measured` three times on `c39b8a9` (97,875, 88,733 and 88,743 kB) and once on `main` at `0807e9e` (97,390 kB, then 80,715 kB on a re-run), and read 90,724 kB once on `c7c5999`; in every high reading the growth is mimalloc's heap (42,852 to 51,776 kB against 35,648 kB). Measured in the container, six runs of each alternating: `main` 65,658 to 68,692 kB (mean 67,134, heap mean 29,128), this branch 66,020 to 70,603 kB (mean 68,453, heap mean 28,895). The branch's only allocation is heap (`Boxes::residues`) and its heap is no larger; the 1.3 MB between the means is the compositor's shared buffers (`memfd:smithay-client-toolkit`), which vary by 4 MB run to run on either. So the change costs nothing measurable, and GitHub's runners read the same build 17 MB apart from its heap alone, which the container never shows (its heap within 2.2 MB). The owner ruled on 2026-10-15 to find out whether the change costs memory and, if that was inconclusive about GitHub's readings, raise the ceiling: 104 MB is the highest reading, 97,875 kB, plus about 9%. The target still warns from 76 MB, so growth stays visible; why GitHub's heap sometimes reads 12 MB higher is not known (a guess: freed pages mimalloc has not yet returned when the test samples).

## grab-scope

**2026-10-15 · grab-scope (owner-testing.md bug 21): a press grabs only for popups on its own monitor.** A popup grabs when the diff that opens it carries a fresh press (`SceneDiff::press`, decisions.md m6-w2-surface), and a logic step's whole diff carries the press that started it: its handlers and two-way writes, and every `on change` they set off, in every monitor's instance of a bar. The owner's island raises a brightness activity in each instance whose card is closed when `brightness.level` changes, so a slider dragged in one monitor's card opened a popup on each other monitor, marked with the slider's press; their grab took the pointer (Hyprland sends it only to the grab's surfaces) and the card being dragged in folded. Telling a press's own handlers from what they set off would mean tracking causes through logic, and an `on change` that opens a menu next to what was clicked is a fair use of the grab; what is never right is a grab on another monitor than the one pressed. So the surface manager records the layer surface each press landed on (the pointer's, or the one with the keyboard for a key; `UserAction::on`), and a popup grabs with it only when its own layer surface is that one or another on the same monitor (a panel the click opened) (`State::press_reaches`). A press on no surface the manager knows reaches any, as before.

## fillet-clip

**2026-10-16 · fillet-clip: a clip above the `attach:` target lets its fillets through.** A test shell's `panel { attach: top; stack { clip: true; … box { bg: $surface; radius: 18 } } }` drew no fillets: the target is the outermost painted box touching the edge, here the card inside the clipping stack, and its fillets lie beside its box, so outside the stack's clip, which cut them away (a stack painting the card itself, or one without `clip`, drew them). The spec said only that the painted box gets fillets, so the reading was open between a checker warning ("fillets come only from a box no clip holds") and drawing them. Drawing them removes a concept: `clip:` keeps meaning "hold the content to this box", and the fillets stay the surface's, not content (they lie in its overhang, past every box). So each clip open above the target (its `PushClip` group, a `clip: true` box, a `scroll`, `list` or `pages`, or a box whose size springs) takes in, once the target is drawn, the fillets and the square corners they meet at those of the target's two corners on the edge that lie on or inside its box, within half a pixel (`fillet::corners`: a square of the clip's largest radius, at least the fillet's, inside the target's box, so a rounded clip does not round the corner a fillet joins and leave it a detached horn), mapped into the clip's space and wound like it so the union has no seam. What a clip lets through is bounded by its box: the square ends where the clip does along the edge, and the square and the fillet both end where it does away from the edge, so a card overflowing a short clip (a toast collapsing to `height: 0`), a narrow one, or one it slid out of (`pages`, a scroll) leaves no tabs or stray fillets past it; the fillet is cut there rather than shrunk, as the clip cuts the card (review of the first version, which let both corners through every clip whole). Only the target's fill passes: when the clip's group closes, every run of its items around that fill that opens no group the fill is drawn in (what is drawn before it, the target's own content and what follows it) is wrapped in a clip of the box again, in the transform it is drawn under (`Flattener::hold_to_box`, which finds that fill by its item index, kept in step with the items inserted before it), so a box drawn after the card, one inside it, or one under a translucent card stays inside the clip's box, while the groups the fill is drawn in (opacity, transforms, layers, clips of its ancestors and its own) keep their order and the card its z-order. Where that held content meets the box's edge away from the corners it is clipped twice by the same outline, so its antialiased edge pixels there are a shade lighter; only a surface whose target sits under a clip has those clips (an outer clip of the box ∪ corners with full coverage along the box's edge would end that, but would let the layer effects of the groups between the clip and the target leak past the box). A layer effect the target or an ancestor between it and the clip draws when its group closes (a filter's spread) may still reach into the corners. The target's record covers the corners so its damage repaints them. Proven by `crates/strand-render/tests/fillet.rs::a_clip_above_the_card_lets_its_fillets_through` (one and two clips, a box overflowing the clip still cut), `::a_rounded_clip_keeps_the_cards_corners_on_the_edge_square` (no gap along the edge, one and two clips), `::only_the_cards_fill_passes_the_clip` (a box after the card, in it, under a translucent card), `::a_clip_lets_through_only_the_corners_it_reaches` (a short clip, a narrow one, a card slid out of one, square and rounded; PNG references `fillet_short_clip`, `fillet_slid_out_of_clip`), `::a_clipped_cards_fillets_repaint_with_it` and `crates/strand-render/src/fillet.rs::tests::a_clip_lets_through_only_the_corners_it_reaches`.

## letters-placement

**2026-10-16 · letters-placement: where `letters` goes is a schema entry, and a `letters` anywhere else is `check::misplaced`.** A test shell found `docs/reference/elements.md` saying `text` "takes no children" while the only working form is `text "x" { letters { y: … } }`, and `letters { text "x" { … } }` checking clean and animating nothing. The placement lived in a special case in the checker (`rendered_child` let a `text` hold a `letters`), and m4-effects-paint-w2 had left a `letters` outside a `text` drawing nothing without an error, so neither the reference nor the checker knew it. spec.md 6.1 makes which children an element may hold schema entries, so builtin.schema now says it: `letters` is `flags leaf only_in text`. `only_in` already makes a `letters` outside a `text` (around one, on its own, at a component's root) a `check::misplaced` error, as for `start` outside `split`; a leaf may hold any element whose `only_in` names it, which replaces the special case; and `letters` is a leaf because its props apply to each letter and a child of it would draw nothing. One mistake, one diagnostic: a misplaced element's children are not also reported, so `letters { text "x" }` is the one error, and `check::misplaced` now says where to write the element (`text … { letters { … } }`). The reference generator names what a leaf still holds ("It takes no children but `letters`") beside `letters`'s "may appear only directly inside `text`", and design.md's effects row writes the whole form. Tests: `tests/negative/letters_outside_text.strand`, `checker.rs::a_text_holds_letters_and_nothing_else` (a `letters` with a child) and `strand-dev reference::tests::where_an_element_goes_is_on_its_page`.

## list-scroll-regrow

**2026-10-16 · list-scroll-regrow: a reveal stands until the pointer scrolls, and is placed again whenever the list's view changes size.** A launcher's filtered list whose height follows its rows (`height: n > 0 ? 40 * n : 1`) came back scrolled by a row after a query that matched nothing was cleared, and stayed so until the next change. The router selects the first row as the rows come back and reveals it (`Renderer::reveal_index`) at once, but the content-sized surface keeps its short size until the compositor configures it, so the first layout gave the list a view of a few pixels: the 40 px row was scrolled to its bottom edge (39 px), and nothing undid that once the view grew to 200, as an offset inside the content is kept. A reveal is now recorded in the list's `ScrollState` (the row, its global index and the offset before it) and placed again, from that offset, by the next layout pass and by every pass that changes the list's view or remeasures the rows; a pointer scroll (wheel, touchpad) ends it, so a view the user scrolled keeps its offset as it resizes, and a row gone from the list ends it too (what selects next reveals again). Placing it from where the view was, not from the current offset, is what lets the view go back: the least scroll that shows the row in the view the list has now. Alongside, a row taller than the view is revealed at its top, not its bottom (as GTK and browsers do), since its top is where its content starts. Keep-selected-visible holds in every view size: a view that shrinks scrolls to keep the revealed row in view.

## change-optional-chain

**2026-10-16 · change-optional-chain: `on change` over a record's key fires when the record switches.** `on change clipboard.history.first?.id { … }` never ran on a new copy, while `on change clipboard.history.first`, `… ?? -1` or a `let` bound to the chain did. The optional chain was not the cause: a target that is a field of a keyed record re-baselines when the record's identity changes (wave2-vm: `on change` identity), and for the key field itself the value is the identity, so every change was classed as a switch and none fired (`audio.sink.id` never fired on a sink switch either). spec.md 8.4's rule exists so a switch does not pass for a change of the field watched; a watched key has no change but the switch, and watching it says the switch is what is wanted. So a target whose field is the record's key, or holds it (the first step of a path key: `app` in `Hit`'s `key app.id`, whose value changes whenever the hit's identity does), compares values only (`lower::handler`), in `on change` and `on change … after` alike; other fields of a keyed record (`clipboard.history.first?.text`, a hit's `score`) still take a switch as their baseline. Whether a list query's item switch (`first`, `last`, `[i]`) should re-baseline the way an object reference's does is left to the owner (owner-testing.md, Docs and traps 3). Bindings, `if` and `let`s never used the identity rule (`tests/instantiate.rs::on_change_over_an_identity_fires_on_a_switch`). A handler with several targets used to compare them under one combined key, so a key watched beside a field of its own object (`on change clipboard.history.first?.id, clipboard.history.first?.text`, `hits.first?.app, hits.first?.score`) still never ran on a switch: the field's identity changed with it and re-baselined the whole handler. Each target is now paired with its own identity and the handler runs when some target changes while its identity stays (`strand_core::Runtime::on_change_each`, `on_change_after_each`; architecture.md): `audio.sink.volume, audio.sink.muted` still takes a sink switch as its baseline, while a plain target beside a field (`audio.sink.volume, x`) runs when it changes in the switch's tick (`strand-core/tests/handler_semantics.rs::on_change_each_judges_each_target_by_its_own_identity`).

## nav-remount

**2026-10-16 · nav-remount: `nav:` names the list as it is once the change is done.** A launcher whose input steers `nav: m == b ? lb : la` beside `pages current: m` lost its arrows on switching pages, and a constant `nav: lb` into a page lost them once the page had gone and come back. The `nav` binding turns the element it names into its scene node when its memo runs, and which node an element has is no signal: the memo ran when `m` changed, before the page swap mounted `lb`, gave `Unset` as it had at the first mount (when `la` was not mounted yet either), so nothing changed and render kept the unmounted `la`'s node; and a constant `nav: lb` never runs again, so a remounted `lb` (a new node) was never named, while the old node's id could be reused for another node. Making each element's node a signal would cost one per element for a handful of props; instead a prop's memo now also gives the element it names (`PropOut::node`), and the instance keeps every such prop (`Ctx::node_props`, which replaces the bind-time-only `late_nodes`) and sets it at the end of each tick, once everything is mounted, to the node the element has then, or unsets it while it has none. A node-valued prop thus follows its element across mounts, remounts and rekeys, whether or not the expression changes in the same step. Render already moves the keys to a new `nav` list and selects its first row (`nav_moves_to_a_list_mounted_in_the_same_diff` holds that); spec.md 6.7 says what `nav` names.

## launch-env

**2026-10-16 · launch-env (G9): the variables that address one shell stay with it; `STRAND_STATE_DIR` names its state directory.** A second shell beside the first (a launcher of its own, a test shell) needs its own socket and its own state, and the only ways were `STRAND_SOCKET` (spec section 13) and overriding `XDG_STATE_HOME`/`XDG_CACHE_HOME`/`XDG_CONFIG_HOME` for the process. Every program a shell starts inherited both: a terminal opened from the second shell answered `strand set` with that shell, not the display's, and an app it launched kept its own state and caches under the test shell's homes. Restoring the session's XDG values is not possible (the shell never saw them), and keeping a launch's environment apart from the shell's would add a concept. So the shell's own variables are named for it and never passed on: `STRAND_STATE_DIR` names the state directory itself (default `$XDG_STATE_HOME/strand`; absolute only, as the XDG variables), resolved in one place, `strand_core::persist::state_dir`, by every store and by `strand export`; and `strand_services::child::child_env` (was `activation_env`, which every spawn site already called) removes `STRAND_SOCKET` and `STRAND_STATE_DIR` beside the activation token from every program the shell starts: app launches, declared actions' commands, `exec` sources, `file` `run:` commands and the overlay's editor. Every other variable passes as the shell got it. The split is by what the variable addresses, not by who started the program: a declared action that runs `strand toggle …` from a second shell reaches the display's shell too, and one that means its own shell names the socket in its argv (`["env", "STRAND_SOCKET=…", "strand", …]`), since its author chose that socket. No `STRAND_CACHE_DIR`: the only cache is the last-good build, keyed by the config directory's canonical path, so shells of different configs never share an entry and sharing the directory costs nothing; and no config variable, since `strand run dir` already names the config. `strand help` gains an environment section listing the two (crates/strand-services/tests/apps.rs::a_launch_never_inherits_the_variables_that_address_this_shell, crates/strand/src/run/exec.rs::tests::a_command_never_inherits_the_variables_that_address_this_shell, crates/strand-core/tests/state_dir.rs::the_stores_follow_strand_state_dir_ahead_of_xdg_state_home, each failing on 25348b69; crates/strand-services/src/child.rs::tests::a_launch_carries_its_token_and_never_an_inherited_one, crates/strand-core/tests/persist.rs::strand_state_dir_names_the_state_directory_itself).

## morph-cross-surface

**2026-10-16 · morph-cross-surface: a node that starts a shared morph shows the props it was created with at their values.** A test shell's launcher icon (a 940-wide panel) flying into a droplet its 880-wide OSD mounts started some 40 px left of and above the icon. The surfaces' origins and the box carried between them were right (the icon's box, moved by the difference of the two origins, lands where it was drawn on screen); the droplet's own `x: (mw - 38) / 2` and `y: 14`, written by logic in the diff that created it, sprang from 0 under the flight. `Animator::paint` shows a node entering for the first time at the values it was created with ("a node drawn for the first time has no value on screen to spring from") by asking whether it is entering, and a morph that starts takes the node out of the entering set so that its enter pose does not play; it then counted as an old node whose props logic had just changed from unset, and every animated prop it was created with sprang (its offsets moved the flight's start, its colour faded in). Design says the morph plays "in place of its `enter` pose", not in place of being new: a node that starts a morph now drops those creation writes as an entering node does (`Animator::shared_morph`), so only the morph moves it. Nothing in design.md changes; the cross-surface case only showed it because the earlier tests wrote their nodes' props with instant transitions.

## shadow-slice

**2026-10-16 · shadow-slice: a shadow on a box large enough for its blur is drawn from slice tiles that do not depend on the box's size, on both backends.** The owner's launcher card springs its width, height and bottom radius on every mode switch and carries `shadow: $elevation.xl` (0 16px 48px) with corners 18, 18, R, R. The paint cache keyed a shadow's pixmap by its exact rect, so every frame of a resize missed: the CPU raster blurred the whole extent again (four times, once per quadrant under a clip, with unequal radii, and directly until a second whole frame for one over 2 MB), and the GPU backend built and uploaded a new pixmap of the shadow's size each frame. vello's blurred rounded rect is a distance field, `0.5 × (erf((min_edge + d)/σ) − erf(d/σ))` scaled by a term of the box's long side, where `d` past a corner's reach (`r1 = hypot(r, 2σ)` from each edge) is the distance outside the nearer edge, or `max(u, v)` deep inside, whatever the radius. For a box at least `2 × 4σ` across, whose `r1` vello does not clamp to half its short side and whose scale term is flat, every size-dependent term is within 3e-6 of its limit (vello's erf of 4), under a thousandth of a level in a u8 channel. Such a shadow is now cut per quadrant into a base tile (a square corner's field from `2.5σ + 2` px outside to `4σ + 2` px inside each edge, drawn padded past its inner edges: the edges' 1-D profiles and the flat middle) and a corner tile of the quadrant's own radius (out to `r1 + 2`) over it, the quadrants meeting between the corners' reach, where all four fields are the same. Tiles are rendered by vello's own `fill_blurred_rounded_rect` on a virtual box large enough for the same flat terms, and keyed by blur, colour, radius and the edges' sub-pixel phase, never by size (layout snaps boxes to whole pixels, so a card's phases stay put while it springs). This is the 9-slice design.md's paint table already names for glows (`Glow` is drawn as a shadow, so glows on boxes slice too), with the corner kept apart from the base so that a springing radius rebuilds only its corner tiles. Each quadrant is the field of its own corner's radius, as the quadrant draw was, so per-corner radii need no clip. Kept as they were: a shadow under a `scale`/`rotate` transform (slices meet on whole pixels; it keeps its whole pixmap, smoothly sampled), a box under the size bound or so round that vello clamps its corners (pills: their field follows the size), and a blur under 0.25 px (f32 rounding moves a near-step edge); those use the whole pixmap or the direct draw with the old rules. Cache rules: a base tile is cached at first sight; a corner tile is held uncached (`PaintCache::recent`) and cached when a later frame asks for it again, so a radius springing frame by frame builds two small tiles a frame and never evicts the cache's entries, and a still one is built once (how long it is held: the review paragraph below). The GPU lowering now counts as a frame of the paint cache (`begin_frame` in `lower_frame`) so the same rule holds there. Sizes: the launcher's eight tiles at 1.5× hold 1,388 kB against 3.7 MB for its whole pixmap, which a resize used to rebuild every frame; base's cache churned to 30.7 MB in the bench below. Equivalence: `cache.rs::sliced_shadows_match_the_direct_blur` compares 96 shapes (uniform, square, launcher and mixed radii; three sizes and blurs; fractional edges; scale 1 and 1.5) with the direct draw: at most one level in one channel, on 0.0004% of pixels at worst; no pixel reference changed. The GPU draws the sliced card within one level of the CPU (`gpu.rs::a_sliced_shadow_on_the_gpu_matches_the_cpu`). Work: `paint.rs::a_resizing_card_draws_its_shadow_from_the_same_tiles` resizes `elevation.lg` and `elevation.xl` cards at 1.5× for 12 frames and asserts no pixmap is built and no shadow pixel blurred after the first frame (`Renderer::blurred_shadow_px`, new, counts tile and pixmap pixels built and extents drawn directly); on 558d26e6 it fails at the first resized frame (4 builds against 2). `gpu.rs::a_resizing_shadow_is_lowered_from_the_same_tiles` fails there with "frame 2 uploaded 1". Three tests counted one pixmap per shadow and now count tiles (`paint.rs`: `elevation_shadow_lists_are_drawn_and_cached` 4 → 18, `shadows_no_frame_used_go_once_idle` 4 → 18, `moved_shadows_reuse_their_pixmap` 1 → 8: md and lg's 2px layer slice, the 24px and 48px layers' 80-wide boxes are too small for their blur); what they assert (a second frame builds nothing, a moved shadow reuses its tiles, a repaint matches) is unchanged. Timing, not a gate (`cache_bench.rs::resizing_shadow_frame_cost`, `--profile timing`, container, the launcher card at 1.5× resized every frame, 200 frames, two runs each): 558d26e6 mean 10.6 ms, p50 7.3, p95 16.8; now 3.9 ms, p50 3.9, p95 4.1 (size only) and 5.0 ms, p50 5.0, p95 5.3 with the bottom radius springing too; a still card repainted whole costs 5.1 ms from base's cached pixmap and 4.9 ms from the tiles (3.9 ms with no shadow), so a resizing shadow now costs what compositing it does. End to end (the owner's launcher, `target/try/tools/shots-keys.sh` with `perf/tab.steps`, CPU at 940 × 640 @1.5, raster of surface 2's frames of at least 20,000 px, base and this binary interleaved, two rounds): base p50 20.1 / 19.9 ms, p95 65.2 / 54.7 ms; now p50 14.9 / 15.0 ms, p95 48.4 / 36.1 ms (a first run 14.0 / 46.0; the coordinator's base 22.0 / 64.8 and no-shadow 8.5 / 24.1). The rest of the gap to no shadow is damage, not raster of the shadow: a box with a shadow damages its shadow's whole extent when it resizes, where a plain box damages only along its edges (`NodeRecord::geom`), and the springing radius's two corner tiles cost about 1 ms a frame. Narrowing a shadowed box's damage to the band that changes is a separate change. An experiment that skipped the casting box's inside when drawing the slices (where the clip lets nothing through) measured nothing and was dropped. architecture.md's paint-cache paragraph and `cache.rs`'s entry say how shadows are cached now; design.md is unchanged (its paint table already says "cached as 9-slice or pixmap").

**2026-10-16 · shadow-slice (review): a corner tile waits for any later frame, within a 4 MB hold; tiles over 2 MB are not sliced.** The first rule held a corner tile only until the next `begin_frame`. Those frames belong to the one paint cache every surface shares (each CPU prepare and, since this change, each GPU lowering), so when a second surface painted between two frames of the card (a bar's clock, another monitor, an OSD), the tile was gone before the card asked again, and a still radius rebuilt its four corner tiles every frame, about 1–2 ms at the launcher's σ = 36 px, where the old path had ended up with a cached pixmap. Now a held tile is cached when any later frame asks for it, as `seen_before` does for gradients. Held tiles are bounded by bytes, not frames: at most `RECENT_BYTES` (4 MB, a few dozen of the launcher's corner tiles at 1.5×), oldest first, never the current frame's, and freed when idle with the rest. They count in `PaintCache::bytes` (`Renderer::paint_cache`), so the reported memory includes them. Per-surface frame counters were the alternative. They would put a surface identity into a cache that both backends share by key and would still drop a tile between a surface's own partial frames, so the byte bound is simpler. Size: a base tile was cached at first sight whatever its size, which skipped the large-entry rule (`EAGER_ENTRY_BYTES`); with `MAX_BLUR` at 1000 a frame's four base tiles could pass the 32 MB budget. A shadow whose tiles would pass 2 MB (a blur over about 110 px, or a huge radius) is no longer sliced: it keeps its whole pixmap under the large-entry rule. So one shadow's tiles hold at most 16 MB. Tests: `cache.rs::other_surfaces_painting_between_frames_do_not_lose_corner_tiles` interleaves one to three other surfaces' frames (a bar's shadow, an OSD whose radius springs) between a card's frames and asserts that a still radius builds its tiles once and a springing one settles; under the one-frame rule it fails at the first frame ("rebuilt the card's tiles", 28 builds against 24). `shadows_at_the_slicing_bound_match_the_direct_blur` adds 72 shapes at the bound, where the flat terms are tightest: the shortest box `slice_plan` takes for each blur, in quarter pixels, with that box a quarter pixel shorter refused, and the roundest corner it takes on a box 12σ across (alone and on all four corners), at 1.5× with fractional edges, both ways round. The worst is one level, on 4 pixels. `small_round_or_sharp_boxes_are_not_sliced` checks the 2 MB bound (σ 125 refused, σ 100 sliced). Bench (`resizing_shadow_frame_cost`, two runs): size springing is unchanged at 3.9 ms mean, 8 builds. Size and radius together now take 4.1 ms (p95 5.2) with 104 builds, against 5.0 ms and 400 builds. That gain is the bench's: its radius repeats every 60 frames, so held tiles come back. A real spring never repeats a radius and still builds two tiles a frame. The end-to-end launcher run was not repeated. Its only other surface, the bar, paints 10 times against the card's 435, so the old rule lost tiles on a handful of frames.

## gpu-first

**2026-10-16 · gpu-first (OWNER RULING): anything that animates draws on the GPU from its first large frame, and the device is kept warm for the session wherever one can exist.** Asked why Strand's animations feel less snappy than their Quickshell (about 300 MB PSS against Strand's 67 MB), the owner said: "That seems trivial since we're already way below quickshell. Why wouldn't we default to GPU for everything if it were available?", and then: "Okay lets do that then I expect a very material change in speed." This applies the standing rule that speed beats size and that memory budgets are tripwires re-based with a measured reason, never caps. The rule replaces M4's promotion, which promoted a surface after 500 ms of large frames and only at a frame with no spring in flight, so the owner's spring-driven launcher morphs never reached the GPU, and which dropped the device 30 s after its last use, so the next animation paid for its creation. As implemented in `strand-render/src/promote.rs`, after the review of d636d051:
- **Promotion.** A surface switches to the GPU at its first large frame (0.2 Mpx damaged) while it animates (a spring, a transition, a swap crossfade or a scroll in flight), or at the third large frame in a row (each within 250 ms of the last) of a clock-driven paint. The frame on which an animation settles never promotes.
- **Demotion, on damage.** A promoted surface goes back to the CPU once it has been settled for 3 s, at a still frame or at the one wake it asks for. Settled means small or no damage, as the ruling says: d636d051 counted any spring in flight as hot, so the launcher's 80 px turning cover (`t`-driven, so a spring every frame) kept it on the GPU for good, repainting 1.35 Mpx a frame there. Now a small spring frame is hot only when the CPU draws it slowly: the small spring frames the CPU drew took `CHEAP_FRAME` (4 ms) or more (since review 2, the median of the last five, once three came, each drawn over at most twice its own damage). That is the launcher's case, where the CPU re-rasterises the blurred card for the cover's 7.5k px of damage in 13–19 ms against the GPU's 9–10 ms full frame, so the GPU stays the faster backend there and keeps the surface; with the media paused the launcher goes back after 3 s. The cost is learned from a CPU frame, so a surface promoted at its first frame (a panel opening) still goes back once before it is known.
- **Re-promotion settles longer.** A surface promoted again within 30 s of going back waits 15 s (`AGAIN_FACTOR` 5) before it goes back again, so someone switching modes every few seconds is not handed to the CPU, with a full CPU repaint, between switches (the review's low item). Measured below: one CPU spell after the first settle, none after.
- **The device.** `strand run` asks for it as it configures (`Renderer::warm_gpu`, `BackendChange::Start`, which replaces `Drop`), off the frame path, but only where a device can exist: a `/dev/dri/renderD*` node, or a software adapter accepted (`STRAND_GPU_SOFTWARE=1`, the test tier). Elsewhere it calls `Renderer::gpu_absent` and builds no Vulkan instance. An answer of no adapter, or only a software one refused, is final for the process (`Device::Absent`), so a machine that can never have a device never probes again; the review measured d636d051 at 93 MB idle with lavapipe's LLVM mapped and nothing gained, and re-probing at each animation 30 s apart. Its thread draws one warm-up frame and builds the present blit for both formats before `Ready`, so the first animation compiles nothing. Nothing drops it. Lost devices, `LOST_CAP` and the 30 s retry for other failures stay.
- **The Vulkan loader filter.** A loaded driver stays mapped for the process, and the loader loads every installed manifest: on a stock Ubuntu with `mesa-vulkan-drivers`, d636d051 mapped eight drivers and LLVM (lavapipe and RADV link it) beside the Intel GPU it used. Before any thread starts, the binary sets `VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE` to keep out lavapipe and SwiftShader (unless a software adapter is accepted), the drivers of PCI vendors with no render node here, and the platform GPUs' drivers when every render node's vendor was read; it appends to an inherited value, sets nothing when the environment chose drivers itself, and gives the variable back to spawned programs as it found it. The variable is the loader's own (1.3.234 on); an older loader ignores it and loads as before.
- **The adapter.** `PowerPreference::LowPower` replaces `HighPerformance`: with the device held for the session, a hybrid laptop would otherwise keep its discrete GPU out of runtime suspend all session and present across GPUs. The compositor's dmabuf-feedback main device would be exact, but the adapter is chosen before any surface exists.
- **Present path.** A promoted surface presents through the WSI wherever the compositor takes the GPU's buffers (Hyprland, a GLES2 or Vulkan sway, or lavapipe on any sway) and reads back only where it cannot (ANV under a pixman-rendered sway, lock surfaces). The review rerun found a stall d636d051 had: a presented surface whose content size changed (the launcher's 1410↔1479 px mode switches) was held for the configure at its new size, which cannot come before its next present commits the new size, and nothing woke the loop at the hold's end, so the launcher froze about 0.5 s on those switches (13 frames in the 700 ms after the Tab, against the CPU's 43). 47a3cd04 then stopped holding presented surfaces, which drew the new layout into the old size (review 2 below holds them again and has the GPU thread commit the new size); any hold on one wakes the loop at its end (`GpuHost::wait`).

Refinements kept from d636d051, each closest to "anything that animates": the 0.2 Mpx floor stays, because below it the CPU frame is about 2 ms and the GPU's fixed costs do not win. Clocks wait for three large frames, so a lone content change does not promote. A panel's first frame is promoted naturally (full damage, its enter spring) but not drawn on the GPU before its first commit, because the hand-off needs a committed surface. With no GPU, behaviour is unchanged, now including memory.

**Measured** with the owner's launcher (`target/try/launcher`, `perf/tab-idle.steps`: an idle report at boot, open, Tab through every mode twice 700 ms apart, a report 5 s later; and `perf/tab-gap.steps`, six Tabs 4.5 s apart), release builds of 3a638d14 and this change (and d636d051 once), on the laptop's Intel GPU (ANV, Mesa 25.2) through `gpu.sh` under a GLES2-rendered headless sway at 60 Hz. That is present mode (`STRAND_GPU_PRESENT=1`; under the default pixman sway ANV can only read back). The launcher is 1410×960 at scale 1.5. Runs were interleaved new, base, new, base with the mock player playing, then base, new, base, new paused (so the turning cover does not dominate). Figures are from the timestamped logs, per frame, in the 700 ms after each Tab: the CPU's large (mode-switch) frames from base's `damage` lines against every GPU frame (`gpu-frame` lines, the GPU thread's CPU part plus the GPU's run).
- **Mode-switch frames, ms p50 / p95 / p99 / max.** Base on the CPU, playing: 9.60 / 26.84 / 67.23 / 98.33 and 10.23 / 22.77 / 45.06 / 126.45; paused: 11.39 / 23.94 / 40.19 / 52.45 and 10.38 / 25.87 / 45.90 / 116.82. New on `gpu-present`, playing: 4.59 / 12.41 / 14.38 / 15.87 and 4.68 / 13.29 / 16.03 / 18.76; paused: 4.16 / 11.97 / 14.93 / 15.72 and 4.94 / 14.04 / 16.16 / 19.27. The worst frame went from 52–126 ms to 16–19 ms on a quiet host; review 2 below gives the figures under load, where it does not hold. Counting every frame in the windows on both sides, not base's large frames alone, the median is not won (review 2): the gain is the tails, the stalls and the frames delivered.
- **Frames drawn per 700 ms window.** New 42–44 in every window; base drops to 28–37 in one or two windows a run. Tab to the first new frame: base up to 116–136 ms, new at most 25 ms after the first switch (36–51 ms on the first, paused).
- **Main thread.** Its work per frame in the windows went from base's p95 18–19 / p99 29 ms to 3.2–3.9 / 3.5–4.0 ms.
- **Spaced switches** (paused, 4.5 s apart). Base: large frames 9.21 / 28.32 / 77.36 / 108.63 ms. New: the launcher went back to the CPU 3.3 s after the first Tab, drew 2 CPU frames (17–30 ms) at the next Tab before it was presented again (0.13 s later), then, promoted again within 30 s, stayed for every later switch: GPU frames 4.29 / 14.61 / 16.76 / 20.09 ms.
- **Steady state.** With the cover turning, outside the windows: base 13.4 ms p50 (the CPU re-rasterising the card), new 9.6–9.8 ms p50 on the GPU. Paused, after the tabs: new goes back to the CPU, base and new both draw nothing.
- **Not won.** The GPU's own run is about 0.3 ms; the rest of a full 1.35 Mpx GPU frame, 8.6–9.8 ms p50, is vello_gpu's CPU-side encoding on the `strand-gpu` thread. Mode-switch p50 (4.2–4.9 ms) fits a 120 Hz panel's 8.33 ms; their p95 (12–14 ms) and a full-surface repaint's p50 do not. That encoding is the next lever.
- **Memory, idle at boot.** With the loader limited to the Intel driver (`gpu.sh`'s `VK_DRIVER_FILES`): base 37.0–37.3 MB, new 57.9–58.6 MB. With the loader searching every installed driver as on a desktop, software not accepted: base 36,964 kB, d636d051 95,407 kB (eight drivers and LLVM mapped), new 60,470 kB (Intel's two). After the ten switches: base 72–77.5 MB, new 108–118 MB.

**Budgets: two legs.** The review found the warm-only gates of d636d051 no longer tripwires: a margin taken as a percentage of a figure that is mostly lavapipe and LLVM (about 190 MB) let a 50 MB regression in the shell pass. Now:
- **Cold**, no render node and no software adapter accepted, so nothing is asked for and nothing Vulkan is mapped (asserted, with "GPU: no GPU render node" logged): the old gates, the bar 42 / 48 MB (41,294 kB measured, release), the full shell 76 / 104 MB (75,034 and 86,820 kB with 161 entries in two runs, over the target and under the ceiling as on `main`: 3a638d14 measured 90,157 kB in the same container), debug 96 MiB (75,166 kB); `demo.rs` and `services.rs`' bars keep 48 MB and 92 MiB debug (59,751 and 61,420 kB debug). The cold legs skip where a render node exists (`gpu.sh`).
- **Warm**, CI's lavapipe device: the measurement plus about the cold gates' absolute headroom, not a share of LLVM. The bar 232 / 242 MiB (232,089 and 229,230 kB measured), the full shell 296 / 324 MiB (296,351 kB with 161 entries, 274,308 kB with 4), debug 288 MiB (269,462 kB). The device is asserted up and never dropped.

**2026-10-16 · gpu-first (review 2): loaded-host figures, the median, a presented surface's new size, and three small fixes.** The second review of 47a3cd04 reran the paused A/B while the owner's own load ran on the laptop (a Playwright Chromium and Node, load average 20–69) and found isolated GPU-path frames of 282, 612 and 630 ms (the `strand-gpu` thread's CPU part, the first presented frame after the attach and two mid-window) and one 700 ms window with 2 frames, worse than anything base did there (its worst frame 128 ms); and that the headline p50 compared base's large frames with every GPU frame.
- **Where a slow frame's time goes.** Under `STRAND_LOG=debug` the `strand-gpu` thread now logs a frame slower than `strand_gpu::SLOW_FRAME` (40 ms) with its phases (upload, passes, scene build, texture, render encode, acquire, submit, present), its uploads, and the thread's time on a core, waiting for one, and major faults from `/proc/thread-self` (`strand_gpu::thread_stats`); render logs a slow paint on the main thread the same way, and an attach, resize, release, commit or pass taking as long. The cost while the debug log is off is the frame's few `Instant`s.
- **The cause was not found.** No GPU-only stall was reproduced. With a busy loop on every core inside the container the worst GPU frame was 66 ms and no GPU-thread frame reached 40 ms; under the host's own IO pressure that day (`some` 42–46 %, 11 GB of swap in use), with the container held to 350 MB beside a 250 MB hog touching its pages, and with three `vkcube`s in mailbox mode on the same GPU, every window drew 39–44 frames and no frame passed 49 ms. Only all of them at once slowed the GPU path, and then base far more (below). There the slow-frame lines showed the time as waiting for a core (`runqueue` 9–134 ms in a frame against 7–33 ms run), largest in the submit phase, with major faults on the first frame (172), not as work of ours or a pipeline compiled late; so the reviewer's 0.6 s frames, with the cause unknown, are recorded as observed, and the debug lines are there for the next one. Thread priority (asking rtkit for the frame threads) is the lever that would help both paths under CPU contention and is left open.
- **Figures** (paused, `tab-idle.steps`, present mode, frames in the 700 ms after each Tab: every GPU frame's `gpu-frame` time against every CPU frame's flatten + raster, ms p50 / p95 / p99 / max; frames per window). Quiet host, this commit and 3a638d14 interleaved twice: new 3.58 / 9.70 / 11.01 / 13.29 and 3.74 / 9.38 / 11.27 / 13.06, 42–43 frames in every window; base 2.29 / 17.20 / 40.88 / 70.63 and 2.30 / 17.14 / 41.00 / 70.82, two windows a run down to 29–31 frames with an 81–86 ms gap. So the median is the CPU's (a GPU frame repaints the whole surface, a CPU frame only its damage) and the win is the tail (p99 41 to 11 ms), the stalls and the frames delivered; the reviewer's own logs said the same (all-frame p50 base 4.67 / 4.79 / 3.20 / 3.27 against new 4.59 / 4.68 / 4.16 / 4.94). Loaded (all three loads above at once, interleaved twice): new 12.46 / 47.04 / 68.77 / 101.34 and 12.08 / 40.62 / 99.49 / 135.61, 12–37 frames a window, the longest gap 210 and 258 ms; base 8.41 / 117.39 / 360.14 / 446.23 and 11.50 / 170.51 / 288.22 / 315.18, 2–27 frames a window, the longest gap 520 and 391 ms. Under the reviewer's load: new as above, base's worst 128 ms. PSS idle at boot 57.3–57.9 MB new against 36.9–37.0 MB base; after the ten switches 111–117 against 75.6–76.7 MB.
- **A presented surface's new size** (the review's low item, checked). Burst captures and the frame log of six growing switches (1410 to 1479 px) showed 47a3cd04 drawing the new layout into the old size in two of the six (a 1410 px frame with the new layout's flatten time 14–23 ms after the Tab), and grim's first capture of each switch off-centre and clipped on the far side, as the review expected. The hold is back for presented surfaces, and the size the manager leaves pending (it does not commit a surface the GPU thread presents) is committed by the thread: `GpuRequest::Commit(surface)` presents the surface's last frame again, sent when render hands the surface changes to the manager (`Renderer::take_surface_changes`), once per size. In the same six switches the first new-layout frame then came at the new size every time, 19–34 ms after the Tab (base 24–31, 47a3cd04 14–28 with the wrong size). Growing switches pay that frame of latency; others do not. The alternative, committing from the manager, would race the WSI's own attach and commit on the same surface.
- **The slow-spring cost** is the median of the last five small spring frames the CPU drew, once three came, each over at most twice its own damage (a buffer of age 2), so a preempted raster, or the full repaint after a demotion or of a late readback, does not hold a cheap spring on the GPU (`one_slow_spring_frame_does_not_hold_a_surface_on_the_gpu`, which fails on 47a3cd04). It still does not age while the surface is on the GPU: a surface that kept its slow small spring would go back only when the spring rests.
- **Render nodes sysfs hides.** `render_vendors` reads the vendor of every render node in sysfs or in `/dev/dri`, and a node with none readable (a sandbox hiding sysfs but passing the device) makes the vendors unknown, so no hardware driver is filtered out and the probe cannot answer `NoAdapter` (final) for want of one. The reviewer's other half, `strand-dev inspect`'s editor inheriting `VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE`, needed no change: `strand-dev` is its own binary without `process_setup!`, so it sets nothing, and strand starts it only through `child_env`, which gives the variable back.
- **A failed warm device is started again once at its retry** (`promote::Device::retry_at`, `Renderer::gpu_wake`): a kept-warm device that failed for a reason that may pass, or was lost, asks for one wake at its 30 s retry and starts again, so the next animation does not wait for it; if that start fails too, it is asked for on demand only, so an idle shell whose device never starts is not woken every 30 s (`a_failed_warm_device_is_started_again_once_at_its_retry`, which fails on 47a3cd04).
- **Budgets.** Nothing here changes memory (the phase marks allocate only with the debug log on). The warm gates' headroom on GitHub's 4-core runners is still unmeasured: if the first `budgets` job misses, it is re-based with that run's figures and its number here, as m5-open-budgets and seam-snap were.


**2026-10-16 · gpu-first (exit): a GPU thread still running at exit ends the process with `_exit`.** The first full local `ci` on 185d47ee failed at step 23: `demo.rs::strand_run_keeps_a_replugged_monitors_bar` sent SIGTERM a few seconds after boot under the whole suite's load, lavapipe was still compiling the warm device's pipelines, the GPU thread did not end within `GPU_SHUTDOWN` (3 s, the existing hung-driver path that leaks the manager), and the process then died with SIGSEGV (status 139) in the normal exit: the C library's exit handlers and the driver's static destructors (LLVM) ran under the still-running thread. Before gpu-first a device existed only while something animated, so this path was all but unreachable at a SIGTERM. Now `run::run`, when the thread was left running, joins the logic thread and the compiler (state is on disk), prints its error if any, flushes the logger and stdio and ends with `libc::_exit` (`exit_beside_gpu_thread`). Waiting longer was rejected: a hung driver would hold the exit forever, which is what the 3 s bound exists for. No test hook holds the GPU thread on purpose, so the proof is the failing `ci` run (the warning "the thread did not end within 3 s" then status 139) and the full `ci` that passes on the fix.

## syncobj-lend

**2026-10-16 · syncobj-lend: a surface lent to the GPU thread takes no buffer until it is handed off or taken back (owner-testing.md bug 22).** On the gpu-first build the owner's Hyprland ended Strand's connection with `wp_linux_drm_syncobj_surface_v1` error 4, "Missing acquire timeline", after it had worked for a moment. Promotion lends a surface's `wl_display` and `wl_surface` to the GPU thread (`State::raw_handles`), and until its `Attached` reply the manager went on painting and committing shm frames, by design (M4: the device could take 100 ms or more to start). Mesa's Vulkan WSI turns explicit sync on for a surface it builds a swapchain on when the compositor offers `wp_linux_drm_syncobj_manager_v1` (Hyprland does; CI's sway 1.9 does not, and CI's Hyprland has no hardware GPU, so the WSI never ran against it), and from then the compositor refuses a buffer committed with no acquire point. Before gpu-first a surface was promoted only at a settled frame, so in practice nothing was painted in the window; promoted at the first frame of an animation, a frame usually was. The manager now attaches no buffer to a lent surface (`draw` returns; a bare commit acking a configure, which carries no buffer, still goes) and draws the frames it skipped at `take_back`; `hand_off` is unchanged. The cost is the window itself: the surface holds its last frame while the swapchain is built, a few milliseconds with the device kept warm (gpu-first). The other direction was already safe: `Release` drops the target and with it the `wgpu::Surface` (the `VkSurfaceKHR`, whose destruction destroys Mesa's syncobj surface) before `Released`, so the first shm frame after `take_back` goes to a surface with explicit sync off. Test: `crates/strand-surface/tests/gpu_handoff.rs::a_lent_surface_takes_no_buffer_until_it_is_taken_back` (fails on e5f3a178: "a buffer was committed to a lent surface", 2 against 1); `a_surface_destroyed_after_its_handles_were_lent_waits_for_take_back` no longer expects a lent surface to be committed.

## gpu-regions

**2026-10-16 · gpu-regions: a frame drawn on the GPU sets its opaque, input and blur regions as pending state for its present (owner-testing.md bug 23).** With gpu-first the owner's island closed as soon as the pointer left the area the closed island covered. A `trigger: hover` popup that draws nothing itself takes input only where its content drew in the last frame (m6-owner-fixes), and the surface manager sends that region, with the opaque and blur regions, in `draw` after each shm paint. A handed-off surface is never painted there: `run/gpu.rs` paints it with `Renderer::paint_gpu` and sends the frame to the GPU thread, so every region stayed as the last shm frame left it, the closed island's, while the island grew on the GPU. The fix keeps the manager the only place that speaks the region requests: `State::sync_presented(surface)` runs the same three syncs (`sync_opaque`, `sync_painted_input`, `set_blur`) for a handed-off surface, sending only what changed and committing nothing, and the host calls it after each frame it sends; the GPU thread's present commits them with the frame, or the next one if the requests reach the socket after it (both threads share one `wl_display`, so its queue keeps their order). The alternative, sending the regions inside the `GpuRequest::Frame` for the GPU thread to set before presenting, would put a second speaker of the manager's protocol state on another thread. Latent since M4; promotion at the first frame of an animation (gpu-first) exposed it. Test: `crates/strand-surface/tests/gpu_handoff.rs::a_handed_off_surface_takes_input_where_its_gpu_frame_drew`.

## flip-open

**2026-10-17 · flip-open: a layout pass that a text's arrival causes glides what it moves from where it was drawn (owner-testing.md bug 24).** Turning Focus on in the owner's island mounted its glyph in the crown's status row, and the music bars beside it jumped out of the island and fell back as they slid left. Bug 14's fix lays a frame out, waits up to `ESTIMATE_WAIT` for text the worker has not shaped, and lays it out again, so "a correction from an estimate is no layout change at all once no frame is laid out by one". But the FLIP that a structural change asks for (`flip`, taken by the next layout pass) was taken by the first pass, laid out by the estimate: the glyph's name, seventeen letters at 0.55 em, wrapped into ten lines in its 14 px box, made the row about 170 px tall, and the bars' glide started from where they had been drawn to where that pass put them. The second pass put them back on their level and started no glide, so the first glide's offset stood: they were drawn far above their box and fell into it. The structural change's scope (its `flip` parents, `flip_all`) now stays open on the surface (`flip_open`) until every text on it is shaped (`flatten_surface`'s `settled`), and a layout pass after a text arrived (`text_arrived`, set by `deliver`) glides what it moved in that scope from the previous pass's boxes; glides add (`Motion::shift`), so each box starts where it was drawn. Nodes laid out first since the surface last painted (`unpainted`) are left out: the mounted glyph was never drawn where its estimate was, and would otherwise glide in from there. It covers a text that arrives after the frame's wait too: the frame drawn by the estimate is then where the correction glides from, a drift that settles rather than a jump. Of the alternatives, holding a moving surface's frame for its text would stall every animation on it (the bars dance), and laying unshaped text out at no size would move its siblings twice (its gap first). Test: `crates/strand-render/tests/morph.rs::a_mounted_text_moves_its_siblings_from_where_they_were_drawn` (fails on b293b8ef: the bars drawn at y 2 against 9 on the first frame).

## hidden-text

**2026-10-17 · hidden-text: text under a node drawn hidden is asked for and waited on as visible text is (owner-testing.md bug 25).** Turning Focus off in the owner's open island brought the unread count back as a reading with `enter { opacity: 0; x: -6 }`, and the rest of the status row dropped out of the island and fell back. Flattening returns early from a node drawn at `opacity` 0 or `scale` 0 (nothing it draws can show), so the texts under it were never in the frame's text list: not requested, not waited on by the estimate wait (m6-owner-fixes, bug 14), not kept from pruning. Layout does not skip them: a hidden box still takes its room, so it placed them by their estimates (`notifications`, one Material Symbols glyph, as thirteen letters wrapped into eight lines in 16 px), and the frame's FLIP glide aimed every sibling at that layout. The shaped sizes came once the pose let the node be drawn, a frame later, after the scope that would have corrected the glide (flip-open) had closed, since the frame's text list said everything was shaped. Such a node now walks its subtree for text only (`Flattener::hidden_texts`): each `text` and button label's unbounded spec, read from its props in its token scope with the font it inherits, as the visit reads them, and nothing else (no items, clocks, hits, or `reveal`, `stagger` and `lean` state, which would start a hidden subtree's animations early). An `input`'s text depends on its focus and keeps its estimate; time-bound text is read without the node's time. The cost is a walk of hidden subtrees on fresh frames, and their layouts are kept while hidden (they take room in layout; a launcher that keeps its modes mounted under `opacity: 0` keeps their text shaped instead of reshaping it on each switch). Test: `crates/strand-render/tests/morph.rs::text_entering_faded_out_moves_its_siblings_once` (fails on ff92415c: the siblings drawn at y 2 against 7 on the first frame).

## eval-sandbox

**2026-10-17 · eval-sandbox: the animation evaluation sandbox is a Cargo workspace of its own, `eval/`, beside the root one.** Bugs 24 and 25 (owner-testing.md) were found by eye in the owner's shell; the sandbox runs scenario scripts on a virtual clock and checks every frame's nodes, so the next of their kind is caught before it ships. It is evaluation tooling, not product: placed under `crates/` it would be a member, so `--workspace` builds, tests and clippy would compile it and its feature would unify into the product's strand-render. Its own workspace (`eval/Cargo.toml` with `[workspace]`, the precedent of `spikes/gpu-present` and `spikes/xdg-activation`) is outside the root's `members`, so root resolution, `affected` and the shipped binary never see it. The costs, and what pays them: it cannot inherit `[workspace.dependencies]`, so it names the Strand crates by path (their own `.workspace = true` fields resolve in the root workspace they belong to); it keeps its own `Cargo.lock`, seeded from the root's and held to the same versions by `scripts/eval/check-lock.sh` (no third-party dependency the root lock lacks); its profiles and lints are copies of the root's, kept equal by `eval/tests/drift.rs`; and every command runs from the repository root with `--manifest-path eval/Cargo.toml`, so `run.sh`'s `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target/container` and the shared sccache serve both. Outside the root workspace the Strand crates build as dependencies, at `[profile.dev.package."*"]`'s opt-level 2, which makes the sandbox's frame costs meaningful at the price of a slower rebuild after a strand-render edit. `scripts/eval/check-isolation.sh` (with a self-test) holds the boundary: no `crates/*/Cargo.toml` names `strand-eval`, a path into `eval/` or `eval-hooks` beyond strand-render's own feature line, the root resolution never enables `eval-hooks`, and every `cfg(feature = "eval-hooks")` is in strand-render (counted, so growth shows in review).

**2026-10-17 · eval-sandbox: strand-render's hooks are a cargo feature, `eval-hooks`, not a runtime flag.** The sandbox needs to see what each frame drew per node (the laid box, the drawn box, the motions moving it and whether they are authored) and to make inline text late on purpose; the owner wants the product free of evaluation code. A feature compiles the hooks out of every product build: no crate of the root workspace enables it, so feature unification cannot turn it on, a release `strand` holds none of it (measured on this branch: `strings` on `cargo build -p strand --release` finds no `strand_render::probe` symbol, `Router::set_now`, `Animator::motions` or any of the probe's type and method names; a bare `grep -c probe` counts 20 strings, all older than the hooks: openssl_probe, the compiler's `mount::probe`, a theme swap's `Play::probe`, std's `small_probe_read`), and root clippy with `--all-features` (ci.sh step 9) still lints the hook code. A runtime flag would ship the code and a branch in every node's flatten. The hooks are cfg'd blocks at the plan's sites, not a macro: they read as what they are, and `check-isolation.sh` counts them. What changed from the plan, as the code required: `impl Renderer` for the probe lives in `renderer/probe.rs` (Renderer's fields are private to `renderer`), the types in `src/probe.rs`; the frame trace's switch reaches `flatten()` through a cfg'd `Extras::trace` (no signature change); a node's `visual` box is its drawn box (snapped to the physical pixels it covers) through the transform it is drawn under, axis-aligned, rather than its ink bounds (a row that paints nothing has none, a shadow widens them); `laid` is a plain rect, as unplaced nodes are not traced; `OffsetParts` also carries a shared morph's translate; a drag's lift counts as authored x and y (the pointer moves it on purpose; its spring back is the glide's, which is derived); and `ENTER` is not read before `Animator::paint` as the plan had it, since a frame flattens up to six times and the first flatten takes the enter, leaving the traced (last) one without it: the animator keeps a cfg'd set of nodes whose enter pose started, and reports `ENTER` while their pose's springs run (never under reduced motion, which shows the node at once). The frame trace is pushed in `paint_frame` after the hit list is kept, so frames with empty damage are traced too, and a GPU paint runs the same path.

**2026-10-17 · eval-sandbox: lateness is inline shaping plus a hold, not a delayed worker.** A text worker answering within `ESTIMATE_WAIT` produces, in one frame, a layout pass by the estimate, the layouts' delivery and a second pass by the shaped sizes; inline shaping does the same (`flatten_surface` flattens, `request_text` shapes and delivers, the loop flattens again), so the deterministic Inline backend is the worker's in-time order, the regime bugs 24 and 25 showed in (their morph.rs tests use the worker with the wait). Text later than the wait cannot be made deterministic through the worker (its waker fires after `send`, on its own thread), so the Inline arm can hold the layout it made: the request stays in `pending`, the slot keeps what it had (nothing, for new text), and layout and flatten treat the text exactly as a late worker's (placed by its estimate and drawn as nothing, or drawn from its last layout as a stand-in) until `Renderer::release_text` hands it to `deliver`, the worker's own delivery path; released between frames with `update`, it is the runtime's `text_ready` wake. The hold changes nothing unless the sandbox turns it on.

**2026-10-17 · eval-sandbox: the input router reads its clock through `now()`, which `Router::set_now` can pin.** Hover popups open after their `delay` and close after `HOVER_GRACE` by the wall clock (the two `Instant::now()` reads in input.rs), and the owner's island is `trigger: hover`, so a scenario on virtual time needs the router on it too. A clock trait threaded through the router would add a concept for one caller; a private `fn now(&self)` that returns the wall clock, or under `eval-hooks` the time `set_now` pinned, keeps every product build's behaviour identical (without the feature it is `Instant::now()`) and is the only non-cfg'd change the hooks make.

**2026-10-17 · eval-sandbox: what cargo does with a second workspace sharing `target/container`, measured.** Inheritance: `cargo metadata --manifest-path eval/Cargo.toml` resolves every path dependency's `.workspace = true` fields in the root workspace (strand-render and the rest report version 0.0.0, edition 2024, rust-version 1.97, publish false), with eval/ the only member of its own workspace, so the plan's fallback (a root member `crates/strand-eval`) is not needed. No thrash: after an eval build, `cargo build -v -p strand-render` in the root reports 0 units compiling and 210 fresh (strand-render among them), and after a root `clippy --all-features` the eval build reports 0 compiling and 255 fresh; the two workspaces' units differ by profile and features (strand-render at opt 0 without the hooks in the root, at opt 2 with them in eval), so they sit side by side rather than replace each other. The cost is disk, not time: eval adds its own copies of the Strand crates and of the third-party crates whose features differ there. sccache: the first eval build in `target/container` sent 64 compile requests, 47 executed, 15 hits and 32 misses (third-party units with eval's own features); the Strand crates, path dependencies, compile incrementally as the root's members do and are not cacheable in either workspace (15 such calls in eval, 5 for root strand-render), which is why the plan's fallback target directory would cost most: sccache keys on `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`'s value (run.sh keeps it the relative `target/container` so worktrees share the cache), and a build of eval into `target/container-eval-probe` hit nothing (248 Rust misses, 2 min). Third-party versions: clap with `derive` and its default features would have added nine packages the root lock lacks (clap_derive, anstream and its parts), so eval uses clap's builder API with `std`, `help`, `usage`, `error-context` and `suggestions`, and the seeded eval/Cargo.lock adds no package but strand-eval itself (`scripts/eval/check-lock.sh`). Profiles: copying the root's `[profile.release.package.*]` levels for packages eval's graph does not have made cargo warn about each of 17 on every command, so eval/Cargo.toml leaves those out and `eval/tests/drift.rs` compares against the root's sections filtered by eval/Cargo.lock's package names. The GitHub rust-cache behaviour with the second workspace is measured when the `eval` job lands.

**2026-10-17 · eval-sandbox: a scenario is a TOML header, the config's files and a steps script, none of it Strand syntax.** A scenario has to say three things: the shell under test, what happens to it, and what counts as a failure. The shell is plain `.strand` text in `=== <path>.strand` sections, or a file or directory named by `config`. What happens is one verb per line (`set`, `pointer`, `text late 1 where "…"`, `rest`; docs/eval.md). Writing those as Strand (a test block, a `strand test` dialect) would add a second use of the language with its own semantics, which design.md's "does it remove a concept, or add one?" rules out; the script stays a tool's input, and values are read as `strand set` reads them (`parse_text` against the target's type), so nothing new is learned to write `set dnd false`. Choices the plan left open: `#` starts a comment only when it stands alone (a whole-line `# …` or ` # …` after a step), so `#bars` is a selector and `#ff8800` a colour; `expect` always runs, whatever `checks` lists; a `[services]` value may be a TOML string, number or bool, all read as text; `[allow]` entries need a non-empty `why`, and `expect_fail` a reason. Where a scenario lives decides what it may name: anything outside `eval/scenarios/local/` (curated, regressions, tests, matrix cells) may name only files inside `eval/` and the bundled fonts, and the parser refuses the rest with the file and line, so an owner's config or fonts cannot reach a gate by accident. The `id:` selectors rest on spec.md 6.3: `id: name` is valid on any element and names it across its component or surface (`Instance::identity` reports it).

**2026-10-17 · eval-sandbox: the driver runs a scenario in one process on a virtual clock, and what it needed beyond the plan.** `harness::run` compiles the scenario's `.strand` sections from an in-memory `SourceMap` (named as in the scenario, so diagnostics say `shell.strand:3 (scenario line 5)`), not from a temporary directory through the loader as the plan had it: nothing reaches the disk, and a `config` path or directory is read into the same map. It boots `Instance::from_build` on the schema mock with one screen (`Mock | DP-1`, the scenario's width, height and scale) and the `[services]` values set before the first `step`, and drives the renderer and the router as morph.rs's `Shell` does, at tick `k`'s time `T0 + k·period` (logic's wall clock `UNIX_EPOCH + MOCK_TIME + t`, the router pinned by `set_now`). Text waits are zeroed (`set_first_frame_wait`, `set_new_text_wait`, `set_estimate_wait`): what is late is the scenario's to say. Three changes from the plan, as the code required. The hold was all or nothing (`set_text_hold(bool)`), so `text late 3 where "iiii"` would have held every other text one frame too; strand-render's eval-hooks gain `set_text_hold_with(Option<HoldPick>)`, a filter on node and text that `set_text_hold(true)` is now the always-true case of, cfg'd like the rest and counted by `check-isolation.sh` (no product code changes). A `late N` rule releases a text N ticks after it was first held, which is N paints while its surface wants frames (a pending text keeps it wanting them) and stays defined when it paints none. A selector in `expect hidden #focus` names a node already gone, so selectors resolve against the live tree first and then against the nodes the run has seen (by id, origin or text; a kind path needs the tree), and an error says `matches no node mounted now or seen before` at the step's line. What shows at tick `k` is a timeline: a surface's rows stand until it paints again. A node shows when present, not `opacity0`/`scale0`, effective opacity at least 0.02, a visual area of at least one pixel and on its surface; an exiting ghost (`inert`) shows, so a node blinking out mid-exit is still seen, but bystander and envelope leave ghosts alone (they are leaving on purpose). `tol = max(edge_px, 1/scale)`. **bystander** and **envelope** are the plan's (a node shown at `s` and `e`; bystander on axes whose laid value is unchanged, opacity within 0.01 and scale within 0.005 when they end where they started; envelope on the other geometry axes with `ov = max(3 px, overshoot·|e−s|)`, 0.35 by default, leaving keyframes, lean, jelly and time-driven motion out). The bug-24 shape (y 9→21→9 with laid y unchanged) fails bystander on y; it fails envelope on x, where its glide carried the estimate's offset past its way left, since envelope only holds axes that move in layout (a y that does not is bystander's): both checks are what morph.rs's bug-24 test asserts by pixels. **teleport** compares consecutive shown frames; its retarget arm fails a glide whose drawn box moves with its layout's jump (|Δdrawn − Δlaid| ≤ tol on a layout jump over a pixel), the bug-24 class at a retarget, and a jump with no motion at either frame is an `info`, never a failure; it is skipped per segment under reduced motion and outright when the run reduces it. **vanish**: vanish (gone and back within 3 ticks, nothing exiting, entering or authoring opacity or scale at either side), flash (one frame between frames it does not show, keyframes and time aside), blank (damage and no item) as the plan has them; **pop-in** cannot be the plan's "within 0.05 of the pose on the first visible frame": a pose at opacity 0 is invisible by definition, and the driver's first frame of `enter { opacity: 0; x: -6 }` is already one frame into its springs (opacity 0.14, x −4.44 on focus-off, the time the frame is presented). It fails when the node's first frame does not report `ENTER` (the pose was not played) or its first shown frame is more than half its way from the pose to rest (opacity, or the spring's x/y share); a node at rest at once is the skipped pose this catches. **twin** re-runs with motion reduced from tick 0 and compares each settled segment's rest: the nodes shown (by key, keyframed and time-driven ones aside), their visual boxes within tol and opacity within 1/255; `twin_pixels` is parsed but compares nothing yet. **determinism** runs a curated scenario (or one asking) twice and compares digests, naming the first tick apart; **budget** holds per frame and surface the deterministic costs; **reference** fails a run matching (by digest, or every node's path within tol) a recording marked `bad` and makes a `good` one that changed CHANGED, a warning. `expect still|moves <sel> [axis]` looks from the segment's `s` (plus `from`) to the step, `visible|hidden` at the step. Findings of one node, axis, segment and kind fold into the first with a count. An `[allow]` entry exempts its nodes and their subtrees for its check and must name a node the run saw (else it fails, so a stale allow shows); an `intend` exempts its axes in its segment. `expect_fail` makes a failing check XFAIL and a passing one XPASS, which fails the gate ("now passes, remove expect_fail"). `regions` and `cpu-gpu` report skip until their legs land. `check_scenario` runs the scenario, its twin and the determinism re-run; a twin that cannot run is a twin failure, not a lost report.

**2026-10-17 · eval-sandbox: the GPU leg, `cpu-gpu` and `regions`, and where they differ from the plan.** *The GPU leg* (`eval/src/gpu.rs`) is the shell's warm start and present path with the compositor taken out: `Renderer::warm_gpu`, `strand_gpu::Gpu` spawned and its `Ready` delivered, then every surface promoted as it is configured, set to `GpuPresent` and attached without Wayland handles (readback); each paint is `Renderer::paint_gpu`, its frame sent and its `Pixels` copied into the surface's buffer before the tick goes on, so a run stays a function of its scenario. Three things the shell does are left out, on purpose, and said in the module: promotion's wall-clock rules (`set_promotion(false)`; a surface stays on the GPU for the run), `Presented` (never delivered, so the frame-time statistics are the CPU's) and `shader` passes (dropped and noted in the run's notes). It needs nothing of the product beyond the plan's footprint: every call is public API of strand-render with its `gpu` feature and of strand-gpu. *`backend both` is two runs, not one in lockstep.* The plan had one process drawing each tick twice; but a frame's paint changes the renderer's state (its damage history, `painted_time`, the flatten cache), so a second paint of the same tick is not the first one's twin, and two renderers in one harness double every input path. Two deterministic runs on the same virtual clock have the same ticks by construction, and `cpu-gpu` compares them tick by tick: the surfaces painted and wanting frames, every node by (surface, key) (boxes within 0.01 px, opacity within 1e-4, motions, hidden reasons and text states equal), the `Painter` regions, and the pixels, re-premultiplied from the PNGs, within crates/strand-render/tests/gpu.rs's tolerance (6 a channel, at most 2% past it). The plan's `cpu_gpu_allow` list is the existing `[allow]` with `checks = ["cpu-gpu"]`: one mechanism, and it masks the node's box out of the pixel comparison too. `backend cpu|gpu` as a step switches the shown surfaces from their next frame; `both` is the header's only (a step cannot mean two runs). `strand-eval run --backend cpu|gpu` runs one leg of any scenario, and the matrix has a `gpu` effect (`backend = "both"`) so every effect is crossed with the GPU leg. Without a device the check is skipped, saying so, unless `STRAND_REQUIRE_GPU=1` (the container and CI), which makes it a failure, as the GPU tests do. Both legs flatten the same scene in the same renderer, so the regions they report cannot differ: `cpu-gpu` is no detector for bug 23, which lived in the surface manager's present path, out of the sandbox's reach; docs/eval.md says so. *`regions` gates, opt-in, instead of shipping as info.* The plan said to ship it as info unless design.md stated its semantics. design.md does not, but docs/spec.md section 6.7 does (decisions.md m6-w2-surface): a `trigger: hover` popup that draws nothing itself takes input only in the boxes of its top-level elements that draw, as drawn this frame. That is a stated rule, so the check holds it when a scenario names it: every shown top-level element that draws content is inside the input region (or each of its children is, the `hit: none` case), and every rect of the region is a box drawn this frame. Each frame's regions are in the trace (`Frame.regions`, in the digest) for both checks and the viewer. `hover-island-regions.scn` holds a hover island whose card springs wide and back, and passes; the checks' tests hold a region lagging the card two frames, which fails.
